text: A few years ago, the idea of a creative computer sounded like science fiction. Today, computer programs can paint pictures, write stories and [[compose]] music in seconds. In 2018, a portrait made by a computer program was sold at an [[auction]] in New York for more than 400,000 dollars, much more than anyone expected.

These programs use artificial intelligence, or AI. They are trained on huge collections of pictures, songs and texts made by people. By studying all this material, the program learns which colours, notes and words usually go together. Then it can produce new work in a similar style when someone types a short instruction.

Many people find the results [[impressive]]. But artists have mixed feelings. Some enjoy using AI to try out ideas quickly. Others are angry, because their pictures were used to train the programs without [[permission]], and now the programs can copy their style for free. Several artists have taken AI companies to court.

The bigger question is whether a machine can really be creative. Many experts say that creativity needs [[intention]]: an artist wants to say something about life or about their feelings. A computer has no experiences and no feelings. It only finds patterns in what people have already made.

However, other experts point out that human artists also learn by studying the work of others. For them, AI is a new kind of tool, like the camera was 150 years ago. When cameras appeared, some painters thought art was finished. Instead, photography became an art of its own. Perhaps AI will [[inspire]] new kinds of art too, with people still making the important decisions.

text: Not long ago, creativity was seen as the one skill that machines would never master. That assumption now looks shaky. AI systems can produce a painting in the style of Van Gogh, a song that sounds like a chart hit or a short story with a twist ending, all within seconds of receiving a simple written instruction. In 2018, a blurry portrait generated by an algorithm sold at a New York auction for over 400,000 dollars, around forty times its estimated price.

Behind these results is a technique called machine learning. Instead of being given rules, the system is fed millions of examples – images, recordings, books – and gradually learns the statistical relationships between them: which brushstrokes tend to appear in landscapes, which chords tend to follow each other, which words are likely to come next. When it receives a request, it generates something new that fits those patterns. Crucially, it does not copy any single work, but it could not exist without them.

This is where the [[controversy]] begins. Much of the training material was collected from the internet without the [[consent]] of the people who made it. Illustrators have found that programs can now imitate their [[distinctive]] style, which took them years to develop, and offer it to anyone for free. Several groups of artists and writers have launched [[lawsuits|lawsuit]] against AI companies, arguing that their work has been used to build a product that now competes with them.

The philosophical debate is just as heated. Critics argue that AI cannot be truly creative because it has no intentions, no experiences and nothing to express. It recombines what already exists, they say, rather than imagining something new. Supporters reply that human creativity also depends on influence: every musician learns from earlier musicians, every writer from earlier books.

Many artists are taking a middle path. They use AI to [[generate]] rough ideas, then select, edit and develop the most promising ones by hand. Seen this way, the machine is a powerful [[collaborator]] rather than a replacement. Whether audiences will value such work as highly as purely human art remains an open question, but history offers a hint: photography, once dismissed as mere copying, is now hung in the world's greatest galleries.

text: For decades, creativity was held up as the final frontier of artificial intelligence: computers might beat us at chess or arithmetic, the argument went, but they would never write a moving poem. That [[confident]] claim now looks premature. Generative AI systems can produce a convincing pastiche of Van Gogh, a passable pop song or a short story with a neat twist, all from a single typed prompt. When a hazy portrait created by an algorithm fetched over 400,000 dollars at a New York auction in 2018 – roughly forty times its estimate – it became clear that the art world, at least, was taking machine-made images seriously.

The technology behind this is less mysterious than it appears. A generative model is trained on enormous quantities of human work and learns, in statistical terms, how the elements of that work tend to fit together. Given a prompt, it does not retrieve a stored picture but builds a new one that is consistent with everything it has absorbed. The output is original in the narrow sense that it did not exist before; whether it is original in any deeper sense is precisely what is in dispute.

The most immediate dispute is legal and economic. Much of the data used to train these systems was gathered from the internet without the knowledge, let alone the consent, of its creators. Illustrators and authors have discovered that a model can [[replicate]] their signature style in moments, and that clients who once [[commissioned|commission]] them now generate images themselves. Lawsuits are under way in several countries, and the outcome will shape not only who profits from AI but whether creative work remains a viable career.

Philosophers, meanwhile, have long distinguished between different kinds of creativity. The British researcher Margaret Boden, for instance, separated combining familiar ideas in new ways, exploring the possibilities within an established style, and transforming a style so radically that new things become possible. Current AI excels at the first two. Whether it can achieve the third – the leap that produced Cubism or jazz – is far less certain, since such leaps often involve deliberately breaking the very patterns a model is designed to reproduce.

Sceptics add that art is a form of communication: a painting matters partly because someone chose to make it and meant something by it. A system with no experiences has nothing to say, however [[plausible]] its output. Defenders counter that audiences often respond to work without knowing anything about its maker, and that human artists, too, are shaped by everything they have seen and heard. The boundary between influence and imitation, they argue, has never been sharp.

In practice, many professionals have settled on a [[pragmatic]] compromise, treating AI as a sketchbook rather than a substitute. A designer might generate dozens of rough variations, then discard most of them and refine the few that spark an idea. The final decisions – what to keep, what to change, what the work is ultimately for – remain human. If this pattern holds, AI may [[augment]] rather than replace creative labour, much as photography, once [[derided|deride]] as mechanical copying, eventually became an art form in its own right.

text: For most of the computer age, creativity was the trait we reserved for ourselves. Machines might calculate, sort and even defeat grandmasters at chess, but the capacity to make something genuinely new was regarded as quintessentially human – the last redoubt that automation could not breach. That conviction has [[eroded|erode]] with startling speed. Generative systems now turn out serviceable sonnets, plausible pop songs and paintings in the manner of almost any artist, prompted by nothing more than a sentence. The moment the art market took notice is easy to date: in 2018 a smudged, algorithmically generated portrait sold at a New York auction for more than 400,000 dollars, around forty times its pre-sale estimate.

Stripped of its mystique, the technology is a form of statistical modelling on a vast scale. A generative model is trained on immense corpora of human output and learns the probabilistic relationships among their elements – how shapes cluster in a landscape, how a melody tends to resolve, which phrase is likely to follow another. Asked for something, it synthesises an artefact consistent with those learned regularities. The result is novel in the trivial sense that it has never existed before; whether it is novel in any sense that matters is the crux of a debate that is as much philosophical as technical.

The most pressing quarrel, however, concerns livelihoods. The training data for many such systems was harvested from the open web with scant regard for the wishes of those who produced it. Illustrators have watched their [[idiosyncratic]] styles, honed over decades, become available on demand to anyone with a subscription, while former clients quietly stop commissioning them. A wave of [[litigation]] by artists, authors and publishers now seeks to establish whether such training constitutes fair use or wholesale appropriation. Regulators have begun to weigh in as well: the United States Copyright Office has indicated that images generated entirely by a machine, without meaningful human input, cannot be registered for copyright at all.

Underlying the legal wrangling is an older conceptual puzzle. The cognitive scientist Margaret Boden distinguished three modes of creativity: combinational, in which familiar ideas are joined in unfamiliar ways; exploratory, in which the possibilities of an established style are mapped; and transformational, in which the rules of a style are altered so fundamentally that previously unthinkable work becomes possible. By that measure, current systems are formidable combiners and tireless explorers. Transformation is another matter. The leaps that gave us Cubism or bebop were acts of deliberate transgression, and a model optimised to reproduce the regularities of its training data is, almost by design, inclined to conform rather than to rebel.

Some critics press the point further. Language models, in one memorable phrase, have been called “stochastic parrots”: systems that stitch together plausible sequences without any grasp of what they mean. On this view, art is irreducibly communicative – a painting or a poem matters because a particular person, with a particular history, chose to make it and meant something by it – and an entity without experience has nothing to communicate, however [[polished]] its output. Their opponents find this argument [[disingenuous|disingenuous]]. Audiences routinely respond to anonymous works, they note, and human artists are themselves composites of everything they have absorbed. The line between influence and imitation, on this account, has always been porous; AI merely makes the porousness impossible to ignore.

Away from the seminar room, practitioners have largely opted for [[accommodation|accommodate]]. Designers, musicians and writers increasingly use generative tools as a means of rapid ideation – producing dozens of rough variants, discarding the majority and developing the handful that provoke a genuine idea. Judgement about what is worth keeping, and about what the work is ultimately for, remains stubbornly human. It is also where much of the artistry now resides.

History suggests that such technologies tend to unsettle the arts before they enrich them. Photography was initially disparaged as mere mechanical transcription, and some painters predicted the death of their craft; instead it liberated painting from the duty of accurate representation and became an art form in its own right. Whether generative AI follows the same trajectory will depend less on what the machines can do than on the economic and legal settlement we reach about who is rewarded for the human labour on which they were built. Creativity, in other words, may survive the machines; the question is whether creative [[livelihoods|livelihood]] will.

text: In Japan, there are a lot of old people. More than one in four people are over 65. Many of them live in care homes. But there are not enough nurses and care workers to help them.

So some care homes now use robots. One robot looks like a baby seal. It is soft and white, and it moves its head and makes sounds when you touch it. Old people hold it and talk to it. It makes many of them feel calm and [[cheerful]].
Other robots help in different ways. Some lead exercise classes and sing songs. Some [[remind]] people to take their medicine. Big, strong robots can even [[lift]] people from their beds.
Many residents like the robots. “He's my friend,” one woman said about her robot seal. Care workers are happy too, because their job is very hard and the robots can [[save]] them time.
But not everyone agrees. Some people think robots cannot give real love and care. They are also [[expensive]]. Most experts say robots should help nurses, not take their place.

text: Japan is ageing faster than almost any other country. Nearly 30 per cent of its population is over 65, and the government has warned of a shortfall of hundreds of thousands of care workers within the next few years. The job is physically [[demanding]], emotionally draining and poorly paid, and many young people simply do not want it. Faced with this crisis, Japan has become a testing ground for a different kind of carer: the robot.

The best known is Paro, a furry robotic seal developed in the 1990s. Equipped with sensors under its soft coat, it reacts to being stroked or spoken to by blinking, turning its head and making sounds like a real seal pup. Paro was designed for people with dementia, and several studies have found that interacting with it can lower stress, calm [[agitation]] and reduce the use of some medicines. Because it is an animal rather than a human-like machine, people seem to accept it easily.

Other robots take on more physical or organised tasks. Humanoid robots run exercise sessions and quizzes, and sensors on mattresses can [[alert]] night staff when a resident gets up and is at risk of falling. Researchers have also developed lifting robots that can move a person from a bed to a wheelchair, a task that causes many of the back injuries suffered by care workers.

Yet the results have been more mixed than the headlines suggest. One study that followed Japanese care homes found that robots often created extra work: staff had to move them around, clean them, charge them and keep residents interested once the novelty wore off. In some homes, expensive machines ended up switched off in a cupboard. The robots that succeeded were those that fitted [[seamlessly]] into existing routines.

There are ethical questions, too. Critics fear that robots could become an excuse to [[cut]] staff rather than support them, leaving vulnerable people with less human company, not more. Others ask whether it is right to give someone with dementia a robot pet that they may believe is alive. Supporters respond that the comfort it provides is real, even if the animal is not. Most agree on one point: technology should free carers to spend more time listening, talking and holding hands – the parts of care that machines cannot [[imitate]].

text: Few countries illustrate the demographic pressures of the twenty-first century as vividly as Japan. Close to 30 per cent of its population is over 65, its birth rate has been falling for decades, and the government has projected a shortfall of several hundred thousand care workers in the coming years. Care work is gruelling, emotionally taxing and modestly paid; [[recruitment]] is difficult and [[turnover]] is high. Against this backdrop, successive governments have invested heavily in an idea that once belonged to science fiction: robots that help look after the elderly.

The most widely studied of these is Paro, a robotic harp seal developed in the 1990s by the engineer Takanori Shibata. Beneath its synthetic fur lie sensors that register touch, light and sound, and it responds with blinks, head movements and cries modelled on those of a real seal pup. Clinical trials have reported that interacting with Paro can reduce anxiety and agitation among people with dementia, and in some cases lower their reliance on sedatives. Its designers deliberately chose an animal unfamiliar to most users, so that people would not compare its behaviour with that of a real cat or dog and be [[disillusioned|disillusion]].

Alongside such companion robots are machines with more practical briefs. Humanoid robots lead residents through exercise routines and memory games; bed sensors notify night staff when someone is restless or at risk of falling; and prototype lifting robots can transfer a person from bed to wheelchair, a manoeuvre responsible for many of the back injuries that drive carers out of the profession.

Yet the evidence from real care homes is less [[upbeat]] than the promotional videos. Research by the anthropologist James Wright, who spent months observing a Japanese care facility, found that robots frequently generated work rather than saving it. Staff had to transport them, charge them, troubleshoot them and keep residents engaged once the initial excitement faded. Some devices were quietly withdrawn after a few months. The technologies that endured tended to be modest ones that slipped into existing routines rather than demanding new ones.

The ethical debate is equally [[nuanced]]. Critics worry that robots offer cash-strapped governments a convenient way to reduce spending on staff, leaving vulnerable people with less human contact rather than more. Others raise questions of dignity and honesty: is it acceptable to give a person with advanced dementia a robot animal they may believe to be alive? Proponents counter that the calm and pleasure people experience are genuine, and that withholding comfort on philosophical grounds would be its own kind of unkindness.

What emerges from this experience is not a story of machines replacing people, but of the limits of technological fixes for social problems. Robots can lift, remind, monitor and entertain. What they cannot do is [[substitute]] for the attention of another person – which is precisely what makes care work so valuable, and why many argue that the real solution lies in paying and training human carers better. Used well, robots may give those carers more time for that attention; used badly, they risk becoming an expensive [[distraction]].

text: If any society can be said to be living in the demographic future, it is Japan. Close to three in ten of its citizens are over 65, the fertility rate has languished well below replacement level for decades, and official projections point to a shortfall of several hundred thousand care workers before the decade is out. The work itself is gruelling, emotionally depleting and modestly remunerated; recruitment is a perennial struggle and attrition is high. Reluctant, for a mixture of political and cultural reasons, to rely heavily on immigration to fill the gap, successive governments have instead invested in an alternative with deep roots in Japanese popular culture: the caring robot.

The emblematic example is Paro, a robotic harp seal conceived in the 1990s by the engineer Takanori Shibata. Under its synthetic fur, an array of sensors registers touch, light, sound and posture, and the robot responds with blinks, head movements and plaintive cries sampled from a real seal pup. Its zoological identity was a calculated choice. Because few users have ever handled a seal, they lack the expectations that would make a robotic cat or dog seem [[uncanny]] or disappointing. Trials in care settings have reported reductions in anxiety and agitation among people with dementia and, in some studies, a reduced reliance on psychotropic medication – findings that, while based on modest samples, have been replicated often enough to be taken seriously.

Companion robots are only part of the picture. Humanoid machines conduct exercise sessions and recreational quizzes; pressure-sensitive mattresses and infrared monitors alert night staff when a resident becomes restless; and experimental lifting robots can transfer a person from bed to wheelchair – a manoeuvre implicated in many of the musculoskeletal injuries that drive carers from the profession. Policymakers have presented these technologies as a way of reconciling rising demand with a shrinking workforce.

The ethnographic record, however, tempers the enthusiasm. The anthropologist James Wright, who spent months embedded in a Japanese care facility, found that robots tended to [[displace|displace]] labour rather than reduce it. Staff had to ferry the machines between rooms, recharge and troubleshoot them, and coax residents into engaging with them once the initial fascination had [[waned|wane]]. Several devices were quietly retired within months. The technologies that persisted were those that demanded little and slotted unobtrusively into routines that already existed – a sobering lesson for designers who imagine that innovation alone will transform an institution.

The ethical terrain is [[fraught]] in a different way. Critics warn that robots furnish fiscally constrained governments with a respectable-sounding rationale for trimming staffing levels, so that the frailest members of society receive less human company precisely when they most need it. Others raise questions of dignity and deception: does presenting a person with advanced dementia with an artificial animal they take to be alive [[infantilise|infantilise]] them, or exploit their impairment? Defenders reply that the solace such encounters provide is no less real for its artificial source, and that refusing comfort on grounds of philosophical purity would be its own form of neglect. Between these positions lies an uncomfortable truth: whether a technology dignifies or diminishes depends less on the device than on the intentions of those who deploy it.

Some commentators also caution against reading the Japanese experience as purely technological. Japanese media and fiction have long cast robots as benign companions rather than menacing rivals, which may make residents and families more receptive to them than they would be elsewhere. Transplanting the same machines to societies with more suspicious attitudes might produce quite different results, which is one reason international comparisons of care robotics are so hard to interpret.

What the Japanese experiment ultimately reveals is less the promise of robotics than the limits of technological solutions to social problems. Machines can lift, prompt, monitor and amuse. What they cannot do is offer the [[attentiveness]] of another human being – which is, in the end, what distinguishes care from mere maintenance. If robots free carers to provide more of that attentiveness, they will have earned their place. If they are instead used to justify providing less, they will have [[compounded|compound]] the very crisis they were meant to relieve.

text: It is just a small heart or a thumbs-up, but the like button has changed the way millions of people feel about themselves. Facebook introduced it in 2009 as a quick way to show [[approval]]. Within a few years, almost every social network had copied the idea, and today people tap it billions of times a day.

Why is it so powerful? Part of the answer is in the brain. When something good happens, the brain releases a chemical called dopamine, which makes us feel [[satisfied]] and encourages us to repeat what we did. Likes arrive at unpredictable moments, and that [[uncertainty]] makes them even more exciting – a little like playing a game where you never know when you will win.

Some former employees of technology companies have admitted that apps were designed to keep people coming back. Notifications, red dots and endless scrolling all help to hold our [[attention]] for as long as possible, because more time on the app means more money from advertising.

Researchers are especially concerned about teenagers. At an age when people care a lot about what others think, likes can feel like a public score of [[popularity]]. Studies have linked heavy social media use with lower self-esteem and anxiety in some young people, particularly girls, although scientists still argue about how strong the effect really is.

In 2019, Instagram tried hiding the number of likes on posts in several countries. Later, it let users choose whether to see them. Some people felt more relaxed; others missed the numbers. Psychologists say the most useful step may be personal: noticing how we feel after scrolling, and remembering that a number on a screen does not [[measure]] a person's value.

text: Few inventions have been as small or as influential as the like button. When Facebook introduced it in 2009, it was intended as a simple shortcut: instead of writing “Great photo!”, users could show approval with a single click. Within a few years the idea had spread to almost every platform, and the humble thumbs-up became a kind of social currency, counted, compared and chased by billions of people.

Part of its power lies in the brain's reward system. Pleasant experiences trigger the release of dopamine, a chemical messenger linked to motivation, which encourages us to repeat whatever we were doing. Crucially, dopamine responds strongly to rewards that are uncertain. Because we never know whether a post will receive three likes or three hundred, checking becomes [[compulsive]], in much the same way that a gambler keeps pulling the lever of a slot machine.

This is not entirely accidental. Several former insiders in the technology industry have described how features such as infinite scrolling, push notifications and visible like counts were refined to maximise [[engagement]] – the time and attention users give to an app – because engagement is what advertisers pay for. One of the engineers who helped create the like button later said he regretted some of its effects and limited his own use of social media.

The greatest concern is for adolescents. During the teenage years, the brain is particularly sensitive to social [[feedback]], and a public tally of likes can turn ordinary life into a constant popularity contest. Large studies have found associations between heavy social media use and depression, anxiety and poor body image, especially among girls. However, researchers [[caution]] that correlation is not causation: it may be that unhappy teenagers spend more time online, rather than the other way round, and the average effects are smaller than headlines suggest.

Platforms have experimented with [[remedies]]. In 2019 Instagram began hiding like counts in several countries, later allowing users to switch them on or off. The results were [[ambiguous|ambiguous]]: some users said they felt freer to post, while many content creators, whose incomes depend on visible popularity, objected. For individuals, experts recommend simple habits – turning off notifications, keeping phones out of bedrooms and paying attention to how particular apps make them feel. A like, after all, measures a moment of attention, not a person's worth.

text: It is difficult to think of a smaller piece of design with larger consequences. When Facebook rolled out the like button in 2009, its purpose was modest: to let people signal approval without the effort of writing a comment. Within a few years it had been adopted, in one form or another, by virtually every social platform. The thumbs-up and the heart became a kind of social currency – instantly visible, endlessly countable and, for many users, quietly [[addictive]].

Neuroscience offers part of the explanation. Rewarding experiences prompt the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated less with pleasure itself than with anticipation and motivation. Dopamine responds most strongly to rewards that are [[intermittent]] and unpredictable – the principle behind slot machines. A post might attract a handful of likes or a flood of them, and the uncertainty is precisely what keeps users refreshing the page. Psychologists call this a variable reward schedule, and it is one of the most effective ways known of sustaining a behaviour.

That platforms exploit this is no longer seriously disputed. A number of former executives and engineers have spoken publicly about features – infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, visible metrics – that were optimised to maximise engagement, the currency in which advertisers ultimately pay. Justin Rosenstein, one of the engineers credited with the like button, later described himself as wary of its unintended consequences and installed controls to restrict his own use. Such admissions have fuelled calls for regulation of what critics term the attention economy.

The strongest anxieties concern adolescents. The teenage brain is acutely [[attuned|attune]] to social evaluation, and a public tally of approval can transform everyday life into a perpetual popularity contest. Large-scale surveys have linked heavy social media use to depression, anxiety, disturbed sleep and dissatisfaction with body image, particularly among girls. Yet the scientific picture is contested. Many of the studies are correlational, making it hard to establish the direction of cause and effect, and some researchers argue that the average associations are small – comparable, in one much-cited analysis, to the effect of eating potatoes. Others counter that averages can conceal serious harm to a vulnerable minority.

Platforms have responded with a mixture of genuine experiment and public relations. In 2019 Instagram began concealing like counts in several countries, eventually allowing users to choose whether to display them. The outcome was [[inconclusive]]. Some users reported feeling less pressure to [[curate]] a flawless image; content creators and businesses, whose livelihoods depend on visible popularity, protested; and the company concluded that the change made little overall difference to wellbeing.

Perhaps the most [[durable|durable]] lesson is that design choices are not neutral. The like button was not built to make anyone unhappy, but its effects emerged from the interaction between a simple feature and deep features of human psychology. Experts increasingly recommend modest, practical defences: switching off non-essential notifications, keeping devices out of bedrooms and paying deliberate attention to how specific apps affect one's mood. A like records a fleeting moment of someone else's attention. Treating it as a [[verdict]] on one's value is a mistake the technology makes very easy to commit.

text: Seldom has so slight a piece of design carried such weight. When Facebook introduced the like button in 2009, the aim was almost trivially modest: to spare users the labour of composing a comment when a single click would convey approval. Within a few years the gesture had been [[assimilated|assimilate]] by virtually every social platform. The thumbs-up and the heart hardened into a social currency – instantly legible, endlessly quantifiable and, for a sizeable share of users, quietly compulsive.

The neuroscience helps explain the grip. Rewarding experiences elicit the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter implicated less in pleasure per se than in anticipation, wanting and the drive to repeat. Its response is most pronounced when rewards arrive on an intermittent, unpredictable schedule – the very principle on which slot machines are engineered. Whether a post will draw a trickle of approval or a deluge is unknowable in advance, and that uncertainty is what keeps the thumb returning to the screen. The behavioural psychologist B. F. Skinner documented the potency of such variable reinforcement in laboratory animals decades before anyone had a smartphone.

That the industry has capitalised on this is no longer a matter of serious dispute. A procession of former executives and engineers has testified to the deliberate refinement of infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications and public metrics in pursuit of engagement – the commodity that advertisers ultimately purchase. Justin Rosenstein, one of the engineers credited with the like button, later spoke of its unforeseen consequences and took steps to [[curtail]] his own use. Such confessions have lent [[credence]] to critics of what has been termed the attention economy, in which human attention is the raw material and the product is advertising space.

Nowhere are the stakes higher than in adolescence. The teenage brain is exquisitely sensitive to social evaluation, and a public, quantified tally of approval can convert ordinary life into a ceaseless [[referendum]] on one's standing. Large epidemiological surveys have associated heavy use of social media with depression, anxiety, disrupted sleep and dissatisfaction with body image, with girls apparently more affected than boys. Some prominent commentators regard the evidence as sufficient to justify restrictions on smartphone use in schools and age limits for platforms.

Yet the science remains genuinely contested. Much of the evidence is correlational, so the direction of causation is [[elusive]]: distressed adolescents may gravitate towards screens rather than being made distressed by them. Some researchers have argued that the mean effect sizes are minuscule – in one widely cited analysis, roughly comparable to the association between wellbeing and regularly eating potatoes. Their opponents reply that such averages may mask severe harm concentrated in a vulnerable minority, and that waiting for definitive proof before acting is itself a choice with consequences. The disagreement is less about data than about how much certainty should be required before policy changes.

The platforms' own experiments have proved [[equivocal]]. In 2019 Instagram began hiding like counts in several markets and later made their display optional. Some users reported feeling liberated from the pressure to curate a flawless persona; influencers and businesses, whose incomes depend on conspicuous popularity, protested; and the company ultimately reported that the change had little measurable effect on wellbeing overall. Sceptics noted that the most consequential features – the algorithmic feed and the endless scroll – were left untouched.

If there is a durable lesson, it is that design is never neutral. Nobody set out to make the like button a source of misery; its effects emerged from the collision between a frictionless feature and ancient features of human sociality – our appetite for status and our sensitivity to rejection. The remedies currently recommended are correspondingly modest: disabling non-essential notifications, banishing devices from bedrooms, and cultivating a deliberate awareness of how particular apps alter one's mood. A like is a [[transient]] trace of another person's attention. To mistake it for a verdict on one's worth is an error the technology does everything to make effortless.

text: Lena, a nineteen-year-old student, used to check her phone more than a hundred times a day. She looked at it on the bus, during lectures and even while talking to friends. So when her psychology teacher suggested an [[experiment]] – one week without a smartphone – she was curious but also slightly afraid.

The first two days were difficult. Lena kept reaching for her pocket, and twice she was sure she felt the phone vibrate, although it was at home in a drawer. Psychologists call this “phantom vibration”, and it is surprisingly common. She also realised how much she [[depended]] on her phone for simple things: the time, the weather, directions and her bank card.

Gradually, she began to [[adapt]]. She wore a watch, wrote her plans in a notebook and asked strangers for directions. Without social media, she had a lot of free time, so she started reading novels again. At night, she fell asleep faster, probably because she was not looking at a bright screen before bed.

The biggest [[surprise]] was her concentration. In class she noticed that she was [[actually]] listening instead of half-listening. Interestingly, a study at a university in Texas found that students did worse on tests when their phones were simply on the desk, even switched off, compared with when the phones were in another room. Just having the phone nearby used up some of their attention.

When the week ended, Lena did not throw her phone away. Instead, she made some new rules: no phone during meals, notifications turned off, and the phone charging outside the bedroom. “The phone isn't the problem,” she says. “The problem is using it without thinking. Now I try to use it on purpose, not out of [[habit]].”

text: Before the experiment, Lena estimated that she used her phone for about two hours a day. When she checked the screen-time report, the real figure was almost six. Like many people her age, she reached for it [[reflexively]]: in queues, between lectures, even mid-conversation. So when her psychology lecturer challenged the class to spend a week without smartphones, she agreed partly out of curiosity and partly to prove that she could.

The first forty-eight hours were uncomfortable. She caught herself patting her pocket dozens of times and twice felt a buzz from a phone that was locked in a drawer at home – a [[phenomenon]] known as phantom vibration syndrome, which surveys suggest most heavy users have experienced. More surprising was how many ordinary tasks had quietly moved onto the device: paying for coffee, checking bus times, finding a friend's address, even knowing what day it was.

By midweek, however, she had developed [[workarounds]]. A cheap watch, a paper diary and some cash replaced most of the phone's functions, and she rediscovered the art of asking strangers for help. Without the constant pull of social media, her evenings stretched out. She read two novels, cooked with her flatmates and noticed that she was falling asleep earlier, a change consistent with research on the effect of bright screens on the body's sleep hormone, melatonin.

The most striking change, though, was in her ability to focus. Researchers at the University of Texas found that students performed worse on memory and reasoning tests when their phones were on the desk – even face down and switched off – than when the phones were in another room. They called this a “brain drain”: part of the mind is busy resisting the urge to check the phone, leaving less capacity for the task in hand. Lena found she could read for an hour without [[interruption]], something she had not done since school.

Not everything was positive. She missed a change of room for a seminar because the message was sent by app, and she felt [[isolated]] when friends made plans in a group chat. Being offline in a world built around phones, she realised, has real social costs.

Her conclusion was not that smartphones are bad, but that the [[default]] settings are designed for maximum use, not for the user's benefit. She now keeps notifications off, leaves her phone outside the bedroom and puts it in a bag during lectures. “I still use it every day,” she says, “but now I decide when. It doesn't decide for me.”

text: Lena had always assumed her phone use was moderate – perhaps two hours a day. The screen-time report on her device disagreed: the daily average was closer to six, spread across more than a hundred separate pickups. Like most of her peers, she reached for the phone [[instinctively]] whenever there was a moment to fill – in queues, between lectures, during lulls in conversation. So when her psychology lecturer proposed that the class spend a week entirely without smartphones and keep a diary of the experience, Lena signed up, half intrigued and half determined to prove she was not dependent.

The first two days were more unsettling than she had expected. She lost count of the times she patted an empty pocket, and on two occasions she distinctly felt a buzz from a phone that was locked in a drawer across town. Researchers have documented this “phantom vibration” in a majority of heavy users, and some interpret it as a sign that the brain has become [[primed|prime]] to detect any signal that might be a notification. Just as revealing was the discovery of how many mundane functions she had [[delegated|delegate]] to a single device: payment, timetables, maps, the alarm that woke her, even her sense of what day of the week it was.

By the fourth day, she had assembled a set of analogue substitutes – a cheap wristwatch, a paper diary, a printed map and, somewhat to her embarrassment, cash. Freed from the steady drip of social media, her evenings expanded. She finished two novels, cooked with her flatmates and began falling asleep noticeably earlier. That last change is [[consistent]] with research suggesting that bright screens in the evening delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that signals to the body that it is time to sleep.

The change she had least anticipated concerned attention. A widely discussed study from the University of Texas asked students to complete demanding cognitive tasks with their phones either on the desk, in a bag or in another room. Those whose phones were within sight performed significantly worse, even when the devices were face down and silent. The researchers proposed that resisting the [[pull|pull]] of a nearby phone consumes mental resources, leaving fewer available for the task in hand – a phenomenon they labelled “brain drain”. Lena, who had not read a book in one sitting since school, found herself reading uninterrupted for over an hour.

The experiment was not without its costs, however. Because her university communicated mainly through an app, she missed a room change and arrived at an empty seminar. More painfully, she was absent from plans made in group chats and felt [[excluded|exclude]] from the social life of her course. Opting out of the smartphone, she concluded, is far easier for someone whose friends and institutions do not assume constant connectivity – which, nowadays, is almost nobody.

Her final diary entry was not a rejection of technology but a critique of its design. Many of the features that had kept her hooked – infinite feeds, red badges, sounds that interrupt – are default settings chosen to maximise use, and they can be changed. She now disables all but essential notifications, leaves her phone to charge outside her bedroom and keeps it out of sight during lectures. “I haven't given anything up,” she wrote. “I've just moved from using it [[compulsively|compulsive]] to using it deliberately. The phone works for me again, not the other way round.”

text: Lena had always considered her phone habits unremarkable – two hours a day, she would have guessed, perhaps a little more. The screen-time report on her device was less charitable: an average of nearly six hours, fragmented across more than a hundred separate pickups. Like most of her generation, she reached for the phone [[reflexively]] whenever life offered a moment of empty time – in queues, between lectures, in the small silences of conversation. When her psychology lecturer invited the class to spend a week without smartphones and to keep a reflective diary of the experience, Lena volunteered with a mixture of curiosity and bravado, keen to demonstrate that she was in control.

The opening days proved humbling. She lost count of the occasions on which her hand strayed to an empty pocket, and twice she felt, with complete conviction, the buzz of a phone that was in fact locked in a drawer on the other side of the city. Such phantom vibrations have been reported by a clear majority of heavy users in several surveys, and some researchers read them as evidence that the perceptual system has been recalibrated to treat any ambiguous sensation as a potential notification – a kind of hypervigilance trained into us by the device itself. Equally sobering was the realisation of how much of her daily life had been quietly [[subsumed|subsume]] into a single object: her wallet, her map, her alarm clock, her diary, her music and, it seemed, much of her sense of time.

By midweek, she had improvised a set of analogue substitutes – a wristwatch, a paper notebook, a printed street map and, to her faint embarrassment, coins and notes. Liberated from the drip-feed of social media, her evenings acquired an unfamiliar spaciousness. She read two novels, cooked elaborate meals with her flatmates and found herself falling asleep markedly earlier, an effect consistent with laboratory evidence that exposure to bright screens in the evening suppresses melatonin and pushes back the body's internal clock.

The most [[profound]] change, however, concerned her attention. Researchers at the University of Texas had students complete demanding tests of working memory and fluid intelligence with their phones placed on the desk, in a bag or in another room. Performance declined with proximity: those whose phones were merely visible, even face down and silenced, scored measurably worse. The authors hypothesised that the effort of not attending to a salient object drains the limited pool of cognitive resources available for the task in hand – a cost they memorably named “brain drain”. Subsequent attempts to replicate the finding have produced mixed results, a reminder that striking studies are not always robust. Yet Lena's own experience was unambiguous: for the first time since school, she read for over an hour without once breaking off.

The week also exposed the limits of individual [[abstinence]]. Her university disseminated announcements chiefly through an app, so she missed a change of venue and sat alone in an empty seminar room. More [[corrosive|corrosive]] was her exclusion from the arrangements that coalesced in group chats; she discovered several gatherings only after they had taken place. Opting out, she reflected, is a luxury afforded only to those whose social and institutional worlds do not presuppose constant connectivity – that is, to almost nobody. Framing excessive phone use as a failure of personal willpower, she wrote, conveniently ignores how thoroughly society has been rebuilt around the assumption that everyone is reachable at every moment.

That insight shaped her conclusion. The problem, she decided, lay less in the device than in its defaults. The infinite feed, the red badge that [[nags|nag]], the alert that interrupts – these are design decisions optimised for time-on-device, a metric that serves the platform rather than the person holding it. Crucially, most of them can be overridden. She now silences all but essential notifications, banishes her phone from the bedroom at night and keeps it out of sight during lectures.

“I haven't renounced anything,” her final entry reads. “I've simply moved from compulsion to intention. The phone is a tool again rather than a [[tether]].” It is a modest resolution, but perhaps a more realistic one than the dramatic digital detoxes regularly promoted in the media – and, crucially, one she has managed to sustain.

text: Walk into a modern supermarket and you can scan and pay for your shopping without speaking to anyone. In huge online warehouses, robots move shelves to workers, and software now answers customer questions, writes simple reports and checks documents. It is not surprising that many people ask: will there be any work left for humans?

The worry is not new. In the early nineteenth century, textile workers in England smashed the new machines that were taking their jobs. In 2013, two researchers at Oxford University [[predicted]] that about 47 per cent of jobs in the United States were at high [[risk]] of [[automation]] within twenty years. The number made headlines around the world.

However, many economists think the picture is more complicated. Machines usually take over particular [[tasks]], not whole jobs. A later study by the OECD, an international organisation, looked at the tasks inside each job and estimated that around 14 per cent of jobs in rich countries were at high risk – still a lot, but far fewer than half.

History also shows that technology creates new work. When cash machines appeared in American banks, the number of bank tellers did not fall for many years. Because each branch became cheaper to run, banks opened more of them, and tellers spent more time selling services and helping customers. Jobs such as app developer or social media manager did not exist at all thirty years ago.

Still, the changes can be painful for people whose skills are no longer needed, especially older workers. Experts agree that the most [[valuable]] skills are the ones machines find difficult: communication, creativity, caring for others and solving unexpected problems. Governments and companies, they say, must help people [[retrain]] throughout their working lives.

text: Self-service tills in supermarkets, robots that glide around warehouses carrying entire shelves, chatbots that handle customer complaints, software that drafts contracts: automation has moved from the factory floor into almost every corner of the economy. Unsurprisingly, it has [[revived|revive]] an old fear – that machines will eventually leave most people without work.

The anxiety has a long history. In the 1810s, English textile workers known as Luddites broke into factories and destroyed the mechanical looms they blamed for their poverty. Two centuries later, a 2013 study by the Oxford researchers Carl Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 per cent of American jobs were at high risk of being automated within a decade or two. The figure was quoted so often that it came to [[symbolise|symbolise]] the coming robot age.

Yet the [[prediction]] rested on a particular method: it judged whole [[occupations|occupation]] at once. Later research by the OECD broke jobs down into their individual tasks and found that most occupations contain a mix of routine activities, which are easy to automate, and others – negotiating, persuading, caring – which are not. On that basis it estimated that about 14 per cent of jobs in rich countries were highly automatable, while a further third were likely to change significantly. The lesson is that automation tends to reshape jobs rather than simply delete them.

Economic history supports this more measured view. The economist James Bessen has shown that after cash machines spread across American banks, the number of human tellers actually rose for several decades. Because ATMs made each branch cheaper to operate, banks opened more branches, and tellers shifted from counting notes to selling financial products and building relationships with customers. Technology also creates entirely new occupations: a large share of today's jobs have titles that did not exist in the 1940s.

None of this means the [[transition]] is painless. The benefits of automation often go to companies and highly skilled workers, while those whose routine skills are replaced may end up in lower-paid work. Older workers in particular can find it hard to start again, and whole regions can suffer when a major employer automates.

What, then, should individuals and governments do? Most experts emphasise the skills that machines still [[struggle|struggle]] with: complex communication, creative problem-solving, empathy and physical dexterity in unpredictable environments. Some also argue for stronger safety nets and affordable adult education, so that retraining is a realistic option rather than a slogan. The question, in short, is not whether there will be work, but whether people will be prepared and supported to do it.

text: Automation has escaped the factory. Self-checkout machines now line supermarket aisles, fleets of robots shuttle shelving units around vast fulfilment centres, chatbots field customer complaints, and software can draft legal contracts or summarise medical notes. With each advance, a familiar question resurfaces with fresh urgency: if machines can do so much, what will be left for us?

The fear is as old as industrialisation itself. In the 1810s, English textile workers who came to be known as Luddites smashed the mechanical looms they held responsible for their [[destitution|destitute]]. Two centuries on, a 2013 paper by the Oxford economists Carl Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 per cent of US employment was at high risk of computerisation within a decade or two. The statistic travelled far beyond academia and became a kind of shorthand for the coming disruption – often quoted without the [[caveats|caveat]] its authors attached.

Subsequent research has tempered the alarm. Frey and Osborne assessed occupations as indivisible wholes, but most jobs are bundles of tasks with very different [[susceptibility]] to automation. When the OECD analysed the tasks people actually perform, it concluded that roughly 14 per cent of jobs across its member countries were highly automatable, while around a third faced substantial change. The emerging [[consensus]] among economists is that technology tends to [[erode|erode]] the routine components of work while leaving – and sometimes increasing the value of – the non-routine ones.

The historical record bears this out, sometimes counter-intuitively. As the economist James Bessen has documented, the spread of ATMs in the United States was accompanied not by the disappearance of bank tellers but by a modest increase in their numbers for several decades. Automation lowered the cost of running a branch, banks responded by opening more branches, and tellers' work shifted from handling cash towards relationship banking and sales. More broadly, a large proportion of today's jobs fall under titles that would have been unrecognisable in 1940.

This is not to suggest that the process is benign. The gains from automation have often accrued to capital owners and to highly educated workers whose skills complement new technology, while middle-skill jobs – clerical work, routine manufacturing – have been [[hollowed|hollow]] out. Displaced workers frequently find new employment only at lower wages, and the costs are geographically concentrated: towns built around a single plant can be devastated when it automates or closes. Some economists argue that recent advances in AI, which can perform cognitive tasks once thought safe, may make this round of change faster and broader than previous ones.

Policy responses fall broadly into two camps. One emphasises skills: investing in the abilities machines still find elusive – nuanced communication, creative problem-solving, care and dexterity in messy physical environments – and making adult retraining accessible rather than [[aspirational]]. The other focuses on distribution, from stronger unemployment insurance to proposals for a universal basic income. Most realistic strategies combine elements of both. The central challenge, it increasingly seems, is less a shortage of work than a shortage of mechanisms for helping people move into the work that technology creates.

text: Automation no longer stops at the factory gates. Self-checkout terminals have displaced rows of cashiers, squat orange robots ferry entire shelving units across the floors of cavernous fulfilment centres, conversational software triages customer complaints, and language models draft contracts, summarise case notes and write serviceable code. Each new capability revives a question that has haunted industrial societies for two centuries: if machines can do so much, what will remain for people to do – and how will they live?

The anxiety is venerable. In the 1810s, the textile workers of the English Midlands who rallied under the mythical “General Ludd” smashed the mechanised frames they blamed for their [[impoverishment]]. Their name has since become a byword for irrational technophobia, though historians point out that their grievances concerned wages and working conditions as much as machinery. Two hundred years later, a 2013 paper by the Oxford economists Carl Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 per cent of US employment was at high risk of computerisation within a decade or two. The figure acquired a life of its own, cited as prophecy in countless articles, usually shorn of the authors' careful qualifications.

Subsequent scholarship has been more [[circumspect]]. Frey and Osborne evaluated occupations as monolithic units, whereas most jobs are heterogeneous bundles of tasks that differ markedly in their susceptibility to automation. When OECD researchers examined the task content of actual jobs, they put the share of highly automatable employment across member countries at roughly 14 per cent, with perhaps a third of jobs facing substantial transformation. The weight of economic opinion now holds that technology tends to [[supplant]] the routine, codifiable elements of work while leaving intact – and often enhancing the value of – those requiring judgement, social intelligence or improvisation.

History furnishes some instructive paradoxes. As the economist James Bessen has shown, the proliferation of ATMs in the United States coincided not with the extinction of the bank teller but with a modest rise in tellers' numbers over several decades: cheaper branches meant more branches, and tellers were redeployed from counting cash to cultivating customer relationships. A related insight, known as Moravec's paradox, holds that what humans find hard – advanced mathematics, chess – is often easy for computers, while what we find effortless, such as folding laundry or navigating a cluttered room, remains stubbornly difficult for machines. It is no accident that care workers and plumbers have proved harder to automate than many accountants.

None of this licenses [[complacency]]. Over recent decades the dividends of automation have accrued disproportionately to the owners of capital and to highly educated workers whose expertise complements new technology, while middle-skill occupations – clerical, administrative, routine manufacturing – have been hollowed out, a process economists call job [[polarisation]]. Displaced workers frequently re-enter the labour market at lower wages, if at all, and the damage is geographically concentrated, leaving communities built around a single employer to absorb the shock. There are also grounds for suspecting that generative AI, by encroaching on cognitive and creative tasks previously considered immune, could make the current transition faster and more [[pervasive]] than its predecessors.

Proposed remedies cluster around two poles. The first is human capital: cultivating the capacities machines still find elusive – nuanced communication, creative problem-solving, care and physical dexterity in unstructured settings – and making lifelong retraining a genuine entitlement rather than a pious aspiration. The second is distribution: strengthening unemployment insurance, rethinking the taxation of capital relative to labour, or, more radically, introducing a universal basic income. Pilot schemes of the latter have produced encouraging evidence on wellbeing, though rather less on the question of how such a scheme could be financed at national scale.

Most serious proposals combine both approaches, and with good reason. The historical record suggests that technology seldom produces a permanent shortage of work; what it reliably produces is a period of [[dislocation]] whose length and severity depend on institutions. The real question, then, is not whether machines will leave anything for us to do, but whether our societies will build the bridges that allow people to cross from the jobs that are disappearing to those that have yet to be invented.

text: When we feel [[upset]], many of us try to [[ignore]] our feelings or hide them. We tell ourselves to “just get on with it”. But a growing amount of research suggests that putting our emotions into words is one of the simplest ways to feel better.

In a well-known study at the University of California, people were shown photos of faces with strong emotions, such as anger or fear. When they simply chose a word to describe the emotion, activity in the amygdala – the part of the brain that reacts to [[threats|threat]] – went down. Naming the feeling seemed to [[calm]] the brain's alarm system. The psychiatrist Dan Siegel describes this idea with a short phrase: “Name it to tame it.”

Writing has a similar effect. In the 1980s, the American psychologist James Pennebaker asked students to write about the most difficult experiences of their lives for fifteen minutes a day, on four days in a row. Compared with students who wrote about ordinary topics, they made fewer visits to the health centre in the following months. Many said that writing helped them understand what had happened.

Of course, talking to someone we [[trust]] has extra benefits. A good listener can make us feel less alone and help us see a problem from a new angle. Yet many people, especially young men, find it hard to ask for help because they worry about looking weak.

Experts say that if sadness or anxiety lasts for weeks and makes everyday life difficult, it is important to speak to a doctor or a trained counsellor. Mental health is part of our general health, and asking for support is a sensible step, not a [[failure]]. Sometimes the bravest thing a person can say is simply: “I'm not OK.”

text: “Keep calm and carry on” may make a good poster, but as a strategy for dealing with painful emotions it has serious limits. Psychologists have long observed that people who habitually [[suppress]] their feelings tend to report more stress, not less. A growing body of research points to a simpler and more effective alternative: putting emotions into words.

One of the best-known demonstrations comes from the University of California, Los Angeles. In a 2007 brain-imaging study led by Matthew Lieberman, volunteers looked at photographs of angry or frightened faces. When they chose a word to describe the emotion, rather than a name to describe the person, activity in the amygdala – a region involved in detecting threat – dropped noticeably, while areas associated with self-control became more active. Lieberman called this process “affect labelling”. Remarkably, most participants did not believe that labelling would help, yet their brains suggested otherwise.

Writing appears to work in a similar way. Beginning in the 1980s, the psychologist James Pennebaker asked students to spend fifteen to twenty minutes on four consecutive days writing about their deepest thoughts and feelings concerning a [[traumatic]] or upsetting experience. Compared with a control group who wrote about everyday matters, they later made fewer visits to the doctor. The effect has since been [[replicated|replicate]] in many studies, although its size varies, and researchers think it works partly because writing forces people to turn a chaotic experience into a coherent story.

Talking to another person adds something that neither labelling nor writing can provide: connection. A supportive listener can [[validate]] our feelings, offer a different perspective and remind us that we are not alone. Unfortunately, [[stigma]] still prevents many people from seeking help. Men in particular are less likely than women to talk about their emotional difficulties or to see a professional, and in many countries they account for the majority of suicides.

None of this means that every bad mood requires therapy. Ordinary sadness and worry are part of life. But when low mood or anxiety persists for several weeks and begins to [[interfere]] with sleep, work or relationships, health professionals advise speaking to a doctor or counsellor. As campaigners often point out, nobody hesitates to see a doctor about a broken leg; problems of the mind deserve the same attention.

text: The instinct to keep a stiff upper lip runs deep in many cultures. Faced with grief, fear or humiliation, we are often encouraged to push the feeling down and get on with things. Yet decades of psychological research suggest that habitual suppression is a poor strategy: people who routinely conceal their emotions tend to experience more physiological stress, poorer memory for social situations and, over time, weaker relationships. One of the most [[robust]] alternatives turns out to be disarmingly simple – describing what we feel.

Some of the clearest evidence comes from neuroscience. In 2007 a team at the University of California, Los Angeles, led by Matthew Lieberman, scanned the brains of volunteers as they viewed images of emotionally charged faces. When participants selected a word that captured the emotion – “angry”, say, or “scared” – activity in the amygdala, which helps to register threat, fell markedly, while regions of the prefrontal cortex linked to [[regulating|regulate]] emotion became more engaged. Lieberman termed this “affect labelling”. Strikingly, people consistently underestimate its value: asked in advance, most predict that naming a feeling will make it worse.

A parallel line of research concerns expressive writing. In experiments that began in the 1980s, the psychologist James Pennebaker asked participants to write for fifteen to twenty minutes on several consecutive days about their deepest thoughts and feelings regarding a traumatic or distressing event. Relative to control groups writing about [[innocuous]] topics, they subsequently made fewer visits to health services and reported improved mood. Hundreds of studies later, the benefits appear real but modest and uneven. Analyses of the essays themselves suggest a mechanism: those who improved most tended to move, across the sessions, towards using more causal and insight words – “because”, “realise”, “understand” – as if gradually constructing a narrative that made sense of what had happened.

More recent work by the psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett adds a further [[refinement|refine]]. People differ in what she calls emotional [[granularity]]: the precision with which they distinguish between related feelings. Someone who can tell apart disappointment, resentment and embarrassment, rather than lumping them together as “feeling bad”, appears better equipped to respond to each appropriately, and studies have linked higher granularity to less reliance on alcohol and aggression as coping strategies.

Words spoken to another person bring an additional ingredient: social support. A trusted listener can [[normalise|normalise]] an experience, challenge distorted thinking and provide practical help. Yet seeking such support remains heavily stigmatised in many communities, particularly among men, who are less likely to disclose emotional difficulties or consult professionals and who, in many countries, account for around three-quarters of suicides.

None of this implies that every setback warrants clinical attention; sadness and worry are normal responses to a difficult world. But when low mood or anxiety persists for weeks and begins to [[impair|impair]] sleep, work or relationships, clinicians recommend seeking professional help. The underlying lesson of this research is that emotions are not simply events that happen to us. The act of naming them is itself a form of regulation – one available to anyone, at any time, at no cost.

text: Few cultural reflexes are as deeply entrenched as the injunction to keep a stiff upper lip. Confronted with grief, dread or shame, people are routinely urged to bottle the feeling up and soldier on, as though emotional restraint were a moral virtue rather than a coping strategy with measurable costs. The research is not kind to this tradition. Studies of habitual suppression – the effortful concealment of an emotion once it has arisen – find that it tends to heighten physiological arousal, [[degrade|degrade]] memory for the social interactions in which it occurs and, over time, erode the intimacy of close relationships. Concealment, it seems, does not make the feeling go away; it merely adds the labour of hiding it.

Among the more robust alternatives is one so modest it is easily overlooked: naming the feeling. In a frequently cited 2007 study at the University of California, Los Angeles, Matthew Lieberman and colleagues used functional MRI to monitor volunteers viewing emotionally evocative faces. When participants matched each face to a word describing the emotion it displayed, rather than to a name or gender, activity in the amygdala – a structure central to the rapid appraisal of threat – diminished, while regions of the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex associated with inhibitory control became more active. Lieberman christened the phenomenon “affect labelling”. Tellingly, it operates largely beneath awareness: when asked beforehand, most people predict that dwelling on a feeling by naming it will intensify rather than [[assuage]] it.

Expressive writing offers a parallel, and older, body of evidence. In a series of experiments beginning in the 1980s, the social psychologist James Pennebaker invited participants to write, for fifteen to twenty minutes on consecutive days, about their deepest thoughts and feelings concerning a traumatic or profoundly upsetting experience. Compared with controls who described their shoes or their plans for the day, they went on to make fewer visits to health services and reported improvements in mood. Several hundred replications later, the picture is one of benefits that are genuine but modest and [[inconsistent]] across populations – a useful corrective to the more breathless claims sometimes made on the technique's behalf.

Pennebaker's linguistic analyses of the essays themselves hint at why it works. Participants who benefited most were not those who expressed the most negative emotion, but those whose language changed over the sessions, showing a rising frequency of causal and cognitive words – “because”, “reason”, “realise”, “understand”. The implication is that the benefit lies less in catharsis than in construction: in the gradual assembly of a coherent narrative that renders a chaotic experience [[intelligible]] and therefore bearable.

The psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett has pushed the argument further with the concept of emotional granularity – the precision with which individuals differentiate among related affective states. A person who can distinguish wistfulness from regret, or indignation from humiliation, possesses, in effect, a finer instrument for interpreting their own experience. Higher granularity has been associated with greater flexibility in regulating emotion and with a lower [[propensity]] to resort to binge drinking or aggression under stress. On this view, expanding one's emotional vocabulary is not a literary [[affectation]] but a practical skill.

Speech addressed to another person introduces a further ingredient that neither labelling nor writing can supply: the presence of a responsive other. A trusted listener can normalise distress, gently contest catastrophic interpretations and mobilise practical help. Yet the stigma surrounding emotional disclosure remains formidable, particularly among men, who in many countries are markedly less likely to seek psychological help and who account for roughly three in four suicides. Public campaigns have increasingly targeted precisely this reluctance, framing disclosure as an act of courage rather than of weakness.

None of this licenses the medicalisation of ordinary unhappiness; sorrow and anxiety are appropriate responses to a world that frequently warrants them. But where low mood or anxiety persists for weeks and begins to [[compromise]] sleep, work or relationships, clinicians are unanimous that professional help should be sought. The broader lesson of this literature is a quietly radical one: emotions are not simply weather systems that pass over us. The act of articulating them is itself a means of shaping them – a resource that costs nothing, requires no equipment and is available to almost everyone.

text: “Eat breakfast like a king, lunch like a prince and dinner like a beggar.” Most of us grew up believing that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. It seems like common sense. But scientists are now asking whether this old idea is really based on [[evidence]].

The famous slogan has a surprising history. It became popular in the early twentieth century, partly through magazines and advertisements connected to companies that made breakfast cereals. These companies had a clear interest in [[persuading|persuade]] people that a morning meal was essential.

For a long time, studies seemed to support the idea. People who regularly ate breakfast were, on average, slimmer than people who [[skipped|skip]] it. However, these studies only showed a link, not a cause. Breakfast eaters might also exercise more or sleep better. When researchers did [[experiments|experiment]] – asking one group to eat breakfast and another to skip it – the results were different. In a large review of such studies in 2019, breakfast eaters did not lose more weight. In fact, they ate around 260 more calories a day.

This does not mean breakfast is bad. What we eat matters more than the time we eat it. Sugary cereals and white bread raise blood sugar quickly, but the energy soon disappears. Foods with protein and fibre, such as eggs, yoghurt, oats and fruit, keep us [[full]] for longer.

Children may be a special case. Many schools now offer free breakfasts, and teachers report that pupils concentrate better, behave better and miss fewer days. For adults, nutrition experts give a [[flexible]] answer: if you are hungry in the morning, enjoy a healthy breakfast; if you are not, it is fine to wait until later.

text: Few pieces of nutritional advice are repeated as confidently as the claim that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Parents tell it to children, doctors have repeated it to patients, and it appears on countless cereal boxes. Yet when researchers look closely at the evidence, the picture becomes considerably more [[complicated]].

The phrase itself has commercial roots. It was popularised in the early twentieth century, in part through health magazines and advertising associated with the American cereal industry, which had an obvious interest in making the morning meal seem [[indispensable]]. That does not make the claim false, but it is a reminder to ask who benefits from a piece of “common knowledge”.

For decades, the scientific case seemed strong. Large observational studies found that people who ate breakfast regularly tended to weigh less and have lower rates of heart disease than those who skipped it. The problem is that such studies reveal [[correlations|correlation]], not causes. Breakfast eaters may also be more likely to exercise, smoke less and keep regular hours – any of which could explain the difference.

To separate cause from coincidence, scientists turned to randomised controlled trials, in which volunteers are assigned at random to eat breakfast or to skip it. The results have been [[sobering]] for breakfast enthusiasts. A 2019 review in the British Medical Journal, combining thirteen trials, found that breakfast eaters did not lose more weight; on average they consumed about 260 extra calories a day. A trial at the University of Bath likewise found that breakfast did not speed up [[metabolism]], though it was linked to more physical activity in the morning.

If the timing of the meal matters less than once thought, its content matters a great deal. A breakfast of sugary cereal or white toast produces a sharp rise and fall in blood sugar that can leave people hungry again within hours. Meals containing protein and fibre – eggs, Greek yoghurt, porridge, nuts, fruit – are digested more slowly and tend to keep hunger at bay until lunch.

Children and teenagers may be an exception. Their brains are developing and many go to school hungry, especially in poorer families. Several evaluations of school breakfast programmes have reported improvements in attendance and behaviour, and some in concentration. For adults, however, the [[consensus]] is becoming more relaxed: eat breakfast if you are hungry, choose it wisely, and don't feel guilty if you would rather wait.

text: Some pieces of dietary wisdom acquire the status of self-evident truth. Chief among them is the [[maxim]] that breakfast is the most important meal of the day – a claim recited by parents, echoed by health professionals and printed on the side of countless cereal boxes. Yet the closer one looks at the evidence, the less self-evident it becomes.

The slogan's history is instructive. It gained currency in the early twentieth century, promoted in part by health publications and advertising connected to the burgeoning American cereal industry, whose founders had both commercial and moral reasons for elevating the morning meal. Commercial origins do not in themselves [[invalidate]] a claim, but they should prompt a degree of scepticism about why a particular piece of “common sense” became so common.

For much of the late twentieth century, the scientific literature appeared to [[vindicate]] the slogan. Large cohort studies repeatedly found that regular breakfast eaters weighed less and had lower rates of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease than habitual skippers. But observational associations are notoriously vulnerable to [[confounding]]. People who eat breakfast every day are also, on average, more likely to exercise, less likely to smoke and more likely to keep regular sleeping and working hours. Disentangling the effect of breakfast itself from this cluster of healthy habits is extremely difficult.

Randomised controlled trials, which allocate participants by chance to eat or skip breakfast, offer a cleaner test – and their findings have been distinctly [[deflating|deflate]] for the breakfast lobby. A 2019 meta-analysis in the British Medical Journal pooled thirteen such trials and found no evidence that breakfast aids weight loss; if anything, breakfast eaters consumed around 260 more calories a day and were marginally heavier. The Bath Breakfast Project, a carefully controlled British trial, found that eating breakfast did not boost resting metabolism, although it was associated with more spontaneous physical activity before noon. Neither result suggests that breakfast is harmful; both [[undermine]] the idea that it is uniquely beneficial.

Emerging research in chrononutrition – the study of how meal timing interacts with the body clock – complicates matters further. Some studies suggest that the body handles glucose more efficiently earlier in the day, which would favour eating more in the morning and less late at night. The evidence here is still preliminary, but it hints that the real issue may be less whether to eat breakfast than how food is distributed across the day.

What is far clearer is that composition matters. Refined cereals and pastries cause a rapid spike and subsequent dip in blood glucose, often followed by renewed hunger. Breakfasts rich in protein and fibre – eggs, Greek yoghurt, oats, nuts, fruit – are digested more slowly and promote [[satiety]] for longer. For children, particularly those from low-income households who might otherwise arrive at school hungry, school breakfast schemes have been associated with better attendance and behaviour. For adults, the most defensible advice is pragmatic: eat breakfast if you are hungry, make it a nutritious one, and feel no obligation to force down food you do not want.
