text: Few dietary injunctions have enjoyed the uncontested authority of the claim that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. It is recited by parents, reiterated by clinicians and emblazoned on the packaging of cereals in supermarkets the world over. Its very familiarity, however, has [[insulated|insulate]] it from scrutiny – and scrutiny, when finally applied, has proved unkind.

The aphorism's [[provenance]] alone should give pause. It was popularised in the early twentieth century, notably in health magazines and promotional material associated with the nascent American cereal industry, whose pioneers – some of them sanitarium doctors with zealous views about diet and morality – had every reason to cast the morning meal as indispensable. A commercial pedigree does not [[falsify|falsify]] a proposition, but it ought to prompt the question of how a particular piece of conventional wisdom came to be so conventional.

For decades, epidemiology appeared to bear the slogan out. Large cohort studies consistently reported that regular breakfast eaters were leaner and suffered lower rates of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease than those who skipped the meal. The difficulty is that observational data of this kind are [[riddled|riddle]] with confounders. Habitual breakfast eaters are disproportionately likely to exercise, abstain from smoking, sleep regularly and enjoy higher incomes; breakfast may simply be a marker of an orderly, health-conscious life rather than its cause. Statistical adjustment can reduce such distortions but never entirely eliminate them.

Randomised controlled trials, which assign participants by lot to eat or forgo breakfast, cut through this tangle – and their verdict has been notably deflating. A 2019 meta-analysis published in the British Medical Journal, pooling thirteen trials, found no evidence that breakfast promotes weight loss; on the contrary, breakfast eaters consumed roughly 260 additional calories daily and were, if anything, marginally heavier. The Bath Breakfast Project, a meticulously controlled British study, found that breakfast did not elevate resting metabolic rate, though it was associated with greater spontaneous physical activity during the morning – an effect that roughly offset the extra energy consumed. None of this demonstrates that breakfast is detrimental; it does [[dismantle]] the notion that it confers some unique metabolic advantage.

Nor is the story finished. The burgeoning field of chrononutrition, which examines how the timing of meals interacts with circadian rhythms, has produced intriguing if provisional findings. Insulin sensitivity appears to be higher in the morning than in the evening, so the same meal may provoke a smaller rise in blood glucose at eight a.m. than at nine p.m. If these findings hold, the salient question may turn out to be not whether one eats breakfast but how one's daily intake is distributed – front-loaded or back-loaded – across the waking day. Studies of late-night eating among shift workers, whose body clocks are chronically disrupted, lend the hypothesis some [[circumstantial]] support.

On composition, by contrast, the evidence is considerably more settled. Highly refined cereals and pastries induce a rapid surge in blood glucose followed by a precipitous decline, frequently accompanied by renewed hunger well before midday. Breakfasts rich in protein and fibre – eggs, strained yoghurt, oats, nuts, fruit – are digested more gradually and sustain satiety for longer. In this sense, the cereal box may be not merely the vehicle of the old maxim but part of the problem it claims to solve.

Children constitute a partial exception. For pupils from food-insecure households, who might otherwise arrive at school having eaten nothing since the previous day, breakfast schemes have been associated with improved attendance, punctuality and classroom behaviour – benefits as much social as nutritional. For adults, the most defensible counsel is [[deflationary|deflate]] but liberating: eat breakfast if you are hungry, make it a substantial and minimally processed one, and feel no obligation whatsoever to consume food your body is not asking for.

text: Many parents think teenagers are lazy. They go to bed late and they don't want to get up in the morning. But scientists say this is not the teenagers' [[fault]].

Everyone has a body clock. It tells us when to feel sleepy and when to wake up. When children become teenagers, their body clock [[changes|change]]. They start to feel sleepy about two hours later than before. So a fifteen-year-old who goes to bed at ten o'clock often cannot fall asleep until midnight.
Teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep every night. But school starts early, so many of them sleep only six or seven hours. They feel tired in class and find it hard to [[remember]] things.
In 2016, some schools in the American city of Seattle started an hour later. The students slept more, and their marks got better. They were also late for school less often.

Phones don't help. Their bright light tells the brain it is still day. So doctors give teenagers some [[simple]] advice: put your phone away an hour before bed and try to go to sleep at the same time every [[night]].

text: It is a familiar scene in many homes: a teenager who [[refuses|refuse]] to go to bed before midnight and then can't get up in the morning. Parents often see this as laziness. Scientists, however, say that teenagers' sleep [[patterns|pattern]] are mainly controlled by biology, not by bad habits.

Our sleep is controlled by a body clock, a natural 24-hour rhythm. In the evening, the brain releases a hormone called melatonin, which makes us feel sleepy. During puberty, this release happens later – often around two hours later than in younger children or adults. As a result, many teenagers simply do not feel tired until eleven or even later, however early they go to bed.

The problem is that school timetables do not [[match]] this biology. Experts recommend that teenagers get between eight and ten hours of sleep a night, but if they fall asleep at midnight and get up at half past six, they get much less. Lack of sleep affects concentration, memory and mood, and it has been linked to a higher [[risk]] of accidents and depression.

Some places have taken action. In 2016, schools in Seattle moved their start time from 7.50 to 8.45 in the morning. Researchers found that students slept on average 34 minutes more each night, their grades improved and fewer students were late or absent. In 2019, California became the first US state to pass a law requiring most high schools to start no earlier than 8.30.

Technology makes the situation worse. The blue light from screens delays melatonin even more, and exciting messages or games keep the brain [[alert]]. Sleep experts suggest switching off devices an hour before bed, keeping the bedroom dark and cool, and trying to get up at a [[similar]] time at weekends, so that the body clock does not move even later.

text: Few household battles are as predictable as the one between parents and teenagers over bedtime. The teenager insists they are not tired at ten o'clock; the parents insist they will be exhausted in the morning. Both are right – and, according to sleep scientists, the teenager is not simply being [[stubborn]].

Human sleep is governed by two systems. The first is the circadian rhythm, an internal clock that runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle and signals night-time by releasing the hormone melatonin. The second is sleep pressure, a need for sleep that builds up the longer we are awake. During adolescence both systems shift. Melatonin is released up to two hours later than in childhood, and sleep pressure builds more slowly, so teenagers can stay awake comfortably until late at night. This is not a [[quirk]] of modern life: the same delay has been observed in many cultures and even in other mammals.

Unfortunately, school [[schedules|schedule]] are designed around adults. Sleep organisations recommend that teenagers get eight to ten hours a night, yet surveys in many countries show that a large proportion get fewer than seven on school nights. The [[consequences|consequence]] go well beyond yawning in class. Chronic sleep loss impairs attention and memory, makes it harder to control emotions and has been associated with higher rates of depression, obesity and car accidents among young drivers.

A growing number of school districts have responded by starting later. When Seattle moved the start of its secondary schools from 7.50 to 8.45 in 2016, researchers who tracked students before and after the change found that they slept a median of 34 minutes longer, their grades rose and punctuality improved, particularly in schools serving poorer neighbourhoods. California has since made later starts a legal requirement for most high schools. Critics point to the practical costs – bus timetables, sports training and parents' working hours – but supporters argue that these are small compared with the benefits.

Families can also help. Screens [[emit]] blue light that suppresses melatonin, and exciting content keeps the brain switched on, so experts advise switching devices off an hour before bed. Another useful idea is to limit “social jet lag” – the habit of sleeping until midday at weekends, which effectively moves the body clock several time zones west and makes Monday morning even more painful. Teenagers may never become [[enthusiastic]] early risers, but understanding their biology can turn a nightly argument into a shared problem to solve.

text: Every evening in countless households, the same negotiation takes place. A teenager insists that they are wide awake at ten o'clock; a parent warns that they will be impossible to wake at seven. For generations, the [[standoff]] has been framed as a question of discipline. Sleep science suggests it is better understood as a question of biology – and, increasingly, of public policy.

Sleep is regulated by the interplay of two processes. The circadian system, an internal clock with a period of roughly 24 hours, times our daily rhythms and signals the onset of night through the release of melatonin. Alongside it runs homeostatic sleep pressure, a drive for sleep that accumulates during waking hours and dissipates during sleep. Adolescence alters both. The evening rise in melatonin occurs as much as two hours later than in childhood, and sleep pressure builds more slowly, enabling teenagers to remain alert well into the night. This delay appears to be [[innate]] rather than cultural: it has been documented across societies with very different lifestyles and in several other mammalian species.

The difficulty is that the institutions surrounding teenagers have not adjusted. Health bodies recommend eight to ten hours of sleep for adolescents, yet in many countries a majority of secondary-school students fall short on school nights. The [[ramifications|ramification]] extend well beyond drowsiness. Chronic sleep restriction degrades attention, working memory and emotional regulation; it has been linked to elevated risks of depression, obesity and risk-taking; and drowsy driving is a significant cause of crashes involving young motorists. Some researchers have argued that early school start times represent one of the most widespread, and most easily corrected, public health problems facing young people.

Evidence that later starts make a difference is accumulating. When Seattle delayed secondary school start times from 7.50 to 8.45 in 2016, a study that measured students' sleep with wrist-worn monitors found a median increase of 34 minutes per night, together with higher grades and fewer late arrivals and absences – gains that were most pronounced in schools serving low-income neighbourhoods, where the [[disparity]] in outcomes narrowed. In 2019 California went further, passing legislation that requires most public high schools to begin no earlier than 8.30. Opponents raise legitimate logistical concerns, from bus routes and after-school sport to the needs of working parents, but advocates contend that such obstacles are [[surmountable]] and the benefits substantial.

Households, too, can [[mitigate]] the problem. The blue-enriched light emitted by screens suppresses melatonin, while stimulating content keeps the mind aroused; experts therefore recommend a screen-free hour before bed and a dark, cool bedroom. Equally important is limiting what the chronobiologist Till Roenneberg has called “social jet lag”: the mismatch between the body clock and social obligations, which teenagers aggravate by sleeping until noon at weekends. The effect is akin to flying several time zones west every Friday and back again every Monday. Teenagers are unlikely ever to become [[eager]] early risers, but recognising the biological basis of their behaviour can transform a nightly conflict into a problem that families, schools and policymakers share.

text: In homes across the world, the same nightly drama unfolds. A teenager protests that sleep is impossible at ten; a parent predicts, correctly, that the same teenager will be inert at seven. For generations the dispute has been cast as a contest of wills, with lateness and lethargy read as symptoms of indiscipline. The science of sleep tells a more [[exculpatory]] story – one in which the adolescent body, not the adolescent character, is largely responsible, and in which the institutions that structure teenagers' days bear a share of the blame.

Sleep is the product of two interacting processes. The circadian system, orchestrated by a cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus, keeps time on a cycle of roughly 24 hours and heralds the night by triggering the secretion of melatonin. In parallel, homeostatic sleep pressure – mediated in part by the accumulation of the molecule adenosine – mounts with every waking hour and is discharged by sleep. Puberty perturbs both. Evening melatonin onset is delayed by up to two hours relative to childhood, while sleep pressure accrues more slowly, so that adolescents can sustain alertness late into the night with little apparent effort. This phase delay has been documented in industrialised and pre-industrial societies alike, and in rodents and primates, which makes explanations based purely on screens or permissive parenting [[untenable]].

Institutional timetables have proved stubbornly [[impervious]] to this biology. Expert bodies advise eight to ten hours of sleep for adolescents, yet in many countries most secondary pupils fall well short on school nights, rising for early buses at an hour that, in circadian terms, corresponds to the middle of an adult's night. The consequences are not confined to yawning and irritability. Chronic sleep restriction compromises attention, working memory and the regulation of emotion; it is associated with elevated rates of depression, obesity and risky behaviour; and drowsiness contributes materially to road accidents involving young drivers. Some public health researchers regard early school start times as among the most pervasive yet [[tractable]] threats to adolescent wellbeing.

Where policy has changed, the evidence is encouraging. In 2016 Seattle's public school district moved secondary start times from 7.50 to 8.45. A study that monitored students with wrist-worn activity trackers before and after the change found a median gain of 34 minutes' sleep per night, accompanied by improved grades and fewer instances of lateness and absence. Tellingly, the improvements were most marked in schools serving disadvantaged neighbourhoods, suggesting that sleep deprivation may [[exacerbate]] existing educational inequality. California subsequently legislated, in 2019, to prohibit most public high schools from starting before 8.30. The objections – the cost of reconfiguring bus networks, the disruption to after-school sport and employment, the strain on working parents – are not frivolous, but advocates argue they amount to problems of coordination rather than of principle.

The domestic environment can either compound or relieve the problem. Light from screens, rich in blue wavelengths, suppresses melatonin, while the emotional charge of messaging and gaming sustains arousal; hence the near-universal recommendation of a screen-free hour before bed. Subtler, but no less consequential, is what the chronobiologist Till Roenneberg has termed “social jet lag”: the discrepancy between the timing dictated by the body clock and that imposed by social obligations. Teenagers who compensate for weekday deprivation by sleeping until noon at weekends shift their internal clocks later still, so that Monday morning arrives with the physiological force of a transatlantic flight.

Recognising the biological roots of adolescent sleep does not mean abandoning boundaries. It does mean reframing the question. Teenagers will probably never be [[sprightly]] at dawn. But once their behaviour is understood as a predictable feature of development rather than a moral failing, the nightly confrontation can give way to something more productive: a negotiation between families, schools and policymakers about how to arrange the world so that young people can get the sleep their bodies demand. Viewed in this light, the late-rising teenager is less a [[culprit]] than a casualty of a timetable designed for someone else.

text: Most of us know that exercise keeps our hearts and bodies healthy. What is less well known is how quickly it can affect the brain. You don't need months of training: even a few minutes of movement can make a [[measurable]] difference.

In 2018, researchers at the University of California, Irvine asked young adults to pedal gently on an exercise bike for ten minutes. Then they scanned their brains and gave them a memory test. Compared with people who had simply rested, the cyclists showed stronger connections between parts of the brain involved in memory, and they [[recalled|recall]] details more accurately.

Walking seems to help creativity too. In a study at Stanford University, students who walked – either outside or on a treadmill facing a blank wall – came up with about 60 per cent more creative ideas than when they were sitting. Many famous thinkers, from Charles Darwin to Steve Jobs, liked to walk while they thought or held meetings.

Over longer periods, the effects can be even greater. In one study, older adults who walked for forty minutes three times a week for a year saw the hippocampus, a part of the brain important for memory, grow slightly larger, while it shrank in people who only did stretching. Regular exercise has also been shown to reduce [[symptoms|symptom]] of depression and anxiety.

So how much do we need? The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least 150 minutes of [[moderate]] activity a week. That might sound like a lot, but it can be [[divided|divide]] into short periods: a [[brisk]] walk to work, cycling to the shops, taking the stairs. For a busy brain, the best kind of exercise is simply the one you will actually do.

text: The benefits of exercise for the heart, lungs and waistline are familiar to almost everyone. Its effects on the brain have received far less public attention, even though the evidence is now [[substantial]]. Perhaps the most surprising finding is how little exercise it takes to make a difference.

In a 2018 study at the University of California, Irvine, healthy young adults spent just ten minutes pedalling slowly on an exercise bike – an effort so light that it barely raised their heart rate. Immediately afterwards, brain scans showed increased communication between the hippocampus, a region central to memory, and areas involved in detailed recall. On a memory task that required them to distinguish between very similar images, the exercisers outperformed those who had rested. The researchers [[speculated|speculate]] that brief activity might be a practical way to give the brain a quick boost before studying.

Movement also appears to free up creative thinking. Psychologists at Stanford asked volunteers to think of unusual uses for everyday objects, either while sitting or while walking. Walking increased the number of original ideas by an average of around 60 per cent, and the effect [[persisted|persist]] for a short time after people sat down again. Remarkably, it did not matter whether participants strolled outdoors or on a treadmill facing a blank wall; the movement itself seemed to be what counted.

Over months and years, the changes can be structural. In a well-known trial, older adults who walked briskly for forty minutes three times a week saw the volume of their hippocampus increase by about 2 per cent over a year, roughly reversing a year or two of normal age-related decline. A comparison group who did only stretching exercises experienced the usual shrinkage. Exercise is thought to [[stimulate]] the production of a protein known as BDNF, which supports the growth and survival of brain cells and is sometimes described as “fertiliser for the brain”.

There are emotional benefits too. Numerous studies have found that regular activity can ease symptoms of mild to moderate depression and anxiety, in some cases as effectively as other standard treatments, although it is not a [[substitute]] for professional care in more serious cases.

The practical message is reassuring. The World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, but this does not need to be done in long, [[gruelling]] sessions. Short bursts – a brisk walk between meetings, cycling instead of taking the bus, a few flights of stairs – all add up. For the brain, consistency appears to matter more than intensity.

text: Public messages about exercise tend to dwell on the body: stronger hearts, healthier weights, lower blood pressure. The brain is a comparative afterthought, even though a substantial body of research now suggests that it is among the organs most [[responsive]] to physical activity. What has surprised researchers most is not the scale of the effects but the modest doses at which they begin to appear.

Consider a 2018 experiment at the University of California, Irvine. Healthy young adults pedalled at a deliberately gentle pace for just ten minutes – an intensity comparable to a leisurely stroll. Functional brain imaging carried out immediately afterwards revealed heightened connectivity between the hippocampus and cortical regions involved in fine-grained memory, and on a demanding task that required participants to tell apart near-identical images, the exercisers outperformed a control group who had sat still. The authors suggested that such brief, low-effort activity might serve as a readily [[accessible]] way to prime the brain before learning.

A parallel line of work concerns creativity. Psychologists at Stanford University measured divergent thinking – the generation of varied, original ideas – by asking participants to propose unconventional uses for common objects. Walking boosted creative output by around 60 per cent compared with sitting, and the benefit lingered briefly after participants sat down. Strikingly, it made no difference whether people walked through a leafy campus or on a treadmill facing a blank wall, suggesting that the physical act, rather than [[novel]] scenery, was responsible.

Sustained activity appears to produce structural change. In a widely cited randomised trial, [[sedentary]] older adults who undertook brisk forty-minute walks three times a week showed an increase of roughly 2 per cent in hippocampal volume over a year, effectively offsetting one to two years of age-related atrophy, whereas a stretching-only control group continued to decline. One proposed mechanism involves brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, a protein that promotes the growth of new neurons and the connections between them, and whose levels rise with aerobic exercise.

Studies in schools point in the same direction. Short bouts of physical activity during lessons – sometimes called “active breaks” – have been associated with better on-task behaviour in children, particularly in the period immediately afterwards. The effects on academic results are less consistent, but few researchers believe that a few minutes of movement could harm learning, and many teachers report that pupils return to their desks calmer and more focused.

The psychological benefits are similarly well documented. Meta-analyses have found that structured exercise can [[alleviate]] symptoms of mild to moderate depression to a degree comparable with established treatments, and that it reduces anxiety in many people. Researchers caution, however, that exercise should complement rather than replace professional treatment for more severe conditions, and that motivation itself can be a casualty of depression.

For anyone pressed for time, the practical implications are encouraging. The World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, but there is little evidence that it must be [[accumulated|accumulate]] in long sessions. Brisk walks between appointments, cycling rather than driving, or climbing stairs instead of taking the lift all count. The emerging message from neuroscience is that the most effective exercise regime is not the most intense one but the most [[sustainable]].

text: Exercise is usually sold to us as a matter of bodily maintenance: cardiovascular fitness, metabolic health, a trimmer silhouette. The brain features, if at all, as an afterthought. Yet a burgeoning literature suggests that the brain is among the most exercise-sensitive organs we possess – and that, contrary to the punishing [[ethos]] of much fitness culture, its responsiveness begins at doses so modest as to be almost [[negligible]].

A 2018 study at the University of California, Irvine illustrates the point. Young adults pedalled for ten minutes at an intensity deliberately calibrated to be undemanding – roughly the exertion of an unhurried stroll. High-resolution functional imaging conducted immediately afterwards revealed enhanced coupling between the dentate gyrus, a subregion of the hippocampus implicated in distinguishing similar memories, and cortical areas involved in detailed recall. On a pattern-separation task requiring participants to discriminate between near-identical images, the exercisers [[eclipsed|eclipse]] a seated control group. The authors proposed, with appropriate caution, that such brief and effortless bouts might prime the brain for subsequent learning.

Creativity appears similarly susceptible. In experiments at Stanford, participants generating unconventional uses for mundane objects – a standard measure of divergent thinking – produced roughly 60 per cent more novel responses while walking than while seated, with a residual benefit persisting briefly after they stopped. That the effect was indistinguishable whether people walked through a sunlit campus or on a treadmill facing a featureless wall implies that ambulation itself, rather than environmental stimulation, was the active ingredient – lending empirical support to the habits of the many writers and philosophers who have insisted that they think best on foot.

With sustained practice, the changes become anatomical. In a randomised controlled trial that has become a touchstone of the field, previously sedentary adults in their sixties and seventies who walked briskly for forty minutes three times a week exhibited an increase of around 2 per cent in hippocampal volume after a year, whereas participants assigned to stretching and toning showed the decline typical of ageing. The gains correlated with rising serum levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a protein that fosters neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity and which aerobic activity reliably [[upregulates|upregulate]]. Whether such structural gains translate into durable protection against dementia remains an open and actively investigated question.

The classroom offers a revealing test case. Interventions that break up long periods of sitting with brief “active breaks” have been associated with improved on-task behaviour among children, particularly in the minutes that follow, although their effects on attainment are inconsistent and sometimes negligible. The heterogeneity is instructive: it suggests that the cognitive dividends of movement may be acute and short-lived, more akin to a fresh cup of coffee than to a permanent upgrade – which is, if anything, an argument for distributing activity throughout the day rather than confining it to a single session.

The affective benefits are no less [[compelling]]. Several meta-analyses have concluded that structured exercise reduces depressive symptoms to an extent broadly comparable with psychotherapy or medication in mild to moderate cases, and that it has anxiolytic effects as well. Researchers are careful to add two caveats. First, exercise ought to supplement rather than supplant professional care for severe illness. Second, the very anhedonia and fatigue that characterise depression can make exercise feel impossible – which is precisely why advice to “just go for a run” can sound, to someone who is unwell, more like reproach than encouragement.

Perhaps the most liberating implication concerns dose. The World Health Organization's guideline of at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week is often perceived as [[daunting]], yet there is scant evidence that it must be discharged in long, continuous sessions. Accumulated fragments – a brisk walk between meetings, a cycle commute, a few flights of stairs – appear to confer much of the benefit. Seen through the lens of neuroscience, the ideal regime is not the most heroic but the most habitual: the one that can be woven so [[seamlessly]] into ordinary life that abandoning it would feel stranger than continuing.

text: In some places in the world, many people live to 100 years old. One of these places is Okinawa, a group of islands in Japan. Another is Sardinia, an island in Italy. Writers call these places “blue zones”.
What is the [[secret]] of these long lives? Researchers visited the blue zones and found some [[similar]] habits.

First, people move a lot every day. They don't go to the gym, but they walk, work in their gardens and do housework. Second, they eat a lot of vegetables, beans and fruit, and not much meat. In Okinawa, people have a saying: stop eating when you are 80 per cent full.

Third, family and friends are very important. Old people often live with their children and grandchildren. They meet friends every day and are not [[lonely]]. Fourth, they have a reason to get up in the morning. In Okinawa, this is called “ikigai”.

Of course, genes are important too. But scientists think our daily habits can make a big [[difference]]. We can all walk more, eat more vegetables and spend time with people we love. These are simple [[changes|change]], and they are free!

text: Around twenty years ago, the writer Dan Buettner and a team of scientists went looking for places where people live unusually long, healthy lives. They found five: Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy, Nicoya in Costa Rica, Ikaria in Greece and a community in Loma Linda, California. They called them “blue zones”, because one of the first researchers marked them on a map with a blue pen.

These places are very different from each other, but their older residents share some habits. The first is natural movement. Most of them have never been to a gym, but they walk up hills, grow vegetables and do physical work every day. Exercise is not a separate [[activity]] – it is part of life.

The second is diet. Meals are based on beans, vegetables, whole grains and nuts, with meat eaten only a few times a month. People also tend to eat [[moderately]]. In Okinawa, older people repeat a saying before meals that reminds them to stop when they are about 80 per cent full.

The third, and perhaps the most surprising, is social life. Older people in the blue zones are rarely [[isolated]]. They live close to their families, belong to religious or social groups and meet friends regularly. Many also have a strong sense of [[purpose]] – a reason to get up in the morning, which Okinawans call “ikigai”.

Not everyone is [[convinced]]. Some researchers point out that birth records in some places may not be completely reliable, and that genes also play a part. But the habits themselves are supported by plenty of other research. Moving every day, eating mostly plants, keeping close [[relationships|relationship]] and having a purpose are good advice wherever you live.

text: In the early 2000s, the journalist Dan Buettner, working with demographers and doctors, set out to find the places on Earth where people live the longest, healthiest lives. The team identified five regions with unusually high numbers of people reaching ninety or a hundred in good health: the Japanese islands of Okinawa, the mountainous Barbagia region of Sardinia, the Nicoya Peninsula in Costa Rica, the Greek island of Ikaria and a Seventh-day Adventist community in Loma Linda, California. They became known as the “blue zones” – a name that came, rather [[prosaically]], from the blue ink used to circle villages on a map.

The regions differ in climate, culture and religion, yet the researchers noticed striking [[parallels|parallel]] in how their oldest residents lived. Few of them had ever exercised in a formal sense. Instead, physical activity was built into everyday routines: herding goats up steep hillsides, tending vegetable gardens, kneading bread, walking to visit neighbours. Their diets were largely plant-based, centred on beans, whole grains, vegetables and nuts, with meat reserved for special occasions. Portions were modest; older Okinawans traditionally recite the phrase “hara hachi bu”, a reminder to stop eating when the stomach is about 80 per cent full.

Equally important, the researchers argue, was social and psychological life. Elderly people in the blue zones tend to live with or near their families, remain respected members of their communities and take part in religious or social groups. In Okinawa, many belong to a “moai”, a lifelong circle of friends who support each other practically and emotionally. A sense of purpose – called “ikigai” in Okinawa and “plan de vida” in Nicoya – gives people a reason to stay [[engaged]] with the world.

The blue zones idea has been enormously popular, inspiring books, cookery programmes and even town planning projects in the United States. But it has also attracted criticism. Some demographers have questioned whether the extreme ages recorded in certain places are [[accurate]], since birth certificates can be missing or incorrect, especially for people born more than a century ago. Others note that genetics, as well as wealth and access to healthcare, also influence how long people live, and that habits observed in a few places cannot [[prove]] what causes long life.

Even so, most of the blue zones habits are [[backed]] by independent research. Regular moderate activity, a diet rich in plants, strong social connections and a sense of meaning are all associated with lower rates of disease and death. The lesson may not be that we should all move to a Greek island, but that a long life is built from ordinary daily choices – and from the communities that make those choices easier.

text: Few health ideas of recent decades have travelled as far as the “blue zones”. The term emerged in the early 2000s from work by demographers studying unusually long-lived populations, and was popularised by the journalist Dan Buettner, who, with National Geographic, led expeditions to five places where people appeared to reach ninety and a hundred in remarkable numbers and remarkable health: Okinawa in Japan, the Barbagia highlands of Sardinia, Costa Rica's Nicoya Peninsula, the Greek island of Ikaria and a Seventh-day Adventist community in Loma Linda, California. The name itself has an unglamorous origin – the blue ink with which researchers circled promising villages on a map.

What makes the blue zones compelling is that such different places seem to [[converge|converge]] on similar ways of living. Their oldest inhabitants rarely exercise in any deliberate sense; physical activity is woven into daily life through farming, herding, gardening, walking steep streets and doing domestic work by hand. Diets are predominantly plant-based – beans, whole grains, vegetables, nuts – with meat an occasional extravagance. Calorie intake is modest: older Okinawans traditionally invoke the Confucian-inspired maxim “hara hachi bu”, eating until they are roughly 80 per cent full.

Just as significant, in Buettner's account, are the social and existential dimensions of life. Older people in these regions tend to remain [[embedded]] in multigenerational families and close-knit communities, where age often brings status rather than [[marginalisation|marginalise]]. Okinawans may belong for decades to a “moai”, a group of friends who offer mutual financial and emotional support. And many describe a clear reason for living – “ikigai” in Okinawa, “plan de vida” in Nicoya – which keeps them engaged, active and needed.

The concept has inspired bestselling books, cookbooks, documentaries and a series of American urban projects that tried to [[engineer]] blue-zone habits through walkable streets, community gardens and healthier school meals. Yet it has also drawn serious [[scrutiny]]. Some demographers argue that extreme [[longevity]] claims are disproportionately found in places with poor or incomplete birth records, raising the possibility that ages have been exaggerated through clerical error, missing documentation or even pension fraud. If some of the oldest residents were in fact younger than recorded, the statistical case for certain regions would weaken considerably.

There are methodological concerns, too. Identifying common habits among a handful of long-lived populations is not the same as demonstrating that those habits cause longevity. Genetic inheritance, historical circumstances – including, in some cases, periods of food scarcity – and access to healthcare may all contribute, and lifestyles in several blue zones have changed rapidly with the arrival of fast food and cars, often with measurable effects on health.

None of this, however, [[negates|negate]] the value of the habits themselves, most of which are supported by large independent bodies of evidence. Regular moderate activity, a diet rich in plants and fibre, strong social ties and a sense of purpose are each associated with lower mortality. The deeper lesson of the blue zones may be less about a secret formula than about environment: in these places, healthy choices were rarely heroic acts of willpower, but the default options of the community. Making healthy behaviour the easy choice, rather than the virtuous one, may be the most transferable insight of all.

text: Few concepts in popular health writing have proved as seductive, or as commercially fertile, as the “blue zones”. The phrase originated in demographic research in the early 2000s – it refers, rather mundanely, to the blue ink used to circle clusters of long-lived villages on a map of Sardinia – and was carried to a global audience by the journalist Dan Buettner. With the backing of National Geographic, Buettner assembled teams of demographers and physicians and identified five places that seemed to produce [[centenarians|centenarian]] at exceptional rates: Okinawa, the Barbagia highlands of Sardinia, the Nicoya Peninsula in Costa Rica, the Aegean island of Ikaria and a Seventh-day Adventist enclave in Loma Linda, California.

The appeal of the idea lies in its apparent universality. Communities separated by oceans, languages and faiths appeared to converge on a common repertoire of behaviours. Their oldest members rarely exercised in any deliberate sense; activity was [[intrinsic]] to daily life, embedded in herding, terraced farming, bread-making and the steep walk to a neighbour's door. Diets were overwhelmingly plant-based, built on legumes, whole grains and garden vegetables, with meat an occasional indulgence. Consumption was restrained: elderly Okinawans traditionally invoke the precept “hara hachi bu”, ceasing to eat at roughly 80 per cent of satiety.

Buettner's account places equal weight on the social fabric. In these communities, old age was not a passage into irrelevance but often a source of standing; elders lived among multiple generations and retained recognised roles. Okinawans formed “moai”, lifelong cohorts of friends who pooled resources and offered emotional support, while a pronounced sense of purpose – ikigai in Okinawa, plan de vida in Nicoya – sustained engagement with the world well into the tenth decade.

The commercial afterlife of the concept has been [[prodigious]]: bestselling books, branded recipes, a streaming documentary and municipal programmes across the United States that sought to retrofit blue-zone conditions through walkable streets, community gardens and the restriction of fast-food outlets. Scholarly reception has been more [[ambivalent]]. The demographer Saul Newman, among others, has argued that claims of extreme longevity cluster disproportionately in regions with deficient civil registration, low literacy and high poverty – precisely the conditions in which ages are most easily misreported, whether through clerical error, the loss of documents or the fraudulent claiming of pensions in a dead relative's name. Proponents counter that the original blue zones were subjected to rigorous age validation; critics reply that validation is only as good as the archives on which it relies.

Even where the data are sound, inference poses difficulties. Isolating a handful of exceptional populations and cataloguing what they have in common is a classic recipe for [[spurious]] causal conclusions: a shared habit may be incidental rather than explanatory. Genetic endowment, the selective emigration of the young and the less robust, historical episodes of caloric scarcity and the quality of local healthcare are all plausible contributors. Moreover, the zones themselves are [[ephemeral]]: as processed food, motor vehicles and sedentary work have arrived, several have seen obesity and diabetes rise among younger generations, a reminder that longevity is the product of a whole life course rather than a fixed property of a place.

Yet the scepticism, however warranted, does not [[impugn]] the habits themselves, nearly all of which are corroborated by large and independent epidemiological literatures. Habitual moderate activity, a diet dominated by plants and fibre, dense social networks and a sense of meaning are each associated with reduced mortality. The most durable insight of the blue zones may therefore be structural rather than personal. In these places, healthy behaviour was seldom an act of heroic self-discipline; it was simply what the environment made easiest. Designing communities in which the healthy option is also the path of least resistance may prove a more reliable route to long life than any secret formula imported from a distant island.

text: A glacier is a very big river of ice. It moves very slowly down a mountain. There are glaciers in many countries, from Switzerland to Peru to Pakistan.

Today, most glaciers in the world are getting smaller. The world is getting warmer, so the ice [[melts|melt]] faster than new snow can [[replace]] it. In Switzerland, the glaciers lost about ten per cent of their ice in just two years.

This is a big problem for people. In summer, water from melting glaciers goes into rivers. Millions of farmers use this water for their fields, and cities use it for drinking. When the glaciers are gone, there will be less water in dry [[seasons|season]].
Melting ice can also be [[dangerous]]. Sometimes a lake of melted water grows behind a wall of ice and rocks. If the wall breaks, the water floods the villages below.

In 2019, people in Iceland held a funeral for a glacier called Okjökull. They put a sign on a rock. It says that in 200 years, all their glaciers may be gone. It is a message to the future: we know what is [[happening|happen]], and we must act.

text: Glaciers look solid and permanent, but they are always moving. Formed from snow that has been pressed into ice over hundreds of years, they slide slowly down mountain valleys like frozen rivers. For thousands of years, the snow that fell each winter more or less balanced the ice that melted each summer. That [[balance]] has now been broken.

Because of global warming, glaciers in almost every mountain range are shrinking. The [[decline]] has been especially fast in the European Alps: Swiss scientists reported that the country's glaciers lost around ten per cent of their total volume in just two years, 2022 and 2023, after hot summers and winters with little snow.

This matters far beyond the mountains. Glaciers act like water towers. They store water as ice in winter and release it slowly in summer, when rain is often [[scarce]]. In Asia, rivers that begin in the Himalayas – such as the Indus and the Ganges – [[supply]] water to hundreds of millions of people. In the Andes of South America, cities such as La Paz in Bolivia depend partly on glacier water during the dry season.

At first, faster melting can actually mean more water in rivers. But scientists warn of a moment called “peak water”: once a glacier becomes too small, the amount of meltwater starts to fall, and farmers and cities lose a [[reliable]] supply. Melting also creates new dangers. Lakes can form behind natural walls of rock and ice, and if these walls suddenly break, floods can destroy villages in minutes.

In 2019, Icelanders held a funeral for Okjökull, the first Icelandic glacier lost to climate change. A plaque at the site is called “A letter to the future”. It ends with a simple [[warning]]: only we know whether we did what was needed.

text: From a distance, a glacier looks like the very definition of permanence: a vast, silent body of ice that has filled its valley for millennia. Up close, it is a dynamic system, constantly fed by snowfall at its upper end and losing ice through melting at its lower end. For most of human history, these gains and losses roughly [[cancelled|cancel]] each other out. Today, in almost every mountain range on Earth, the losses are winning.

The [[retreat]] is particularly visible in the Alps. After the exceptionally hot summer of 2022 and another poor year in 2023, Swiss monitoring scientists calculated that the country's glaciers had lost about a tenth of their remaining volume in just two years – more than had melted in the three decades before 1990. Similar trends have been recorded from Alaska to the Andes and across the vast ice fields of High Mountain Asia, a region sometimes nicknamed the “Third Pole” because it holds more ice than anywhere outside the polar regions.

The consequences extend far downstream. Glaciers function as natural reservoirs, storing winter precipitation and releasing it during the warm, dry months when crops need it most. Rivers fed partly by Himalayan ice, including the Indus, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra, sustain agriculture and drinking water for hundreds of millions of people. In the Andes, the cities of La Paz and El Alto in Bolivia rely on glacial meltwater during droughts, and several small glaciers that once [[buffered|buffer]] dry seasons there have already disappeared.

Paradoxically, rapid melting can increase river flows for a time, creating a false sense of [[abundance]]. Hydrologists describe a point called “peak water”, after which a shrinking glacier can no longer supply as much meltwater and summer flows decline, sometimes sharply. Many Andean and Central Asian glaciers are thought to be at or beyond this point. Melting also brings [[hazards|hazard]]. Lakes of meltwater can build up behind unstable dams of rock and debris; when these give way, the resulting floods can sweep away bridges, roads and homes with little warning.

In 2019, a group of Icelanders and scientists climbed the volcano Ok to hold a memorial for Okjökull, the first Icelandic glacier to lose its status as a glacier. A bronze plaque, titled “A letter to the future”, predicts that all of Iceland's main glaciers may follow within the next 200 years. Its final line is a challenge rather than a [[lament]]: “Only you know if we did it.” Scientists stress that the future is not yet fixed; every fraction of a degree of warming avoided will save ice – and the water that depends on it.

text: Seen from a valley floor, a glacier seems the epitome of permanence – a great tongue of ice that has lain there since before human memory. In reality it is a dynamic system in [[precarious]] [[equilibrium]]: snow accumulates and compacts into ice in its upper reaches, the ice flows downhill under its own weight, and at its lower end it melts away. As long as accumulation and melt roughly balance, the glacier holds its position. Across the world's mountain ranges, that balance has tipped decisively towards loss.

The Alps offer a stark illustration. Following the record-breaking heat of summer 2022 and another punishing season in 2023, Switzerland's glacier monitoring network reported that the country had lost around 10 per cent of its remaining glacier volume in just two years – a rate of loss that would once have taken decades. Comparable retreat has been documented from the Rockies to Patagonia, and across High Mountain Asia, the so-called Third Pole, whose glaciers store more fresh water than any region outside the Arctic and Antarctic. A major study published in 2023 estimated that, even if warming were limited to 1.5 °C, around half of the world's glaciers could vanish by the end of the century, most of them small but many of them locally [[indispensable]].

Their importance lies less in their size than in their timing. Glaciers act as frozen reservoirs, [[banking|bank]] precipitation during the cold months and releasing it in late summer, precisely when rainfall is scarce and demand for irrigation peaks. The Indus basin, which supports agriculture across Pakistan and north-western India, draws a substantial share of its summer flow from snow and ice melt. In the Bolivian Andes, La Paz and El Alto have depended on glacial runoff during droughts, and the disappearance of the Chacaltaya glacier – once the site of the world's highest ski run – has become a symbol of what is at stake.

Counter-intuitively, the early stages of glacier loss can increase water availability, as accelerated melting swells rivers. Hydrologists refer to the moment at which this trend reverses as “peak water”. Thereafter, a dwindling glacier yields progressively less meltwater, and late-summer flows can fall steeply just as populations and agricultural demand are growing. Research suggests that many glaciers in the tropical Andes and parts of Central Asia have already passed this tipping point, leaving downstream communities to adapt to a less [[forgiving]] hydrology.

Retreating ice also creates new [[perils|peril]]. As glaciers shrink, meltwater pools behind moraines – loose ridges of rock and sediment left by the ice. Such lakes can burst without warning, unleashing torrents that destroy everything in their path. These glacial lake outburst floods have killed thousands of people over the past century, and the number and size of potentially dangerous lakes in the Himalayas has risen markedly.

In August 2019, mourners gathered on the slopes of the volcano Ok in western Iceland to mark the passing of Okjökull, the first Icelandic glacier declared dead. The plaque they unveiled, “A letter to the future”, anticipates that all of the country's main glaciers may follow within two centuries, and concludes: “Only you know if we did it.” Glaciologists [[underline|underline]] that the outcome is not predetermined. Because glacier loss responds closely to temperature, every tenth of a degree of warming prevented translates directly into ice – and water – preserved.

text: To the casual observer, a glacier is the epitome of geological permanence, an immense and motionless presence that seems to predate memory itself. To the glaciologist, it is a ledger. Snow accumulates and recrystallises into dense ice in the upper reaches; gravity drives that ice slowly downslope; and in the [[ablation]] zone below, it melts, sublimates or calves away. When the two sides of the account balance, the terminus holds steady. For most of the Holocene they did, give or take the [[vicissitudes|vicissitude]] of the Little Ice Age. Across almost every mountain range on Earth, the account is now deeply in deficit.

The Alps have become a grim showcase. After the scorching summer of 2022, compounded by a meagre snowpack, and a further punishing season in 2023, the Swiss glacier monitoring network reported a loss of roughly a tenth of the country's remaining ice volume in two years – attrition that would formerly have taken several decades. Comparable recession has been charted from the Rockies to Patagonia and across High Mountain Asia, the so-called Third Pole, whose glaciers constitute the largest store of fresh water outside the polar ice sheets. A widely cited 2023 study projected that even if warming were held to 1.5 °C, roughly half of the world's glaciers would disappear by 2100; under higher-emission scenarios the proportion rises considerably. Most of those destined to vanish are small, but smallness is no measure of local importance.

What makes glaciers [[consequential]] is less their mass than their timing. They act as frozen reservoirs, sequestering winter precipitation and disbursing it in late summer, when rainfall is sparse and irrigation demand peaks. The Indus basin, the agricultural backbone of Pakistan and north-western India, draws a substantial fraction of its summer discharge from snow and ice melt. In the Bolivian altiplano, La Paz and El Alto have leaned on glacial runoff during droughts; the extinction of the Chacaltaya glacier, once host to the world's highest ski lift, has become an [[emblem]] of what is being lost.

The hydrology of decline is counter-intuitive. In its early stages, accelerated melting augments river flows, lending a deceptive impression of plenty. The inflection point at which this trend reverses – “peak water” – marks the onset of a long decline, as an ever-diminishing ice mass yields ever less meltwater. Evidence suggests that many glaciers in the tropical Andes and parts of Central Asia have already passed it, leaving downstream populations to confront shrinking dry-season flows precisely as their numbers and their irrigated acreage expand. Adaptation is possible – through reservoirs, more efficient irrigation and the protection of high-altitude wetlands that store water – but it is costly, and its burden falls disproportionately on communities that contributed least to the warming.

Retreat also manufactures new hazards. As ice withdraws, meltwater ponds behind moraines, the unconsolidated ramparts of debris deposited by the glacier. These natural dams are inherently unstable, and their sudden failure can [[unleash]] glacial lake outburst floods of devastating force. Such events have claimed thousands of lives over the past century, and satellite inventories show that the number and volume of glacial lakes in the Himalayas have grown substantially in recent decades – a slow-building threat that early-warning systems are only beginning to address.

In August 2019, a small procession of scientists, officials and mourners climbed the volcano Ok in western Iceland to commemorate Okjökull, the first Icelandic glacier to be officially declared defunct. The plaque they installed, “A letter to the future”, predicts that the country's principal glaciers may follow within two hundred years and ends with an unsettling [[ambiguity]]: “Only you know if we did it.” The sentence is at once elegy and accusation. Glaciologists are nonetheless keen to resist [[fatalism]]. Because glacier mass responds closely to temperature, the trajectory remains contingent on emissions; every tenth of a degree of warming forgone is, quite literally, ice – and water – kept in the bank.

text: Since the 1950s, plastic has changed the way we live. It is cheap, light, strong and easy to shape, so we use it for almost everything, from food packaging to car parts. Today the world produces around 400 million tonnes of plastic every year, but less than ten per cent of it is [[recycled|recycle]]. Much of the rest ends up in [[landfill]] or in the natural environment.

Plastic does not rot like food or paper. Instead, sunlight, waves and wind slowly break it into smaller and smaller pieces. Pieces smaller than five millimetres are called microplastics, and even smaller ones are called nanoplastics. Clothes made of synthetic materials such as polyester also [[release]] tiny fibres every time they are washed.

These particles have now been found almost everywhere scientists look: in deep oceans, on mountain tops, in Arctic snow, in table salt, in honey and in tap and bottled water. A 2022 study in the Netherlands found plastic particles in the blood of most of the [[volunteers|volunteer]] tested, and other studies have found them in human lungs.

What this means for our health is still unclear. Some laboratory studies suggest that very small particles could cause inflammation or carry harmful chemicals into the body, but these studies often use much larger amounts than people are exposed to. Researchers say more work is needed before we can [[draw]] firm conclusions.

Meanwhile, many governments are taking action. Some have banned single-use plastic bags, straws or cutlery, and the United Nations has been working on an international treaty to reduce plastic pollution. As individuals, we can help by refusing unnecessary packaging, choosing reusable [[containers|container]] and recycling properly – but experts agree that the biggest changes must come from producers.

text: Few materials have shaped modern life as thoroughly as plastic. Cheap, light, [[durable]] and endlessly mouldable, it has made food last longer, cars lighter and medical equipment safer. Global production has risen from about two million tonnes in 1950 to roughly 400 million tonnes a year today. The problem is what happens afterwards: only around nine per cent of all the plastic ever made has been recycled, and much of the rest has been burned, buried or simply lost into the environment.

Unlike organic waste, plastic does not biodegrade in any meaningful timeframe. Instead, ultraviolet light, heat and mechanical wear [[fragment|fragment]] it into ever smaller pieces. Particles under five millimetres are classed as microplastics; those below one micrometre – far thinner than a human hair – are known as nanoplastics. Some are created deliberately, like the microbeads once common in face scrubs, but most come from the breakdown of larger items, from tyres wearing down on roads and from synthetic textiles [[shedding|shed]] fibres in the washing machine.

Over the past decade, researchers have found these particles in virtually every environment they have examined, from the bottom of the Mariana Trench to fresh snow in the Arctic. They have also turned up in the human body. A 2022 Dutch study detected plastic particles in the blood of seventeen out of twenty-two healthy volunteers, and other teams have reported them in lung tissue and placentas. In 2024, scientists using a new laser-based imaging technique estimated that a litre of bottled water could contain hundreds of thousands of plastic particles, most of them nanoplastics too small to have been counted before.

Whether this exposure is harmful remains an open question. In laboratory experiments, high doses of microplastics can cause inflammation and cell damage, and plastics can carry additives, such as certain softening chemicals, that are known to [[interfere]] with hormones. A 2024 study of patients undergoing surgery in Italy found that those with microplastics in the fatty deposits of their arteries had a higher risk of heart attack and stroke over the following years – although, as the authors acknowledged, this showed an association rather than proof of cause.

Action is under way at several levels. Many countries have banned microbeads and certain single-use items, and since 2022 governments have been negotiating a global treaty to tackle plastic pollution, though talks have repeatedly stalled over whether to limit production itself. Experts generally argue that recycling alone cannot solve the problem; reducing [[unnecessary]] plastic, redesigning products and holding manufacturers responsible for their waste must play a larger role. For individuals, choosing tap water over bottled and washing synthetic clothes less often are small but [[tangible]] steps.

text: Plastic is, in many respects, a triumph of twentieth-century chemistry. Cheap, light, durable and almost infinitely [[versatile]], it has [[revolutionised|revolutionise]] packaging, transport and medicine. Annual production has grown from around two million tonnes in 1950 to roughly 400 million today, and is projected to keep rising. Yet the very property that makes plastic so useful – its resistance to decay – has become its central liability. Of all the plastic ever manufactured, an estimated nine per cent has been recycled; the remainder has been incinerated, landfilled or dispersed into the environment, where it persists for decades or centuries.

Plastic does not so much decompose as disintegrate. Exposure to ultraviolet radiation, heat and abrasion breaks larger objects into progressively smaller fragments. Particles below five millimetres are termed microplastics, and those below one micrometre nanoplastics. Some are manufactured at that size, such as the microbeads formerly added to cosmetics, but the majority are secondary: shed by synthetic textiles in the wash, abraded from car tyres, or [[flaking|flake]] off packaging, paint and fishing gear.

The [[ubiquity]] of these particles has become one of the more unsettling findings of recent environmental science. They have been recorded in the sediment of the Mariana Trench, in Antarctic sea ice, in rainfall over remote national parks and in the stomachs of animals ranging from plankton to whales. Increasingly, they are also being detected in human tissue. A 2022 study from the Netherlands found quantifiable plastic in the blood of seventeen of twenty-two healthy donors; other groups have reported particles in lungs, placentas and breast milk. In 2024, researchers using stimulated Raman scattering microscopy estimated that a litre of bottled water may contain around a quarter of a million particles, roughly nine-tenths of them nanoplastics previously invisible to conventional analysis.

The health implications remain genuinely uncertain. Experiments on cells and animals show that microplastics at high concentrations can provoke oxidative stress and inflammation, and the chemical additives in many plastics – including certain phthalates and bisphenols – are recognised endocrine disruptors. Epidemiological evidence in humans is sparse but beginning to accumulate. A 2024 study in the New England Journal of Medicine followed Italian patients who had undergone surgery to remove arterial plaque; those whose plaque contained detectable micro- and nanoplastics were significantly more likely to suffer a heart attack, stroke or death during the following three years. The authors were careful to note that the study could not establish causation, but it has given new urgency to calls for research.

Policy is struggling to keep pace. Bans on microbeads and certain single-use items have spread widely, and in 2022 UN member states agreed to negotiate a legally binding global treaty on plastic pollution. Negotiations have since become [[mired|mire]] in a fundamental disagreement: a coalition of countries argues that the treaty must cap the production of new plastic, while oil- and petrochemical-producing states insist it should focus on waste management and recycling. Most independent analysts side with the former view, noting that recycling rates have [[stagnated|stagnate]] for decades and that much recycled plastic can only be downgraded into lower-quality products.

For individuals, the most effective measures are unglamorous: drinking tap rather than bottled water, avoiding heating food in plastic containers, and buying fewer, longer-lasting synthetic garments. Yet the scale of the problem means that personal choices can only [[supplement]], not substitute for, changes in how plastic is designed, produced and paid for.

text: Plastic is among the defining achievements of modern chemistry and, increasingly, among its most [[intractable]] legacies. Light, cheap, durable and almost limitlessly adaptable, it has transformed packaging, transport, construction and medicine. Annual output has swelled from roughly two million tonnes in 1950 to some 400 million today, with forecasts pointing higher still. Yet the attribute that underwrites plastic's usefulness – its stubborn resistance to degradation – is precisely what makes its afterlife so problematic. Of all the plastic ever produced, an estimated nine per cent has been recycled; the rest has been incinerated, entombed in landfill or released into ecosystems in which it may persist for centuries.

Rather than decomposing, plastic disintegrates. Ultraviolet radiation, thermal cycling and abrasion fracture larger items into fragments of diminishing size: microplastics, below five millimetres, and nanoplastics, below a micrometre. A minority are engineered at that scale, such as the exfoliating microbeads once ubiquitous in cosmetics, but most are secondary – fibres sloughed from synthetic garments in the wash, particulates ground from tyres on tarmac, flakes [[shed]] from paint, packaging and fishing nets.

The [[pervasiveness]] of these particles is now one of the more disquieting facts of environmental science. They have been retrieved from sediment in the Mariana Trench, from Antarctic sea ice and from rain falling on protected wilderness; they have been found in organisms throughout the food web, from zooplankton to baleen whales. Humans are no exception. A 2022 Dutch study quantified plastic in the blood of seventeen of twenty-two healthy donors, and particles have since been documented in lung tissue, placentas and breast milk. In 2024, researchers deploying stimulated Raman scattering microscopy – a technique capable of identifying particles at the nanoscale – estimated that a litre of bottled water may harbour roughly a quarter of a million plastic particles, the overwhelming majority of them nanoplastics that earlier methods had simply been unable to see.

What this exposure means for human health is a question science has only begun to address. In vitro and animal studies indicate that high concentrations of micro- and nanoplastics can induce oxidative stress, inflammation and cellular damage, and several additives routinely compounded into plastics – certain phthalates and bisphenols among them – are established endocrine disruptors. Translating such findings to realistic human exposures is fraught: doses in laboratory studies often exceed environmental levels by orders of magnitude, and contamination of samples is a persistent methodological hazard. Nonetheless, the first clinical signals are emerging. A 2024 study in the New England Journal of Medicine followed Italian patients who had undergone carotid surgery; those whose excised arterial plaque contained detectable plastics had a markedly elevated risk of heart attack, stroke or death over roughly three years. The authors were scrupulous in noting that the design could not [[establish]] causality, but the finding has sharpened demands for systematic research.

Governance has lagged behind the science. Bans on microbeads and selected single-use items have proliferated, and in 2022 the UN Environment Assembly mandated negotiations towards a legally binding global treaty. Those negotiations have since foundered on a fundamental [[cleavage]]. A coalition of states contends that no agreement worth the name can avoid capping the production of virgin polymers; a bloc of petrochemical producers insists that the remedy lies downstream, in improved waste management and recycling. The weight of independent analysis favours the former position. Global recycling rates have [[languished|languish]] for decades, much collected plastic is exported to countries ill-equipped to process it, and mechanical recycling typically degrades polymers, so that today's bottle becomes tomorrow's lower-grade fibre before ending, eventually, as waste.

There are, inevitably, things individuals can do: drinking tap rather than bottled water, refraining from heating food in plastic, and buying fewer but more durable synthetic garments. But to frame the problem chiefly as a matter of consumer virtue is to mistake its [[provenance]]. Plastic pollution is the predictable output of an economic system that makes virgin polymer cheap and its disposal someone else's problem. Durable solutions are therefore likely to be structural – in design standards, extended producer responsibility and limits on production – rather than the cumulative sum of conscientious shopping.

text: For more than a century, most electricity has been produced by burning coal, oil and gas. These fossil fuels are the main cause of climate change. In the last fifteen years, however, something remarkable has happened: electricity from the sun and the wind has become cheaper than electricity from fossil fuels in most parts of the world.

The fall in prices has been [[dramatic]]. Between 2010 and 2020, the cost of electricity from large solar farms fell by almost 90 per cent, and onshore wind became around 70 per cent cheaper. As factories produced more panels and turbines, they became more efficient, and prices kept falling. Today, solar and wind are the fastest-growing sources of power on the planet.

But they have one big weakness. Unlike a gas power station, which can be switched on whenever it is needed, solar and wind are [[variable]]: they produce electricity only when the sun shines or the wind blows. [[Demand|demand]], on the other hand, often peaks in the early evening, just as solar power disappears.

This is where batteries come in. The price of lithium-ion batteries – the same technology used in phones and electric cars – has also fallen by around 90 per cent since 2010. Power companies can now build huge batteries that charge up during sunny afternoons and [[discharge]] in the evening. In 2017, a giant battery in South Australia became famous for reacting to power cuts in less than a second. In California, batteries now supply a large share of electricity in the evening peak.

Batteries are not the only solution. Countries are connecting their grids with long power lines, so that electricity can travel from windy areas to calm ones. Old technologies help too: in “pumped hydro” systems, water is pumped uphill when electricity is [[plentiful]] and released through turbines when it is needed. Together, these tools are making a [[clean]] power system more realistic than ever before.

text: For most of the past century, keeping the lights on meant burning something – usually coal, oil or gas. The [[shift]] away from these fuels was long assumed to be expensive. That assumption has collapsed. Between 2010 and 2020, the cost of electricity from utility-scale solar fell by nearly 90 per cent and onshore wind by around 70 per cent, driven by mass production, better technology and fierce competition. In most countries, building new solar or wind capacity is now cheaper than building new fossil-fuel plants, and the two technologies account for the bulk of new power capacity installed worldwide each year.

Cheapness, however, is not the same as reliability. Electricity grids must match supply and demand second by second, and solar and wind are intermittent: output depends on the weather and the time of day. In places with a lot of solar power, such as California, engineers talk about the “duck curve” – a graph of demand on the grid that dips in the middle of the day when solar panels are producing heavily, then rises steeply in the evening as the sun sets and people come home. Meeting that evening [[surge]] has traditionally required gas plants that can be fired up quickly.

Increasingly, batteries are taking over that role. The cost of lithium-ion battery packs has dropped by roughly 90 per cent since 2010, largely thanks to the electric car industry. Grid-scale battery installations can now absorb [[surplus]] solar power in the afternoon and release it in the evening. California has added thousands of megawatts of battery storage in just a few years, and on many evenings batteries have become one of the largest single sources of power on its grid. Batteries also [[stabilise|stabilise]] the grid by responding almost instantly to sudden changes: when a coal plant in South Australia failed in 2017, a newly built battery reacted within fractions of a second.

Lithium-ion batteries, though, typically store energy for only a few hours. Coping with a windless week in winter requires other tools. Long-distance transmission lines can carry power from regions where the wind is blowing to regions where it is not. Pumped hydro storage, which moves water between two reservoirs at different heights, already provides the vast majority of the world's stored electricity. Researchers are also exploring longer-duration options, from iron-air batteries to “green” hydrogen made using renewable electricity. Demand can also become more [[flexible]], with electric cars and heat pumps programmed to charge or run when power is cheap and plentiful.

None of these solutions is perfect on its own, and building enough grid connections is proving slow. But taken together, they suggest that the old objection to renewables – that the sun sets and the wind drops – is becoming a solvable engineering problem rather than a fundamental [[barrier]].

text: Within a remarkably short span, the economics of electricity have been turned on their head. For most of the twentieth century, decarbonising the power sector was assumed to entail a heavy premium. Then the costs of renewable generation went into free fall: between 2010 and 2020 the price of electricity from utility-scale solar photovoltaics dropped by close to 90 per cent and onshore wind by around 70 per cent, propelled by economies of scale, [[incremental]] engineering improvements and intense global competition. Today, in the large majority of markets, new solar and wind capacity undercuts new coal or gas plants on cost, and the two technologies dominate the world's annual additions of generating capacity.

Low cost, however, does not [[equate|equate]] to dependability. A power grid must balance supply and demand continuously, and solar and wind output fluctuates with the weather and the hour. The challenge is neatly captured by the “duck curve” observed in California: net demand – total demand minus solar output – sags in the middle of the day and then climbs steeply at dusk, as panels fall idle just when households switch on lights, ovens and televisions. Historically, that ramp has been met by gas-fired “peaker” plants that can start within minutes.

Batteries are rapidly [[eroding|erode]] that role. Lithium-ion pack prices have fallen by roughly 90 per cent since 2010, a decline driven largely by the scale of electric vehicle manufacturing. Grid operators can now install vast battery arrays that soak up midday surplus and discharge it through the evening peak. California has deployed many thousands of megawatts of storage within a few years, and on some evenings batteries now rank among the largest single contributors to its supply. Batteries also provide services that are less visible but no less valuable: because they respond in milliseconds, they can [[cushion]] the grid against sudden faults. South Australia's Hornsdale Power Reserve demonstrated this in 2017, injecting power within fractions of a second when a coal plant unexpectedly tripped offline.

Yet the typical lithium-ion installation stores only a few hours' worth of energy, which is enough to shift solar power into the evening but not to bridge a cold, still week in winter – the period Germans evocatively call Dunkelflaute, or “dark doldrums”. Addressing such episodes requires a broader [[portfolio]]. High-voltage transmission lines can move power across hundreds or thousands of kilometres, exploiting the fact that the wind is usually blowing somewhere. Pumped hydro, which stores energy by moving water between reservoirs at different elevations, still accounts for the overwhelming share of global storage capacity. Longer-duration technologies, from iron-air batteries to hydrogen produced by electrolysis, are under development, though most remain costly. Meanwhile, “demand response” – shifting when electric cars charge or heat pumps run – can turn consumers into active participants in balancing the grid.

The obstacles that remain are increasingly institutional rather than technological. In many countries, the queue of renewable projects awaiting grid connection runs to years, permitting new transmission lines is slow and contentious, and electricity markets designed around fossil-fuel plants do not always reward flexibility. These are serious [[impediments|impediment]], but they are of a different order from the old objection that renewables simply cannot keep the lights on after dark. The question is no longer whether a predominantly renewable grid is [[feasible]], but how quickly the rules can be rewritten to build one.
