text: Seldom has an industry's cost structure been upended as swiftly as that of electricity generation. For decades, decarbonising the power sector was presumed to [[entail]] a steep premium, to be justified on environmental grounds alone. That presumption has been demolished. Between 2010 and 2020 the levelised cost of electricity from utility-scale solar photovoltaics fell by close to 90 per cent and that of onshore wind by roughly 70 per cent, a decline propelled by economies of scale, iterative engineering gains, cheaper finance and ferocious competition among manufacturers. Across most of the world, new solar and wind capacity now undercuts new fossil-fuelled plant, and together they account for the lion's share of generating capacity added each year.

Cheapness, however, is not [[synonymous]] with firmness. A grid must reconcile supply and demand from moment to moment, and the output of solar panels and wind turbines waxes and wanes with the weather and the diurnal cycle. California's “duck curve” renders the difficulty graphically: net load – demand minus solar generation – slumps through the middle of the day before rearing steeply at dusk, as output collapses precisely when households return home. That evening ramp has historically been met by gas-fired peaking plants, prized for their ability to fire up at short notice and paid handsomely for doing so.

Batteries are steadily [[usurping]] that function. The price of lithium-ion packs has dropped by around 90 per cent since 2010, a trajectory owed chiefly to the scale of electric vehicle production. Grid operators can now commission battery arrays measured in hundreds of megawatts that absorb the midday [[glut]] and discharge it into the evening peak. California has installed many thousands of megawatts of storage in a handful of years, and batteries now feature on some evenings among the largest single contributors to its supply. Their value is not confined to energy arbitrage. Because power electronics respond in milliseconds, batteries furnish so-called ancillary services – frequency regulation, synthetic inertia – that keep the grid stable after sudden disturbances. South Australia's Hornsdale Power Reserve became something of a cause célèbre in 2017 when it injected power within fractions of a second of a coal unit tripping offline, faster than the conventional plant obliged to respond.

Lithium-ion storage nevertheless has a structural limitation: most installations hold only a few hours of energy, sufficient to time-shift solar output into the night but wholly inadequate for prolonged lulls. Germans have a word for the [[bane]] of the renewable grid planner – Dunkelflaute, the “dark doldrums” of windless, overcast winter days that can persist for a week or more. Contending with such episodes calls for a diversified toolkit. High-voltage transmission can pool resources across continental distances, exploiting the statistical likelihood that the wind is blowing somewhere. Pumped hydro, which stores energy by shuttling water between reservoirs at different elevations, still accounts for the overwhelming majority of installed storage worldwide. Longer-duration chemistries such as iron-air batteries, and hydrogen produced by electrolysis and burned or converted back to power, are in development, although their costs and round-trip efficiencies remain [[sobering]]. Demand-side flexibility – vehicles that charge when power is abundant, heat pumps that pre-heat buildings – could quietly provide much of the balancing that was once the preserve of power stations.

Increasingly, the binding constraints are not physical but institutional. In many jurisdictions, renewable projects languish for years in queues for grid connection; new transmission corridors face protracted permitting battles and local opposition; and wholesale markets designed around dispatchable thermal plant often fail to remunerate the flexibility that a renewable system most needs. These are formidable obstacles, yet they belong to a different category from the old objection that the sun sets and the wind drops. That objection has been transformed from an article of faith into an engineering and regulatory agenda. The question is no longer whether a grid dominated by renewables can work, but whether institutions can be reformed quickly enough to build it before the carbon [[budget]] runs out.

text: When a kettle stops working or a zip breaks, the easiest thing is often to throw it away and buy a new one. In many cases, a new product costs less than a repair. But this habit has a price. Every year, the world throws away more than 60 million tonnes of electronic waste, and less than a quarter of it is properly collected and recycled.

In 2009, the Dutch journalist Martine Postma decided to do something about it. She organised an event in Amsterdam where people could bring broken items and get help repairing them from volunteers with practical skills. The idea [[spread]] quickly. Today there are thousands of repair cafés in dozens of countries, usually held once a month in libraries, churches or community centres.

The atmosphere is relaxed and [[sociable]]. Visitors sit next to the volunteer and take part in the repair, so they learn something they can use again. Many problems turn out to be simple – a loose wire, a blocked filter or a broken switch. Volunteers say that people often arrive [[frustrated]] and leave proud.

Repair cafés have also become part of a wider movement called the “right to repair”. [[Campaigners|campaigner]] argue that many products are designed in ways that make repair difficult: parts are glued together, special tools are needed and spare parts are expensive or [[unavailable]]. In response, some governments are acting. France now gives many electronic products a repair score from 1 to 10, so that shoppers can compare them, and the European Union has passed rules to make repairs easier and cheaper.

Fixing things will not solve all of our environmental problems. But it reduces waste, saves the energy and materials needed to make new products and helps people feel more confident and [[independent]]. As the repair café slogan says: “Toss it? No way!”

text: In much of the world, repairing things has quietly gone out of fashion. When a toaster stops working or a phone screen cracks, replacing it is often cheaper and quicker than finding someone to fix it. The environmental cost of this habit is [[considerable]]. According to the United Nations, the world generated around 62 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2022, of which less than a quarter was documented as properly collected and recycled. The rest was burned, dumped or handled informally, often in poorer countries, releasing [[toxic]] substances in the process.

In 2009, the Dutch journalist Martine Postma organised a modest experiment in Amsterdam: a space where people could bring broken household items and repair them with the help of volunteers. The format proved remarkably popular. There are now thousands of repair cafés across dozens of countries, typically held monthly in libraries, churches and community halls. Volunteer fixers – often retired engineers, electricians or tailors – sit alongside visitors, explaining what they are doing so that the owner can learn. Organisers estimate that well over half of the items brought in are successfully repaired.

Part of the appeal is social. Repair cafés bring together people of different ages and backgrounds around a shared practical task, and many visitors say they leave with new confidence as well as a working lamp. But the events have also become a focal point for a wider political campaign known as the “right to repair”. Its supporters argue that manufacturers often make repair needlessly difficult by gluing components together, using [[proprietary]] screws, restricting access to spare parts and manuals, or using software to block repairs by independent technicians.

Critics of the industry also point to “planned [[obsolescence]]” – the deliberate design of products with a limited lifespan. The best-known historical example dates from the 1920s, when leading light bulb manufacturers agreed to limit the life of their bulbs to around 1,000 hours. Today the [[accusations|accusation]] are usually less dramatic: batteries that cannot be replaced, or devices that stop receiving software updates after a few years.

Governments have begun to respond. Since 2021, France has required many electronic products to display a repairability score from 1 to 10, and in 2024 the European Union adopted rules requiring manufacturers to offer repair for certain products at a reasonable price and to make spare parts available. Some technology companies, under pressure, now sell parts and tools directly to customers.

Repair alone will not [[resolve]] the problem of waste, and some products are genuinely hard to fix. Yet the repair café movement shows how a simple, local idea can change attitudes – and, eventually, laws. As one volunteer put it, the most important thing being repaired is not the toaster, but our relationship with the objects we own.

text: Somewhere in the second half of the twentieth century, repair fell out of everyday life. As manufacturing moved to low-cost economies and products became cheaper, more complex and more tightly sealed, mending things came to seem old-fashioned, uneconomic or simply impossible. Replacing a broken kettle or a cracked phone screen is often cheaper and easier than finding someone able to fix it. The cumulative consequences are [[stark]]. The United Nations' Global E-waste Monitor estimated that 62 million tonnes of electronic waste were generated in 2022 – enough to fill a line of lorries circling the equator – and that under a quarter of it was formally collected and recycled. Much of the remainder ends up in landfill or is processed informally, frequently in low-income countries, where workers extracting valuable metals are exposed to lead, mercury and toxic fumes.

The repair café emerged as a small act of resistance to this throwaway culture. In 2009 the Dutch journalist Martine Postma staged the first event in Amsterdam, inviting residents to bring broken possessions and mend them alongside volunteers with practical expertise. The format has since spread to thousands of venues across dozens of countries. Its ethos is [[participatory]] rather than transactional: fixers – frequently retired engineers, electricians, seamstresses and bicycle mechanics – explain each step so that owners can learn, and organisers report that a majority of items leave in working order.

Beyond its environmental rationale, the repair café performs a social function that participants often value as highly as the repairs themselves. It brings together people who might otherwise never meet, [[revalues|revalue]] practical knowledge that the labour market has tended to discount, and offers a modest antidote to the sense of helplessness that many feel when confronted with sealed, [[inscrutable]] devices.

The movement has also become the grassroots face of a broader political campaign for a “right to repair”. Advocates contend that manufacturers routinely [[obstruct]] repair through design and policy: components glued rather than screwed together, proprietary fasteners, restricted access to spare parts and diagnostic tools, and “parts pairing”, whereby software refuses to recognise a replacement component unless it has been authorised by the manufacturer. Industry groups counter that such restrictions protect safety, security and intellectual property, and that unauthorised repairs can damage devices.

Suspicion of manufacturers is not without historical [[foundation]]. In the 1920s, the world's leading light bulb producers formed what became known as the Phoebus cartel, agreeing to limit bulb lifespans to around 1,000 hours and fining members whose bulbs lasted longer. Contemporary allegations of planned obsolescence tend to be subtler – non-replaceable batteries, the withdrawal of software support – and harder to prove, but they have fuelled public scepticism.

Legislators are beginning to [[intervene]]. France introduced a mandatory repairability index for many electronic products in 2021, and in 2024 the European Union adopted a directive obliging manufacturers to repair certain goods at a reasonable cost, even after the warranty has expired, and to make spare parts and information available. Several US states have passed their own right-to-repair laws. Repair alone cannot dismantle a consumption model built on rapid replacement, and some products will always be hard to mend. But the trajectory from a single Amsterdam community hall to continental legislation suggests that changing how we treat broken things may also change what manufacturers are permitted to sell.

text: Repair was once so embedded in ordinary life as to be invisible: shoes were resoled, socks darned, radios taken to the corner shop. Over the latter half of the twentieth century, that culture quietly [[atrophied|atrophy]]. As production migrated to low-wage economies, goods became cheaper, more intricate and more hermetically sealed, while the cost of skilled labour in wealthy countries rose. Mending began to look uneconomic, then quaint, then impossible. The aggregate result is now measurable in megatonnes. The UN's Global E-waste Monitor calculated that 62 million tonnes of discarded electronics were generated in 2022, of which under a quarter was formally collected and recycled. The balance is landfilled, incinerated or processed informally, frequently in low-income countries, where workers recovering copper and gold are exposed to lead, mercury and the [[noxious]] fumes of burning cable.

The repair café began as a small, almost whimsical riposte to this throwaway economy. In 2009 the Dutch journalist Martine Postma convened a gathering in Amsterdam at which residents could bring broken belongings and mend them in the company of volunteers. The model proved contagious, propagating to thousands of venues across dozens of countries. Its defining feature is that it is participatory rather than transactional: volunteer fixers – often retired engineers, electricians, tailors and bicycle mechanics – work beside owners and narrate what they are doing, so that each repair doubles as a lesson. Organisers report success rates comfortably above half, though success is measured as much in demystification as in functioning toasters.

Participants frequently describe the social dimension as the real draw. Repair cafés convene people across generations and classes around a shared, tangible problem; they restore esteem to manual knowledge that the labour market has systematically discounted; and they counter the learned helplessness induced by devices whose interiors are deliberately [[inaccessible]]. In this sense they are as much about agency as about ecology.

The movement has also furnished a grassroots constituency for the political campaign known as the “right to repair”. Its proponents catalogue the ways in which manufacturers [[impede]] repair: adhesives in place of screws, proprietary fasteners, the rationing of spare parts and schematics, and the practice of “parts pairing”, in which firmware rejects a functioning replacement component unless it carries the manufacturer's digital authorisation. Industry bodies respond that such controls safeguard users, protect intellectual property and prevent shoddy third-party repairs from tarnishing their brands – arguments that critics regard as a [[veneer]] for protecting [[lucrative]] after-sales revenue.

Scepticism about corporate motives draws on a genuine precedent. In the 1920s the world's principal light bulb manufacturers formed the Phoebus cartel, which standardised bulb life at around 1,000 hours and imposed fines on members whose products lasted longer. Today's allegations of planned obsolescence are generally subtler – sealed batteries, the premature withdrawal of software updates, designs that make a cracked back panel as costly to replace as the device itself – and correspondingly harder to substantiate. Whether such outcomes reflect deliberate strategy or merely the relentless pursuit of thinness and novelty, their effect on lifespans is much the same.

Regulators have begun to act. France introduced a compulsory repairability index for a range of electronic goods in 2021; in 2024 the European Union adopted a directive obliging manufacturers to offer repair for specified products at reasonable cost beyond the warranty period and to make parts and information available; and a growing number of US states have enacted right-to-repair statutes. None of this will by itself overturn an economic model predicated on rapid replacement, and some products will always defy repair. But the trajectory from a single Amsterdam community hall to supranational legislation is instructive. It suggests that the [[mundane]] act of fixing a kettle, multiplied across thousands of Saturday afternoons, can help reopen a question that markets had considered closed: what we are entitled to expect from the things we buy.

text: In 2012, newspapers called it “the year of the MOOC”. MOOC stands for Massive Open Online Course: a university course that anyone can take for free on the internet. Famous universities such as Harvard and Stanford put lectures online, and millions of people from every country [[enrolled|enrol]]. Many experts predicted that traditional universities would soon be out of date.

That did not happen. One reason was a surprising problem: very few people finished. Studies of courses from Harvard and MIT found that only a small [[proportion]] of people who signed up – often around five per cent – completed them. Some only wanted to watch a few videos, which is fine. But many others started with good intentions and simply gave up.

Researchers have found several reasons. Online learners must organise their own time, and it is easy to put things off when life gets busy. There is no classroom, no fixed timetable and often no teacher who knows your name. Learners also miss the [[motivation]] that comes from studying with other people.

The COVID-19 pandemic made these problems clear on a huge scale. In 2020, school closures affected around 1.6 billion students worldwide, and lessons moved onto screens almost overnight. Many teachers and pupils adapted [[impressively]], but studies later found that most students learned less than usual, and children from poorer families, who often lacked devices and quiet places to study, fell furthest behind.

Online learning has not failed, though. It works especially well for adults who are already [[motivated]], and it gives people in remote places access to excellent teaching. Today, many schools and universities use “blended learning”, combining online materials with face-to-face lessons. As one researcher put it, technology can deliver information, but it is human [[contact]] that keeps people learning.

text: When elite American universities began offering free online courses to anyone with an internet connection, the excitement was intense. The New York Times declared 2012 “the year of the MOOC” – the Massive Open Online Course – and some commentators predicted that campus-based universities would soon go the way of the typewriter. Hundreds of thousands of people signed up for single courses in subjects ranging from artificial intelligence to ancient Greek heroes.

A decade later, the [[revolution]] looks rather different. The platforms survived, but their most striking statistic turned out to be how few learners finished. Analyses of courses run by Harvard and MIT on the edX platform found that typically only around five per cent of those who enrolled earned a certificate. Defenders point out that many people never intended to complete a course; they dipped in out of curiosity. Yet even among learners who said at the start that they planned to finish, completion rates were [[disappointingly|disappointing]] low.

Researchers have identified several reasons. Self-paced online study places heavy demands on what psychologists call self-regulation: setting goals, managing time and resisting distraction without external structure. Classrooms provide that structure automatically, in the form of timetables, deadlines and the [[subtle]] pressure of being seen by teachers and [[peers|peer]]. Online learners must create it for themselves, and those who already have strong study habits – typically people with university degrees – benefit most. Ironically, a technology that was meant to make education more equal has often done most for those who were already well educated.

The COVID-19 pandemic subjected these issues to an unplanned global experiment. At the peak of school closures in 2020, UNESCO estimated that around 1.6 billion learners were affected. Teachers improvised remarkably, but research in many countries later documented substantial “learning loss”, especially in mathematics, and widening gaps between richer and poorer pupils, who were less likely to have their own devices, reliable internet or a quiet place to work.

None of this means online education has failed. For motivated adults, people in remote areas and anyone who needs flexibility, it has opened doors that were firmly closed. The more modest lesson is that technology works best as a [[complement]] to human teaching rather than a replacement. Approaches such as blended learning and the “flipped classroom”, in which students watch explanations at home and use class time for discussion and practice, try to combine the strengths of both. Education, it turns out, is not just the [[transmission]] of information, but a social activity – and that is hard to download.

text: In 2012, the future of higher education seemed to have arrived. Prestigious American universities, joined by start-ups backed by venture capital, began offering free online courses to anyone, anywhere. The New York Times christened it “the year of the MOOC”, and a chorus of commentators forecast that the lecture hall would go the way of the travel agent. Individual courses attracted enrolments in the hundreds of thousands – figures no campus could match.

The [[sequel]] proved more sobering. The platforms endured and diversified, but the most widely quoted statistic about them concerned not access but [[attrition]]. A large study of courses offered by Harvard and MIT through edX found that, across several years, only a small fraction of registrants – on the order of five per cent – went on to earn a certificate, and that this figure barely improved over time. Advocates rightly note that many participants never intended to finish; they browsed, sampled a lecture or two and left satisfied. But even among those who declared at the outset that they meant to complete a course, the majority did not.

The explanation lies largely in the demands that unstructured study places on self-regulation – the capacity to set goals, plan, monitor one's progress and persist in the face of distraction. A conventional classroom supplies much of this [[scaffolding]] externally, through timetables, deadlines, the expectations of teachers and the quiet social pressure of peers. Online, learners must construct it themselves. Those best equipped to do so tend to be people who have already succeeded in formal education. The consequence is a troubling [[paradox]]: a technology hailed as a great equaliser has disproportionately served the already advantaged, and a significant share of MOOC certificates have gone to learners who already held degrees.

The COVID-19 pandemic turned this observation into a global natural experiment. At its height in 2020, school closures affected roughly 1.6 billion learners, according to UNESCO, and education migrated to screens almost overnight. Teachers displayed considerable [[ingenuity]], yet subsequent assessments in many countries recorded significant learning losses, particularly in mathematics and among younger children, together with a widening of attainment gaps. Pupils from low-income households were less likely to have a device of their own, a stable connection or a quiet space in which to work, and many also lost access to the meals, routines and pastoral support that schools quietly provide.

It would be wrong to conclude that online learning has failed. For self-motivated adults, people in remote or underserved regions and those balancing study with work or caring responsibilities, it has [[dismantled|dismantle]] real barriers. The more defensible conclusion is that digital tools [[amplify]] existing capacities rather than create them. Models such as blended learning and the flipped classroom, in which students engage with content independently and devote contact time to discussion, problem-solving and feedback, attempt to harness the efficiency of the screen without forfeiting the relational core of teaching. That core – being known, challenged and encouraged by another person – remains remarkably resistant to automation.

text: For a few heady years, the disruption of higher education appeared imminent. In 2012, elite American universities and a clutch of venture-backed start-ups began offering free online courses to all comers, and The New York Times anointed it “the year of the MOOC”. Pundits foresaw the lecture theatre going the way of the record shop; enrolments for single courses ran into six figures, numbers no campus could hope to rival. Education, it seemed, was about to be liberated from the constraints of geography, timetable and price.

What followed was less a revolution than a [[reckoning]]. The platforms persisted and diversified, but the statistic that came to define them concerned not reach but [[retention]]. A multi-year analysis of Harvard and MIT courses on edX found that only around five per cent of registrants earned a certificate – a figure that stubbornly refused to improve. Apologists rightly observed that many participants were browsers, not dropouts, sampling a lecture and leaving content. Yet even among those who professed at the outset an intention to finish, completion remained the exception rather than the rule.

The underlying problem is that unstructured learning makes [[exacting]] demands on self-regulation: the capacity to set goals, monitor progress and sustain effort against the ceaseless allure of distraction. Conventional schooling outsources much of this to its architecture – timetables, deadlines, the gaze of a teacher, the low hum of peer comparison. Remove that scaffolding and learners must erect their own, a feat that comes most easily to those whom formal education has already equipped to perform it. The upshot is a [[perverse]] irony. A technology marketed as a great leveller has, in practice, conferred its greatest benefits on the already credentialled; a substantial share of MOOC certificates have been earned by people who held degrees before they began. This is a textbook instance of what sociologists call the Matthew effect, after the biblical line that to those who have, more shall be given.

The COVID-19 pandemic converted these findings into a planetary natural experiment. At the height of closures in 2020, UNESCO estimated that some 1.6 billion learners had been displaced from classrooms, and instruction migrated to screens with scarcely any preparation. Teachers improvised with considerable resourcefulness, yet assessments in country after country subsequently registered pronounced learning losses – steepest in mathematics and among younger pupils – and a widening of socio-economic attainment gaps. For disadvantaged children, the absence of a personal device or reliable connection was compounded by the loss of what schools provide incidentally: a hot meal, a predictable routine, a trusted adult who notices when something is wrong.

To read this history as a verdict against online learning would nonetheless be [[facile]]. For self-directed adults, for learners in remote or under-resourced regions and for those whose work or caring obligations preclude attendance, digital provision has [[demolished|demolish]] barriers that were once insurmountable. The more defensible inference is that technology acts as an amplifier: it magnifies the capacities and advantages learners already possess rather than generating them from nothing. Pedagogical models that take this seriously – blended learning, or the flipped classroom, in which students encounter content independently and devote precious contact time to discussion, problem-solving and feedback – seek to capture the screen's efficiencies without sacrificing what is irreducibly relational in teaching.

That relational core is easily [[overlooked|overlook]] precisely because it is so ordinary: being known by name, being expected to turn up, being challenged by someone whose good opinion one values. The MOOC experiment revealed, almost by accident, how much of learning depends on such unglamorous social machinery. Information has never been more abundant or more cheaply distributed. What remains scarce, and stubbornly resistant to scaling, is the attention of another human being.

text: For many years, parents told their children: “Go to university and you will get a good job.” Today, more young people go to university than ever before. But many of them are asking an important question: is it still worth it?

University can be very expensive. In some countries, like the USA and the UK, students pay high [[fees|fee]] and finish their studies with a big [[debt]]. They must pay this money back for many years.

On [[average]], people with a university degree still earn more money than people without one. But it depends on the subject and the university. Doctors and engineers usually earn a lot. Some other graduates earn about the same as people who didn't go to university.

There are other ways to start a career. In an apprenticeship, young people work for a company and learn on the job. They get paid, and they don't have a big debt. Some big companies now [[hire]] people for their skills, not for their degree.

So, is university worth it? For many people, yes – and not only for the money. Students meet new people, learn to think in new ways and become more [[independent]]. But it is a good idea to think carefully before you choose.

text: A generation ago, a university degree was seen as a reliable ticket to a good job. Today, more young people than ever go to university – in many countries, around half of all school leavers. But rising costs have made many students and parents ask whether a degree is still a good [[investment]].

The financial cost can be huge. In the United States, total student debt is now well over a trillion dollars, and many graduates spend decades paying back their [[loans|loan]]. In England, students pay more than 9,000 pounds a year in tuition fees, and most leave university owing tens of thousands of pounds.

On average, graduates still earn more than non-graduates over their working lives. However, the average hides big differences. Subjects such as medicine, economics and engineering usually lead to high [[salaries|salary]], while graduates in some other subjects earn little more than people who went straight into work. One British study estimated that around one in five graduates would have been better off, financially, if they had not gone to university at all.

Some economists also argue that employers use degrees partly as a [[signal]]. A degree shows that someone is intelligent and hard-working, even if the job doesn't use what they studied. As more people get degrees, employers ask for them for jobs that never needed them before – a trend sometimes called “degree inflation”.

Meanwhile, alternatives are growing. Apprenticeships allow young people to earn while they learn, and some large companies have [[dropped|drop]] degree requirements for certain jobs, focusing instead on skills. Still, university offers more than a salary. Graduates tend to be healthier, vote more and say they are more satisfied with their lives. The real question may not be whether university is worth it, but whether a particular course is worth it for a particular person – and that [[requires|require]] careful research.

text: For much of the late twentieth century, the case for going to university seemed self-evident. A degree opened doors to professional careers, higher earnings and social [[mobility]], and governments in many countries set ambitious targets to expand higher education. They succeeded: in much of Europe, North America and East Asia, around half of young people now [[enter|enter]] university. Yet as participation has grown, so has scepticism about whether the investment always pays off.

Cost is the most obvious concern. Outstanding student loan debt in the United States has passed 1.7 trillion dollars, more than Americans owe on their credit cards. In England, where annual tuition fees are capped at a little over 9,000 pounds, the typical graduate leaves with debts of more than 40,000 pounds, though repayments depend on income and unpaid balances are eventually written off.

The headline economic return still looks [[favourable]]. On average, graduates earn substantially more than non-graduates over a lifetime, and they are less likely to be unemployed. But averages [[conceal]] enormous variation. Research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies in the UK found that returns depend heavily on subject and institution: medicine, law and economics graduates from selective universities do extremely well, while graduates of some courses earn little more than they would have done without a degree. The same study estimated that roughly one in five graduates would have been financially better off not studying at all.

Economists also debate why graduates earn more. The traditional view is that university builds skills that employers value. An alternative “signalling” theory, developed by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Michael Spence, holds that a degree is valuable partly because it [[certifies|certify]] qualities employers find hard to observe directly – intelligence, persistence, reliability – whether or not the content of the course is relevant to the job. If signalling matters, then as degrees become more common, their value as a signal falls, and employers start demanding degrees for jobs that never needed them, a process known as credential inflation.

Some employers are now [[reversing|reverse]] that trend, removing degree requirements from job advertisements and recruiting on the basis of demonstrated skills. Apprenticeships, which combine paid work with training, are attracting renewed political interest. At the same time, university offers benefits that do not show up in salary statistics: graduates are, on average, healthier, more likely to vote and more likely to volunteer, and many value the intellectual and personal growth of those years for their own sake.

The most useful answer to the question, then, is a conditional one. University is not automatically worth it, nor is it a waste of money. Its value depends on what, where and why one studies – which makes careful, well-informed choices more important than ever.

text: For several decades, the [[proposition]] that university was a sound investment barely needed defending. A degree was the passport to professional employment, a reliable route to higher earnings and a motor of social mobility, and governments across the developed world set out to widen access accordingly. The expansion succeeded on its own terms: in many OECD countries, roughly half of each generation now enters higher education. Yet the very ubiquity of the degree has prompted a question that once seemed almost heretical – whether, for a significant minority, the investment fails to pay off.

The financial stakes have risen sharply. In the United States, outstanding student debt exceeds 1.7 trillion dollars, a sum larger than the nation's credit card debt. In England, tuition fees of over 9,000 pounds a year leave the typical graduate owing more than 40,000 pounds, although the income-contingent repayment system means that many will never repay in full, with remaining balances cancelled after several decades. Such arrangements make the true personal cost [[opaque]] to the eighteen-year-olds who incur it.

Aggregate figures continue to show a substantial graduate premium in lifetime earnings and employment. The averages, however, mask striking [[dispersion]]. Influential work by the Institute for Fiscal Studies, linking tax records to student loan data, found that returns vary enormously by subject and institution: graduates in medicine, economics and law from selective universities enjoy very large premiums, while some courses yield negligible or even negative net returns once fees and forgone earnings are taken into account. The researchers estimated that around one in five graduates would have been better off financially had they not gone to university.

Underlying this debate is a long-running disagreement about why graduates earn more in the first place. Human capital theory holds that university raises productivity by imparting knowledge and skills. The rival signalling hypothesis, associated with the Nobel laureate Michael Spence and popularised more provocatively by the economist Bryan Caplan, contends that much of the premium reflects what a degree reveals – intelligence, conscientiousness, conformity to institutional demands – rather than what it teaches. Most economists accept that both mechanisms operate, but the balance between them matters. If signalling predominates, mass expansion becomes a kind of arms race: each additional graduate [[dilutes|dilute]] the value of everyone else's qualification, and employers respond by demanding degrees for roles that previously required none.

There are signs of a [[backlash]]. A number of large employers have removed degree requirements from many vacancies in favour of skills-based hiring, and policymakers in several countries are promoting higher-level apprenticeships that combine paid employment with accredited training. Critics caution, though, that in practice hiring managers often continue to favour graduates even when the formal requirement has gone.

None of this negates the broader benefits of higher education, which [[resist|resist]] reduction to a wage premium. Graduates are, on average, healthier, more civically engaged and more likely to volunteer, and many regard the intellectual formation of those years as intrinsically valuable. The defensible conclusion is therefore neither the triumphalism of the 1990s nor the cynicism of some recent commentary, but [[discrimination|discriminate]] in the older sense of the word: the ability to distinguish between courses, institutions and personal circumstances. Whether university is worth it is, increasingly, the wrong question; which university, which course and for whom are the right ones.

text: For the better part of half a century, the virtues of a university education were treated less as a hypothesis than as an [[article of faith]]. The degree was a passport to the professions, a guarantor of higher lifetime earnings and an engine of social mobility, and governments across the developed world pursued its expansion with near-evangelical zeal. By its own lights the project has succeeded: in many OECD countries, roughly half of each cohort now proceeds to higher education. Yet the degree's very ubiquity has made respectable a question that would once have seemed faintly heretical – whether, for a sizeable minority, the venture is a poor bargain.

The financial stakes have escalated dramatically. American student debt now exceeds 1.7 trillion dollars, a figure larger than the country's aggregate credit card debt and one that has become a fixture of electoral politics. In England, annual fees of over 9,000 pounds leave the typical graduate with nominal debts in excess of 40,000 pounds, though the income-contingent repayment scheme – under which outstanding balances are eventually written off – means that the system operates less like a loan than like a graduate tax of uncertain duration. This [[convoluted]] design renders the real personal cost all but impenetrable to the school leavers who sign up for it.

In aggregate, the graduate premium remains substantial. But aggregates [[obscure]] a striking dispersion of outcomes. Landmark research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies, which linked anonymised tax records to student loan data, found that returns vary dramatically by subject and institution. Graduates in medicine, economics and law from highly selective universities command very large premiums, while certain courses yield negligible or even negative returns once tuition and forgone earnings are factored in. The authors estimated that around one in five graduates would have been financially better off had they never enrolled – a finding that has been seized upon by sceptics and contested by defenders, but not seriously refuted.

Beneath these figures lies an unresolved theoretical dispute about the source of the premium itself. Human capital theory attributes it to the skills and knowledge that higher education imparts. The signalling account, formalised by the Nobel laureate Michael Spence and pushed to its polemical limit by the economist Bryan Caplan, maintains that a large share of the premium reflects what a degree reveals – cognitive ability, conscientiousness, a willingness to conform to institutional expectations – rather than anything it actually teaches. Few economists believe either mechanism operates alone, but their relative weight has profound policy implications. Where signalling dominates, expansion degenerates into a positional arms race: each new graduate erodes the distinctiveness of everyone else's credential, employers ratchet up their requirements, and young people are obliged to spend ever more to stand still – a phenomenon variously termed credentialism or degree inflation.

There are tentative signs of a [[correction]]. Several large employers have stripped degree requirements from swathes of vacancies in favour of skills-based recruitment, and governments in a number of countries are championing degree-level apprenticeships that combine salaried work with accredited study. Early evidence, however, suggests that formal changes can be [[cosmetic]]: when requirements are dropped, hiring managers frequently continue to select graduates anyway, a reminder that credentials function as cultural shorthand as much as contractual stipulation.

To reduce the value of higher education to a wage differential would, in any case, be [[reductive]]. Graduates are, on average, healthier, more civically active and more likely to volunteer, and many regard the intellectual and personal formation of their student years as valuable in itself, irrespective of any return. The appropriate response, then, is neither the uncritical boosterism of the expansion era nor the fashionable cynicism that has succeeded it. It is [[discernment]]: a recognition that the question “Is university worth it?” admits no general answer, and that the more productive questions are which institution, which course, at what cost and for whom.

text: Many teachers admit that they only truly understood their subject when they had to teach it. Psychologists now have a name for this experience: the “protégé effect”. It describes how people learn better when they study in order to teach others, or when they actually do the teaching.

In a 2014 study at Washington University in St. Louis, students read a short passage. Half were told that they would be tested on it; the other half were told that they would have to teach it to another student. In fact, everyone took the same test – and the students who expected to teach remembered more of the main points and [[organised|organise]] the information better.

Other research suggests that actually teaching is even more powerful than just preparing to teach. When students explained a lesson to a camera, as if teaching an imaginary class, they performed better later than students who simply [[reviewed|review]] the material. Explaining forces us to find the right words, put ideas in a logical order and fill gaps in our knowledge.

The idea is not new. The Roman writer Seneca is often credited with the phrase “docendo discimus” – “by teaching, we learn”. In the 1980s, a German teacher called Jean-Pol Martin developed a method in which students take [[turns|turn]] to teach parts of the lesson to their classmates. Many schools also use peer tutoring, where older or stronger students help others. Studies show that the tutors often benefit as much as the students they help.

You don't need a classroom to use this [[technique]]. The physicist Richard Feynman was famous for explaining difficult ideas in simple language. A popular study method named after him asks you to explain a topic as if to a twelve-year-old. Wherever you [[hesitate]] or use complicated words, you have found a gap to work on. Teaching, it seems, is one of the best ways of [[discovering|discover]] what we really know.

text: Ask experienced teachers when they finally understood their subject, and many will give the same answer: the first time they had to teach it. Psychologists have given this phenomenon a name – the protégé effect – and a growing body of research suggests that it is one of the most [[reliable]] ways to deepen learning.

In a well-known 2014 experiment at Washington University in St. Louis, participants studied a passage about a historical topic. Half were told to expect a test; the others were told they would later teach the material to another student. No teaching actually took place, and everyone sat the same test. Nevertheless, those who had prepared to teach recalled more of the passage, particularly its central ideas, and their notes were better structured. The researchers concluded that simply [[anticipating|anticipate]] the role of teacher changes the way people process information: they search for the main points and organise them coherently.

Later studies suggested that the effect grows stronger when people actually teach. In experiments by Logan Fiorella and Richard Mayer, students who prepared a lesson and then explained it to a video camera outperformed students who only prepared, especially on questions that required them to apply what they had learned. Explaining aloud seems to [[expose]] gaps that silent rereading conceals. It also involves retrieval – pulling information out of memory – which is itself one of the most effective study strategies known.

Educators have long put this principle into practice. Seneca, the Roman philosopher, is traditionally credited with the phrase “docendo discimus”, by teaching we learn. In the 1980s the German teacher Jean-Pol Martin built an entire method, “Lernen durch Lehren”, around students teaching sections of lessons to their classmates. Peer tutoring schemes, in which older or more advanced pupils support others, are now common, and evaluations frequently find that the tutors gain as much as the tutees, both in understanding and in confidence.

The approach has [[limitations|limitation]]. Explaining something badly can reinforce [[misconceptions|misconception]], and the stress of teaching in front of others may distract anxious learners. Teaching also takes time that could be spent covering new material.

Still, the core insight is easy to apply on one's own. The so-called Feynman technique, named after the physicist Richard Feynman, asks learners to explain a concept in plain language, as if to a child, and to return to the source wherever their explanation becomes vague or relies on jargon. The [[underlying|underlie]] lesson is simple: understanding is not something we possess silently, but something we demonstrate when we try to make an idea clear to someone else.

text: It is a commonplace among teachers that they did not genuinely understand their subject until they had to teach it. Cognitive psychologists have given the experience a name – the protégé effect – and over the past two decades have assembled persuasive evidence that preparing to teach, and above all teaching itself, can produce deeper and more [[durable]] learning than conventional study.

A frequently cited 2014 experiment at Washington University in St. Louis illustrates the first half of that claim. Participants read a passage and were told either that they would be tested on it or that they would subsequently teach it to another student. In reality, no one taught; everyone sat the same test. Yet those anticipating a teaching role recalled more of the material, especially its most important points, and produced better-organised notes. The [[mere]] expectation of explaining something to others, it seems, prompts learners to adopt more effective strategies – prioritising key ideas and arranging them into a coherent structure – rather than passively absorbing details.

Subsequent research has suggested that the benefits [[intensify|intensify]] when the teaching is real. In studies by Logan Fiorella and Richard Mayer, students who prepared a lesson and then delivered it to a video camera outperformed those who merely prepared, with the largest gains appearing on transfer questions that required them to apply knowledge to new situations. Two mechanisms appear to be at work. One is generative processing: constructing an explanation obliges learners to connect ideas and supply missing links. The other is retrieval practice: recalling information from memory, rather than rereading it, strengthens the memory itself – one of the best-replicated findings in the science of learning.

The principle long predates the laboratory. The Roman Stoic Seneca is traditionally credited with the maxim “docendo discimus” – by teaching, we learn – and in the 1980s the German educator Jean-Pol Martin developed “Lernen durch Lehren”, a method in which pupils take responsibility for teaching portions of the curriculum to their peers. Peer tutoring programmes have since spread widely, and evaluations often find that tutors' attainment and self-confidence rise at least as much as those of the pupils they support. Researchers have even designed software “teachable agents” – virtual characters that students instruct – in order to harness the effect without requiring a human audience.

The protégé effect is not a [[panacea]]. Learners with shaky understanding may transmit and [[entrench]] their own errors; anxious students may find the social exposure of teaching counterproductive; and time spent explaining is time not spent encountering new material. Effective implementations therefore tend to [[incorporate|incorporate]] feedback from teachers and careful preparation.

For the independent learner, a simple version is readily available. The Feynman technique – named after the physicist Richard Feynman, celebrated for his gift for lucid explanation – invites students to explain a concept in plain language, as though to a novice, and to treat every point of hesitation or [[recourse]] to jargon as a signal to return to the source. Underlying all these approaches is a single idea: understanding is less a private state than a capacity revealed in the attempt to make something intelligible to someone else.

text: Few observations are more [[hackneyed]] among teachers than the confession that they only truly understood their discipline once they were obliged to teach it. Hackneyed, but apparently true. Cognitive psychologists have christened the phenomenon the protégé effect, and a substantial empirical literature now indicates that the anticipation of teaching, and still more the act itself, can yield learning that is deeper, better organised and more transferable than that produced by conventional study.

The anticipatory component was demonstrated with some elegance in a 2014 study at Washington University in St. Louis. Participants studied a prose passage under one of two pretexts: that they would be tested on it, or that they would afterwards teach it to a fellow student. The second instruction was a [[ruse]] – nobody taught, and all sat the same examination – yet those who expected to instruct others recalled more of the material, retrieved its principal ideas more readily and organised their notes more coherently. The mere prospect of an audience, it appears, induces a shift in [[orientation|orient]]: from passive absorption of detail to the active identification and ordering of what matters.

Enacting the role seems to [[compound]] the benefit. In experiments by Logan Fiorella and Richard Mayer, students who prepared a lesson and then delivered it to a video camera surpassed those who merely prepared, with the clearest advantage emerging on transfer problems requiring the application of principles to unfamiliar cases. At least two mechanisms are implicated. The first is generative processing: fashioning an explanation compels learners to articulate connections, supply implicit premises and confront inconsistencies they might otherwise have glossed over. The second is retrieval: reconstructing knowledge from memory, rather than re-encountering it on the page, consolidates that knowledge – the so-called testing effect, among the most robust and widely replicated findings in educational psychology. Notably, the teaching benefit appears [[attenuated|attenuate]] when tutors are permitted simply to read from their notes, which suggests that retrieval, not mere performance, is doing much of the work.

None of this would have surprised earlier educators. The Stoic philosopher Seneca is traditionally credited with the aphorism “docendo discimus”, and in the 1980s the German teacher Jean-Pol Martin elaborated a whole pedagogy, “Lernen durch Lehren”, in which pupils assume responsibility for teaching segments of the curriculum to their classmates. Structured peer tutoring is now widespread, and its evaluations repeatedly find that tutors' gains in attainment and self-efficacy rival or exceed those of their tutees. Researchers in educational technology have gone further, devising “teachable agents” – software characters whose apparent progress depends on what students teach them – which exploit the motivational pull of responsibility for another's learning even when the other is merely a [[simulation]].

The approach is not without hazards. A learner whose grasp is insecure may propagate and entrench misconceptions, both in themselves and in their audience; for anxious students, the exposure of performing before peers can [[swamp]] any cognitive gain; and every minute devoted to explanation is a minute withheld from new content. Successful implementations accordingly pair student teaching with expert feedback and with preparation scaffolded by the teacher.

For the solitary learner, the most portable distillation is the so-called Feynman technique, after the physicist whose lectures were renowned for their transparency: explain the idea in plain words to an imagined novice, and treat every faltering sentence or retreat into jargon as a map of one's own ignorance. The broader moral is epistemological. Understanding, on this account, is not a private possession to be inspected introspectively, but a capacity that becomes visible – to others and, crucially, to ourselves – only when we attempt to render an idea intelligible to someone who does not yet share it.

text: Many people think that learning is only for children. They say, “I'm too old to learn a new language” or “I can't learn the piano at fifty.” But scientists say this is not [[true]].

Our brains can change all our lives. When we learn something new, the brain makes new [[connections|connection]]. Scientists once studied people who learned to juggle with three balls. After three months, some parts of their brains were bigger.
Taxi drivers in London have to learn thousands of streets. This takes years. Scientists found that a part of their brain that helps with memory was bigger than in other people.

Learning is also good for older people. In one study, people over sixty learned new skills like digital photography. After a few months, their memory was better. Learning keeps the brain [[active]] and healthy.

Of course, learning can be slower when we are older. But older people also have a big [[advantage]]: they know a lot about the world. So, it is never too late to start. Choose something you love and [[practise]] a little every day.

text: “You can't teach an old dog new tricks,” goes the English saying. For a long time, scientists believed something similar about people: that the adult brain was fixed, and that serious learning belonged to childhood. Research over the last thirty years has shown that this is far from the whole story.

The brain's ability to change is called neuroplasticity. Every time we practise a skill, connections between brain cells become stronger. In a famous study, adults who learned to juggle showed growth in brain areas involved in movement after just three months of practice. When they stopped juggling, the changes became smaller again – a clear case of “use it or lose it”.

One of the most [[striking]] examples comes from London. To get a [[licence]], the city's black-cab drivers must [[memorise]] around 25,000 streets – a test known simply as “the Knowledge”, which usually takes three to four years to pass. Brain scans showed that experienced drivers had a larger hippocampus, an area important for memory and [[navigation]], than people who didn't drive taxis.

Age does bring some changes. Older adults usually process new information more slowly, and memorising lists becomes harder. But other abilities, such as vocabulary and general knowledge, often keep improving until our sixties or later. Older learners can also use their experience to [[link]] new information to what they already know.

Learning may even protect the brain. In one American study, people over sixty who spent several months learning demanding new skills, such as digital photography or quilting, showed better memory afterwards than those who did easier activities. Today, organisations like the University of the Third Age, which began in France in the 1970s, offer courses for retired people around the world. The message is clear: it is never too late to learn, and the [[effort]] itself is good for us.

text: For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists assumed that the adult brain was essentially fixed: the [[wiring]] laid down in childhood stayed in place, and the only change after early adulthood was gradual decline. The assumption gave scientific weight to a popular belief – that learning is for the young, and that anyone over forty who takes up the violin or a new language is attempting the impossible. Both ideas have been substantially [[revised|revise]].

The key concept is neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganise itself in response to experience. Learning strengthens the connections between neurons that fire together, and repeated practice can even produce visible changes in brain structure. In a 2004 study, adults who spent three months learning to juggle showed an increase in grey matter in regions that process visual motion; when they stopped practising, the gains partly [[reversed|reverse]].

Perhaps the most celebrated evidence comes from London's taxi drivers. To earn a licence, they must master “the Knowledge” – the layout of around 25,000 streets and thousands of [[landmarks|landmark]] – a process that typically takes three to four years. Brain imaging by Eleanor Maguire and colleagues found that experienced drivers had a larger posterior hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, than comparable non-drivers, and that its size increased with years spent in the job. A follow-up study tracked trainees over time and found that those who passed the test showed growth in this region, while those who failed did not.

Ageing does change how we learn, though not always in the ways people fear. Psychologists distinguish between “fluid” intelligence – the speed and flexibility of reasoning with new information – which tends to peak in early adulthood, and “crystallised” intelligence – accumulated knowledge and vocabulary – which often continues to rise into the sixties and beyond. Older learners may need more [[repetition]], but they can draw on a far richer network of existing knowledge to make sense of new material.

There is also growing evidence that sustained learning benefits the ageing brain. In a study led by Denise Park in Texas, older adults who spent around fifteen hours a week for three months learning cognitively demanding skills such as digital photography or quilting improved their memory more than those who took part in social or undemanding activities. Such findings help explain the popularity of initiatives like the University of the Third Age, founded in France in 1973, which now offers courses for retired people around the world.
Learning later in life is rarely effortless. But the evidence suggests that the effort is precisely the point: challenge, not comfort, is what keeps an [[ageing]] brain adaptable.

text: For much of the twentieth century, the scientific consensus held that the adult brain was largely hard-wired. Neural circuits were thought to be laid down in childhood and adolescence, after which the only significant trajectory was one of gradual attrition. This view lent [[credibility]] to a pervasive cultural assumption – that genuine learning is the preserve of the young, and that a fifty-year-old attempting Mandarin or the cello is engaged in a [[quixotic]] enterprise. Both the science and the assumption have since been substantially overturned.

Central to this shift is neuroplasticity: the brain's capacity to restructure itself in response to experience. Synaptic connections that are repeatedly activated become stronger, and sustained practice can produce changes [[discernible|discern]] in brain scans. In a widely cited 2004 study, adults who learned to juggle over three months exhibited increased grey matter in regions specialised for processing visual motion; when practice ceased, the increase partially receded, a vivid illustration of the principle that neural resources follow use.

The most celebrated demonstration, however, involves London's licensed taxi drivers, who must master “the Knowledge” – some 25,000 streets and thousands of points of interest – before they can work. Studies led by the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire found that qualified drivers had a larger posterior hippocampus than matched controls, and that its volume correlated with years of experience. Crucially, a later [[longitudinal]] study followed trainees through the gruelling three- to four-year process: those who qualified showed hippocampal growth, whereas those who dropped out or failed did not. Because the changes emerged during training rather than preceding it, the finding offered unusually strong evidence that learning itself reshaped the adult brain.

Ageing undoubtedly alters cognition, but less [[uniformly]] than popular pessimism suggests. Psychologists distinguish fluid intelligence – the capacity to reason quickly and flexibly with novel information – from crystallised intelligence, the store of knowledge, vocabulary and expertise built up over a lifetime. Fluid abilities tend to peak in early adulthood and decline thereafter; crystallised abilities often continue to grow into the sixties and seventies. Older learners may therefore require more repetition and time, yet they possess a dense network of prior knowledge onto which new information can be [[anchored|anchor]], an advantage that partly compensates for slower processing.

Evidence is also accumulating that cognitively demanding learning confers protective benefits in later life. In the Synapse Project, led by Denise Park at the University of Texas at Dallas, older adults who spent around fifteen hours a week for three months acquiring challenging skills such as digital photography or quilting showed greater improvements in episodic memory than those assigned to socially engaging but undemanding activities. The researchers emphasised that comfort was not enough: the benefits appeared to depend on sustained mental challenge. Related work suggests that lifelong bilingualism and higher educational attainment may help build “cognitive reserve”, delaying the onset of dementia symptoms, though the strength of these effects remains debated.

Such findings help explain the growth of institutions dedicated to later-life learning, from the University of the Third Age, founded in Toulouse in 1973, to the flourishing market in online courses taken by retirees. The broader lesson is not that learning in later life is easy – it is often [[arduous]] – but that the difficulty is itself the active ingredient. The brain, it turns out, remains responsive to demand for as long as we are prepared to make demands of it.

text: For the greater part of the twentieth century, neuroscience lent its authority to a melancholy doctrine: that the adult brain is, in essence, a finished artefact. Its circuitry was held to be fixed by the end of adolescence, after which the only trajectory worth charting was one of slow and [[inexorable]] decline. The doctrine dovetailed neatly with folk wisdom – that the acquisition of a language, an instrument or a demanding discipline is a privilege of youth, and that the middle-aged novice is engaged in something between the admirable and the absurd. Few scientific orthodoxies have been dismantled as thoroughly.

The concept that undid it is neuroplasticity: the brain's capacity to remodel its structure and function in response to experience. Synapses that are repeatedly co-activated are strengthened, unused connections are [[pruned|prune]], and sustained practice can induce structural changes visible on imaging. In a frequently cited 2004 experiment, adults who learned a three-ball juggling routine over three months displayed a transient expansion of grey matter in cortical areas specialised for the perception of visual motion; when they abandoned practice, the expansion partially regressed – a [[graphic]] confirmation that the brain allocates resources according to demand.

The most compelling case, though, comes from the cab ranks of London. Prospective drivers of the city's licensed taxis must commit to memory “the Knowledge”: some 25,000 streets and thousands of landmarks, an ordeal that typically consumes three to four years. Eleanor Maguire and colleagues found that qualified drivers possessed a larger posterior hippocampus – a structure central to spatial navigation – than matched controls, and that its volume scaled with years behind the wheel. Cross-sectional data of this kind leave open the possibility that people with larger hippocampi are simply drawn to the profession. A subsequent longitudinal study therefore followed trainees from enrolment to outcome. Those who qualified exhibited hippocampal growth over the period of training; those who withdrew or failed did not. Because the change post-dated the learning rather than [[antedating|antedate]] it, the inference that sustained study had reshaped the adult brain was unusually secure.

Ageing does transform cognition, but more selectively than fatalism allows. Psychologists distinguish fluid intelligence – the capacity to reason rapidly and flexibly about unfamiliar problems – from crystallised intelligence, the [[repository]] of knowledge, vocabulary and expertise accrued over a lifetime. The former tends to crest in early adulthood and ebb thereafter; the latter frequently continues to rise well into the seventh decade. The older learner may thus need more time and repetition, but enjoys the compensating advantage of a dense semantic network into which new information can be woven – which is why adults often outperform children in the early stages of learning a second language, even if children eventually achieve a more native-like accent.

There is, moreover, mounting evidence that effortful learning confers protection in later life. In the Synapse Project at the University of Texas at Dallas, Denise Park and colleagues assigned older adults to spend around fifteen hours a week, for three months, mastering cognitively taxing skills such as digital photography or quilting. Compared with peers who undertook sociable but undemanding activities, they showed significantly greater gains in episodic memory. The crucial variable appeared to be not engagement as such but sustained challenge. Related research suggests that lifelong bilingualism and extended education may help build “cognitive reserve”, enabling the brain to tolerate pathology for longer before symptoms of dementia emerge – though the size, and in some studies the very existence, of these effects remains [[contested]].

Institutional life has begun to catch up with the science. The University of the Third Age, founded in Toulouse in 1973, now has branches on several continents, and older adults constitute a growing share of the market for online courses. The deeper lesson, however, is not that late learning is easy. It is frequently arduous, and the frustrations of slower recall are real. It is rather that the [[arduousness]] is the mechanism. The adult brain appears to remain plastic for as long as we continue to present it with problems it cannot yet solve.

text: In 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon. Over the next three years, twelve astronauts walked there. Then, in 1972, the visits stopped. Nobody has walked on the Moon since then.

Now many countries want to go back. The USA has a [[plan]] called Artemis. It wants to send astronauts around the Moon and then land near its south pole. China and India have also sent robots to the Moon, and China wants to send people there too.

Why the south pole? Scientists think there is ice there, in deep, dark craters where the sun never shines. Ice is very [[useful]]. Astronauts can drink it as water. They can also make air and rocket fuel from it.
Some people want to build a [[base]] on the Moon where astronauts can live and work for months. The Moon could also be a first step on the way to Mars.
But going to the Moon is very expensive and [[dangerous]]. Some people say we should spend the money on problems here on Earth. Others say that space science helps us all. What do you [[think]]?

text: In December 1972, the astronauts of Apollo 17 left the Moon and returned to Earth. Nobody knew it then, but they would be the last people to walk on its surface for more than half a century. After the excitement of the space race, the costs seemed too high and public [[interest]] faded.

Today, the Moon is popular again. NASA's Artemis programme aims to send astronauts around the Moon and then land them near its south pole, working with space agencies from Europe, Japan and Canada and with private companies. China has landed several robotic missions, including the first ever landing on the far side of the Moon in 2019, and plans to send its own astronauts. In 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 became the first mission to land near the lunar south pole.

Why the south pole? Some craters there are in permanent shadow, so temperatures stay extremely low, and scientists have found evidence that they contain water ice. This could be [[extremely]] valuable. Water is heavy and expensive to [[launch]] from Earth, but on the Moon it could be used for drinking, split into oxygen for breathing, or turned into rocket fuel.

Supporters see the Moon as a kind of training ground. Learning to live there for weeks or months would help prepare for much longer journeys to Mars. The Moon is also a [[unique]] place for science: its rocks keep a record of the early solar system that has been erased on Earth.

There are also less [[comfortable]] reasons. Countries see the Moon as a matter of national pride and influence, and some worry that a new race could lead to [[disputes|dispute]] over the best landing sites. An international treaty from 1967 says that no country can own the Moon, but it was written long before anyone imagined mining it. Returning to the Moon, it seems, raises questions not only for engineers but also for lawyers and politicians.

text: When Apollo 17 lifted off from the lunar surface in December 1972, its crew could hardly have imagined that more than fifty years would pass before anyone followed them. The Apollo programme had achieved its political goal – beating the Soviet Union – and with that rivalry won, the enormous cost of crewed lunar missions became hard to justify. Attention shifted to space stations, robotic probes and the Space Shuttle.

Half a century on, the Moon is once again a destination of choice. NASA's Artemis programme, named after Apollo's twin sister in Greek mythology, is designed to return astronauts to the Moon and eventually establish a [[sustained]] presence there, in partnership with European, Japanese and Canadian space agencies and a growing number of commercial firms. China, meanwhile, has carried out a string of successful robotic missions – including the first landing on the far side in 2019 and the first return of samples from it in 2024 – and has announced plans to land its own astronauts. India joined the club in 2023, when Chandrayaan-3 touched down near the south pole.

That region is the main prize. Because the Moon's axis is only slightly tilted, the floors of some polar craters have not seen sunlight for billions of years and are among the coldest places in the solar system. Orbiting spacecraft have detected signs of water ice trapped in this permanent darkness. If it can be extracted, it would be [[transformative]]: launching a single litre of water from Earth costs thousands of dollars, but ice on the Moon could supply drinking water, oxygen and hydrogen for rocket propellant. Some describe the Moon as a potential “gas station” for deeper space travel.

Scientists also value the Moon for its own sake. Because it lacks the plate tectonics, weather and life that constantly reshape Earth's surface, its rocks preserve a record of the violent early history of the solar system, including the bombardment of the inner planets by asteroids. Samples from new regions could help [[resolve]] long-standing questions about how the Earth-Moon system formed.

Not all of the motives are scientific. Lunar exploration remains a powerful symbol of national [[prestige]], and the renewed activity has an unmistakable geopolitical edge. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty forbids any nation from claiming sovereignty over the Moon, but it says little about extracting resources. The US-led Artemis Accords, signed by dozens of countries since 2020, set out principles for activities such as mining and “safety zones” around landing sites; China and Russia have not joined, and critics fear the rules could [[amount|amount]] to a first-come, first-served claim on the best polar territory.
The return to the Moon, then, is about more than footprints. It is a test of whether humanity can turn a place of exploration into a place of work – and whether it can do so [[cooperatively]].

text: When the crew of Apollo 17 left the lunar surface in December 1972, few would have predicted that the next human footprints there would be more than half a century in coming. Yet the [[logic]] of the Apollo era was always more political than scientific. Once the United States had won the race against the Soviet Union, the staggering expense of crewed lunar missions – at its peak, Apollo consumed more than four per cent of the federal budget – became politically indefensible, and human spaceflight retreated to low Earth orbit.

The Moon is now the focus of a second, more crowded race. NASA's Artemis programme seeks not merely to revisit the Moon but to establish a lasting human presence there, in collaboration with the European, Japanese and Canadian space agencies and a growing roster of commercial partners who build landers and launch vehicles under contract. China has assembled an impressive record of robotic missions, becoming the first nation to land on the lunar far side in 2019 and to return samples from it in 2024, and has set out plans to land its own astronauts. India, Japan and several private companies have also reached the surface, with varying degrees of success.

Most of these efforts converge on the south polar region, and for good reason. Because the Moon's rotational axis is tilted by little more than one and a half degrees, the floors of certain deep craters lie in perpetual shadow, with temperatures plunging below minus 200 °C. Remote-sensing data indicate that these “cold traps” harbour water ice, delivered over billions of years by comets and solar wind. The economic logic is [[compelling]]. Lifting a single kilogram of payload from Earth to the lunar surface costs a great deal, and water is heavy; ice extracted [[in situ]] could provide drinking water, breathable oxygen and hydrogen and oxygen for rocket propellant, potentially turning the Moon into a refuelling depot for missions to Mars and beyond.

The scientific [[rationale]] is no less [[substantial]]. Lacking active plate tectonics, an atmosphere and liquid water, the Moon has preserved a record of the early solar system that Earth's restless surface has erased. Lunar rocks carry evidence of the intense asteroid bombardment that may have shaped the conditions for life on Earth, and samples from previously unexplored regions could test competing theories of how the Moon itself formed – most likely, according to the prevailing view, from debris thrown off when a Mars-sized body collided with the young Earth.

The return to the Moon is also, unmistakably, a geopolitical contest. National prestige, technological leadership and access to resources are all at stake. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits any state from claiming sovereignty over celestial bodies, but it is [[ambiguous]] on the question of extracting and owning resources. The US-led Artemis Accords, signed by dozens of states since 2020, assert that resource extraction does not in itself constitute a territorial claim and propose “safety zones” around operations. China and Russia, pursuing a rival International Lunar Research Station, have not signed, and critics warn that safety zones around scarce ice-bearing craters could [[harden|harden]] into de facto ownership.

Whether the new lunar age proves sustainable will depend as much on diplomacy as on engineering. The Moon offers a rare opportunity to establish rules for a new frontier before conflicts arise rather than after – an opportunity humanity has not always taken on Earth.
