text: When Apollo 17's ascent stage lifted off from the Taurus-Littrow valley in December 1972, its commander remarked that humanity would return “not too long into the future”. The prediction proved spectacularly wrong. The Apollo programme had always been driven less by curiosity than by Cold War rivalry, and once the Soviet Union had been beaten to the surface, the political case for an undertaking that at its height absorbed over four per cent of the US federal budget [[evaporated|evaporate]]. Human spaceflight withdrew to low Earth orbit, and the Moon lapsed into a half-century of neglect broken only by robotic visitors.

That neglect has ended with something approaching a scramble. NASA's Artemis programme – named for Apollo's twin sister – aspires not to a repeat of flags and footprints but to an enduring human foothold, pursued in concert with European, Japanese and Canadian partners and a constellation of commercial contractors supplying landers and launch vehicles. China, proceeding with methodical incrementalism, has achieved the first soft landing on the lunar far side and the first return of far-side samples, and has committed to landing astronauts of its own. India, Japan and several private ventures have also reached the surface, though the litter of crashed landers attests that the Moon remains [[unforgiving]].

Nearly all of this activity converges on the lunar south pole. Because the Moon's spin axis is inclined by barely one and a half degrees, the floors of certain deep craters have languished in shadow for billions of years, attaining temperatures among the lowest measured anywhere in the solar system. Orbital spectroscopy indicates that these cold traps sequester water ice, deposited by cometary impacts and generated by the interaction of the solar wind with lunar soil. Its potential value is hard to overstate. Delivering mass from Earth to the lunar surface is ruinously expensive, and water is among the heaviest of necessities; ice exploited in situ could furnish potable water, breathable oxygen and the hydrogen and oxygen that make up rocket propellant. Enthusiasts envisage a [[cislunar]] economy in which the Moon serves as a fuel depot for voyages to Mars and beyond – though sceptics observe that no one has yet demonstrated that the ice is concentrated enough to be worth mining.

The scientific case stands on its own merits. Bereft of plate tectonics, atmosphere and liquid water, the Moon is a museum of the early solar system whose terrestrial counterpart has long since been recycled by geology. Its cratered surface records the bombardment of the inner planets, and samples from unvisited terrains could adjudicate between rival accounts of the Moon's own origin – most plausibly, in the prevailing giant-impact hypothesis, an [[aggregation|aggregate]] of debris flung out when a Mars-sized protoplanet struck the infant Earth.

Yet to present the return to the Moon purely in terms of science or economics would be disingenuous. It is also a contest for prestige, technological primacy and, potentially, territory. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty forbids national appropriation of celestial bodies, but it is notoriously [[reticent]] about the ownership of extracted resources – a lacuna that seemed academic when no one could reach them. The US-led Artemis Accords, adopted since 2020 by dozens of states, assert that extraction does not amount to appropriation and introduce “safety zones” around lunar operations. China and Russia, developing a rival International Lunar Research Station, have declined to sign. Because the ice-bearing craters are few and small, critics fear that a regime of safety zones could [[ossify|ossify]] into a de facto partition of the most valuable terrain among those who arrive first.

The lunar revival thus poses a question larger than any engineering challenge: whether humanity can devise workable rules for a new frontier before rather than after the competition for it turns [[acrimonious]]. On Earth, the historical precedents are not encouraging. On the Moon, for perhaps the first time, there is still time to do better.

text: Every cell in your body has DNA. DNA is like a book of [[instructions|instruction]]. It tells your body how to grow and work. Half of your DNA comes from your mother and half from your father.

Twenty-five years ago, reading all of a person's DNA took many years and cost billions of dollars. Today it is much faster and cheaper. You can buy a DNA test online, send a little spit in a tube and get the [[results|result]] a few weeks later.
Millions of people have done these tests. Some want to know where their family came from hundreds of years ago. Others want to know if they have a higher [[risk]] of some illnesses.
Sometimes the results are a big [[surprise]]. Some people find brothers or sisters they never knew about. Others find out that their father is not their real father.

DNA tests can be useful, but we should be careful. Your DNA is very [[private]] information, and it also says things about your family. And remember: your genes are not your future. How you live – what you eat, how much you move – is very important too.

text: The first complete reading of the human genome – the full set of DNA instructions inside our cells – was finished in 2003. The project took thirteen years and cost about three billion dollars. Today, a person's whole genome can be read in a day or two for a few hundred dollars, and simpler DNA tests are sold online for less than the price of a pair of trainers.

More than thirty million people have now sent a [[sample]] of saliva to a testing company. Many are curious about their [[ancestry]]: the tests compare their DNA with that of people around the world and estimate where their ancestors came from. Others want health information, such as whether they carry genes linked to certain diseases.

The results can change lives. Some people discover [[relatives|relative]] they never knew existed, including brothers and sisters. Others learn that the man who raised them is not their biological father, or that they were conceived with a donor's sperm. These discoveries can be [[painful]], and many families are not prepared for them.

Health results also need careful [[interpretation]]. A few genes, such as BRCA1, greatly increase the risk of certain cancers, and knowing about them can save lives. But for most common diseases, hundreds of genes each have a tiny effect, and lifestyle matters as much as biology. A “higher risk” may mean a change from 10 per cent to 12 per cent – not a [[prediction]] of illness.

Privacy is another concern. Your DNA reveals information not only about you but also about your relatives, who never agreed to be tested. In 2018, American police identified a murderer from the 1970s and 1980s by finding his distant cousins in a public DNA database. Many people were glad the case was solved, but others worried about how genetic data might be used in the future. Before you spit in a tube, experts say, it is worth reading the small print.

text: When scientists announced in 2003 that they had completed the first full sequence of the human genome, the achievement was compared to the Moon landing. The Human Genome Project had taken thirteen years, involved laboratories on several continents and cost around three billion dollars. Two decades later, a complete genome can be sequenced in a day or two for a few hundred dollars, and cheaper consumer tests that read selected parts of our DNA are sold online and in pharmacies.

The [[appeal]] is easy to understand. Over thirty million people worldwide have mailed saliva samples to direct-to-consumer companies, hoping to learn about their ancestry, their health or simply themselves. Ancestry reports compare a customer's DNA with reference groups from around the world and produce a breakdown of their origins – “28% Scandinavian, 15% West African” – although these percentages are estimates that can change as databases grow.

Less [[anticipated|anticipate]] have been the family revelations. Matching services, which connect customers who share DNA, have reunited adopted people with birth parents and revealed half-siblings scattered across continents. They have also exposed secrets that families had kept for decades: unknown donor conception, adoptions never mentioned, fathers who were not the biological parent. Genetic counsellors report that many customers are emotionally unprepared for such discoveries, which cannot be undone once seen.

Health reports raise different issues. Some genetic [[variants|variant]] carry a high risk – mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, for instance, substantially increase the likelihood of breast and ovarian cancer – and identifying them can lead to life-saving screening. But most common conditions, from heart disease to type 2 diabetes, are influenced by hundreds or thousands of variants, each with a tiny effect, as well as by diet, exercise and environment. Consumer tests may also check only some known mutations, so a [[reassuring]] result can create false confidence. Doctors therefore warn against treating such reports as a diagnosis.

Finally, there is privacy. DNA is uniquely [[revealing]]: it cannot be changed like a password, and it contains information about relatives who never [[consented|consent]] to testing. In 2018, investigators in California identified a suspect in a series of murders from the 1970s and 1980s by uploading crime-scene DNA to a public genealogy website and tracing distant cousins. The arrest was widely welcomed, but it showed that the decision of one person to share their genome can affect an entire family tree. Questions about what happens to genetic data if a testing company is sold or goes bankrupt have only become more urgent.
Reading the book of life has become cheap and easy. Understanding what it says – and deciding who else should be allowed to read it – remains far more difficult.

text: When the completion of the Human Genome Project was announced in 2003, it was hailed as one of the great scientific achievements of the age – the first full reading of the roughly three billion chemical letters that make up human DNA. The effort had spanned thirteen years and cost in the region of three billion dollars. The [[subsequent]] collapse in costs has been even more remarkable than the original feat: a complete genome can now be sequenced in a day or two for a few hundred dollars, while consumer tests that sample selected sites in the genome cost less than a meal out.

Direct-to-consumer genetic testing has accordingly become a mass market. More than thirty million people have posted saliva samples to companies promising insights into their origins, their health and even their taste in coffee. Ancestry estimates, which compare a customer's DNA with reference populations, have proved especially popular, though they are probabilistic [[approximations|approximation]] that depend heavily on which populations happen to be well represented in a company's database – a limitation that has led some customers of non-European descent to receive vaguer results.

The most consequential effects, however, have been familial. By connecting customers who share segments of DNA, matching services have dissolved the anonymity on which many twentieth-century practices relied. Adopted people have found birth parents; donor-conceived adults have identified biological fathers – and, in some cases, dozens of half-siblings fathered by the same [[prolific]] donor. Long-buried family secrets have surfaced with brutal suddenness. Genetic counsellors note that such revelations are irreversible and that the terms and conditions customers click through rarely prepare them for the possibility.

Health reports demand particular caution. For a minority of conditions, single genetic variants are highly predictive: harmful mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2, for example, sharply elevate the lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer, and their detection can prompt potentially life-saving surveillance or surgery. But most common diseases are polygenic, shaped by the cumulative effect of many variants of individually [[negligible]] influence, interacting with diet, activity and environment. “Polygenic risk scores” that attempt to aggregate these effects can shift probabilities only modestly, and their accuracy is markedly lower for people whose ancestry is under-represented in research. Moreover, a consumer test that screens for only a few known mutations may return a falsely reassuring result. Clinicians therefore stress that such reports are not diagnoses and that genes describe tendencies, not destinies.

Privacy concerns are [[compounded|compound]] by the peculiar nature of genetic information. Unlike a password, a genome cannot be reset, and it is inherently shared: it reveals information about parents, siblings and children who have consented to nothing. This was vividly demonstrated in 2018, when Californian investigators identified a suspect in a decades-old series of murders by uploading crime-scene DNA to a public genealogy database and constructing family trees from the distant relatives it matched. Many applauded the result; civil liberties groups warned of a de facto genetic [[surveillance]] network built from the voluntary choices of hobbyists. The financial difficulties of a major testing company in recent years have added a further question – what becomes of millions of genomes if the firm that holds them is sold.
The cost of reading the book of life has fallen by a factor of millions. The [[capacity]] to interpret it wisely, and the rules governing who may read it, have not kept pace.

text: The announcement in 2003 that the Human Genome Project had completed its task was greeted with a rhetoric usually reserved for moon landings. Researchers on several continents had laboured for thirteen years, at a cost of roughly three billion dollars, to [[transcribe]] the three billion or so chemical letters that compose the human genetic code. What followed was a collapse in cost so precipitous that it outstripped even the famous exponential gains of computing: a complete human genome can now be sequenced in a day or two for a few hundred dollars, and consumer tests that sample hundreds of thousands of selected sites retail for less than a restaurant meal.

Direct-to-consumer genomics has duly become a mass phenomenon. Upwards of thirty million people have dispatched vials of saliva to companies promising insight into their ancestry, their health and assorted trivia. Ancestry composition reports, which apportion a customer's genome among reference populations, have proved especially seductive, yet they are probabilistic constructs whose resolution depends on the populations a company has chosen – or been able – to sample. The predominance of people of European descent in many databases has left customers from elsewhere with conspicuously coarser results, an asymmetry that [[replicates|replicate]] older inequities in genetic research.

The most profound consequences, however, have been genealogical. By linking customers who share stretches of DNA, matching services have dismantled the anonymity on which much twentieth-century family practice depended. Adoptees have traced birth parents; donor-conceived adults have identified biological fathers and, in some cases, scores of half-siblings sired by a single prolific donor. Secrets maintained for generations have surfaced in an email notification. Genetic counsellors emphasise that such knowledge is [[irrevocable]] and that the click-through consent customers provide seldom equips them for what they may learn – not least because the people most affected, the relatives on the other end of the match, never consented to anything.

Health information warrants still greater circumspection. For a small number of conditions, single variants carry substantial [[penetrance]]: pathogenic mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 dramatically elevate the lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer, and their detection can justify intensive screening or preventive surgery. Most common diseases, though, are polygenic, arising from the aggregate of innumerable variants of minute individual effect acting in concert with diet, activity and circumstance. Polygenic risk scores that attempt to summarise this complexity offer, at best, modest shifts in probability, and their predictive power deteriorates sharply for people whose ancestry is poorly represented in the underlying studies. A consumer test that interrogates only a handful of known mutations may moreover yield a [[spuriously|spurious]] reassuring result. Hence the insistence of clinicians that such reports are not diagnoses, and that the genome speaks in the language of propensity rather than prophecy.

The privacy questions are sharpened by the peculiar ontology of genetic data. A genome cannot be revoked or reissued, and it is irreducibly collective: to disclose one's own is to disclose fragments of one's parents', siblings' and children's. The point was made with unusual force in 2018, when Californian investigators identified the suspect in a long-unsolved series of murders by uploading crime-scene DNA to a public genealogy website and reconstructing family trees from distant relatives. Public reaction was largely approving; civil liberties advocates, by contrast, discerned the [[contours|contour]] of a surveillance infrastructure assembled not by the state but by the aggregated curiosity of hobbyists. More recently, the financial travails of a prominent testing company prompted anxious questions about the fate of millions of genomes in the event of a sale – questions to which existing law in many jurisdictions offers only partial answers.

The book of life can now be read for the price of a pair of shoes. Our ability to construe it [[judiciously]], and our consensus about who else may turn its pages, lag far behind. Literacy, in this domain as in others, turns out to be the easy part.

A2.title: Why Don't We Remember Being Babies?
A2.sub: We learn so much in our first years. So why do we forget all of it?
text: What is your [[earliest]] memory? Most people remember things from when they were three or four years old. They do not remember anything from before that. Scientists call this "childhood amnesia".

This is strange, because babies learn a lot. They learn to walk, they learn the sounds of a language, and they know their parents' voices. So a lot happens to them, but later the memories [[disappear]].

Are babies able to remember things? An [[experiment]] says yes. Scientists put a toy above a baby's bed. When the baby kicked its legs, the toy moved. A few days later, many babies still kicked their legs. They remembered!
One [[explanation]] is about the brain. A small part of the brain keeps our memories. In babies, this part grows very fast, and new cells may push old memories out.
Another explanation is language. When children can [[describe]] something with words, they can tell it as a story. Stories are easy to remember. Babies do not have these words yet.
[[Culture]] is important too. Some families talk a lot about the past: "What did you do today? How did you feel?" Children in these families often have earlier first memories.
So we forget our first years, but they are still [[important]]. They give us our first [[skills]] and help us become the people we are.

B1.title: Why Can't We Remember Being Babies?
B1.sub: Our first years are full of learning, but almost none of it stays in our memory. Scientists have some ideas why.
text: Think about your earliest memory. For most adults, it comes from around the age of three or four, and it is usually just a [[fragment]]: a smell, a colour, a sound. Everything before that has gone. Psychologists call this "childhood amnesia", and it happens to almost everyone.

The strange thing is that babies have lots of experiences. In the first years of life the brain grows faster than at any other time. Babies learn to walk, [[recognise]] their parents and understand a language. So why do these years [[vanish]] from our memory?

For a long time, scientists [[assumed]] that babies could not make memories at all. But experiments show that this is wrong. In one famous study, three-month-old babies learned that kicking their legs made a toy above their bed move. Several days later, many of them still remembered the trick.

One explanation is about the hippocampus, a small part of the brain which is [[essential]] for storing memories of our own life. In young children it is still growing quickly, and new brain cells are added all the time. Studies with mice suggest that this growth may [[damage]] old memories, so they are slowly replaced.

Language may also be part of the answer. When children can put an event into words, they can turn it into a story, and stories are easier to keep. In one study, children talked about a game months later, but they only used words they had known at the time of the game.
Families and [[culture]] matter too. Children whose parents often talk with them about the past – what happened and how they felt – tend to have earlier first memories.
So our first years are not wasted. We may forget the events, but they [[shape]] our skills, our feelings and the way we get on with other people.

B2.title: Why Can't We Remember Being Babies?
B2.sub: Your first three years shaped who you are, yet almost none of them stayed with you. Scientists are beginning to understand why.
text: Try to recall your earliest memory. For most adults it dates from somewhere around the age of three or four, and it is usually a [[fragment]] rather than a story: the smell of a kitchen, a red coat, the shock of a dog's bark. Everything before that has simply [[vanished]]. Psychologists call this gap "childhood amnesia", and it is so common that we rarely stop to wonder why it exists.

The puzzle is that babies are hardly short of experiences. In the first years of life the brain grows faster than at any other time, and infants learn at a [[remarkable]] speed. They recognise their parents' voices, learn to walk and pick up the sounds of a language. So the problem is not that nothing happens to them; it is that so little of it survives into adulthood.

For decades, many researchers [[assumed]] that babies simply could not form lasting memories. Experiments have shown that this is not quite true. In a well-known series of studies, three-month-old infants learned that kicking their legs made a mobile above their cot move. When they were tested again several days later, many of them still remembered the trick, and older babies remembered for even longer.

One explanation focuses on the hippocampus, a small region of the brain that is [[essential]] for storing personal experiences. In young children it is still developing, and new nerve cells are being added to it at a high rate. Experiments with mice suggest that this rapid growth may [[disrupt]] older connections, so that stored memories are [[gradually]] overwritten. In other words, the memories may be formed but later become impossible to reach.

Language may also play a part. Once children can put events into words, they can organise them into stories, and stories are far easier to keep. In one study, young children who had played an unusual game were asked about it months later. They described it only with words they had already known at the time, never with words learned afterwards – as if the memory were locked in its original, wordless form.

Culture matters too. Studies comparing adults from different backgrounds have found that people raised in families that often talk about past events, and about the child's own feelings, tend to have earlier first memories. Everyday conversations about "what happened today" seem to give children practice in turning experience into lasting memories.

None of this means that our first years are wasted. Even if we cannot recall them, they [[shape]] our skills, our emotions and the way we relate to others. We may have forgotten the events, but in a deeper sense we still carry them with us.

C1.title: The Mystery of Our Missing First Years
C1.sub: Infancy is a period of extraordinary learning, yet it leaves almost no trace in memory. New research is starting to explain this curious blind spot.
text: Ask most adults for their earliest memory and they will offer something from around their third or fourth year – rarely a coherent narrative, more often a [[fleeting]] image: the glare of a kitchen light, a red coat, the sudden bark of a dog. What came before has left no conscious trace. Psychologists refer to this as "childhood amnesia", and it is so [[universal]] that we seldom question it.

Yet the phenomenon is genuinely puzzling. Infancy is hardly uneventful: the brain expands more rapidly then than at any other point in life, and babies acquire skills at an astonishing pace, from recognising familiar voices to mastering the sound system of their first language. The difficulty, then, lies not in a lack of experience but in why so little of it [[endures]].

For much of the twentieth century it was widely assumed that infants were simply incapable of forming lasting memories. That view has proved [[untenable]]. In a classic series of experiments, three-month-olds learned that kicking made a mobile above their cot move, and many still remembered the connection days later; older infants retained it for considerably longer. More recently, a brain-imaging study found signs that the hippocampus is already encoding individual experiences by around the age of one.

If memories are formed, why can't we reach them? One influential account centres on the hippocampus itself. During early childhood it is still maturing, and new neurons are being generated at a high rate. Research on mice suggests that this rapid growth can [[disrupt]] existing circuits, so that earlier memories are gradually overwritten. The memories, on this view, are not so much never made as rendered inaccessible.

Language offers a second, [[complementary]] explanation. Once children can translate events into words, they can arrange them into stories, which are far easier to [[retrieve]]. Strikingly, when young children were questioned months after playing an unusual game, they described it using only the vocabulary they had possessed at the time, never words acquired since – as though the memory had been sealed in its pre-verbal form.

Culture, too, appears to play a role. Cross-cultural research indicates that adults raised in families where past events – and the child's own feelings about them – were discussed frequently tend to report earlier first memories. Everyday conversations, it seems, give children practice in [[consolidating]] experience into autobiographical memory.

Researchers also point out that forgetting is not necessarily a failure. A young brain faces an enormous amount of new information every day, and holding on to every detail could make it harder to recognise general patterns. From this perspective, losing the specific episodes of infancy may be the price we pay for learning what usually happens: that faces mean comfort, that words have meanings, that objects continue to exist when hidden. Some scientists even suggest that the knowledge itself survives in a different form – as skills, habits and expectations – rather than as memories of particular events. We do not remember learning to walk or to understand speech, yet those achievements remain with us every day.

None of this renders our earliest years irrelevant. Though we cannot recall them, they lay the foundations of our abilities, our emotional responses and the way we relate to others. The events may be lost, but their influence remains.

C2.title: The Vanishing Years: Why Infancy Leaves No Memories
C2.sub: The most formative stretch of our lives is also the one we cannot recall. Neuroscience, linguistics and anthropology each offer part of the answer.
text: Press most adults for their earliest recollection and they will offer something [[ephemeral]] from around their third or fourth year: not a story so much as a shard – the glare of a kitchen light, a red coat, the jolt of a dog's bark. Of everything that preceded it, nothing remains. Freud gave the phenomenon a name, infantile amnesia, but its very ubiquity has made it oddly [[inconspicuous]]; we rarely think to ask why it occurs.

The question is less trivial than it seems. Infancy is anything but uneventful. The brain expands more rapidly in those years than at any later stage, and infants acquire knowledge at a pace that would [[confound]] any adult learner, discriminating familiar voices within days of birth and internalising the phonology of their native language long before they can speak it. The enigma, then, is not a dearth of experience but its near-total [[attrition]].

For much of the last century the prevailing explanation was disarmingly simple: infants, it was held, lacked the capacity to lay down durable memories. The empirical record has not been kind to this view. Three-month-olds trained to make a cot mobile move by kicking retained the association for days, and somewhat older infants for weeks. A recent neuroimaging study went further, finding evidence that the hippocampus is encoding discrete episodes by roughly twelve months of age.

If memories are formed, the problem becomes one of access. One prominent hypothesis implicates the hippocampus directly. Throughout early childhood it continues to generate neurons at a prodigious rate, and studies in mice suggest that this neurogenesis can remodel existing circuitry, [[ostensibly]] at the expense of what was stored there. On this account, early memories are not so much absent as [[irretrievable]] – overwritten by the very growth that makes later learning possible.

Linguistic development supplies a further, mutually reinforcing strand of explanation. Narrative is a powerful organising principle for memory, and narrative requires words. In a striking experiment, young children who had played with an unusual apparatus were interviewed months later; they described the episode using only the vocabulary they had commanded at the time, never terms acquired subsequently. The memory, it appeared, remained [[encapsulated]] in the pre-verbal form in which it had been laid down.

Culture adds a third dimension. Cross-cultural studies indicate that adults from backgrounds that encourage elaborate conversation about the past – and about the child's own perspective on it – report earlier first memories on average. Such exchanges appear to [[undergird]] the capacity to transform experience into an autobiographical record.

There is, moreover, a case for regarding this forgetting as adaptive rather than deficient. An infant brain is inundated with novel stimuli, and to retain every particular might impede the extraction of regularities – that faces portend comfort, that sounds cohere into words, that objects persist when concealed from view. Seen in this light, the loss of specific episodes may be the price exacted for generalisation. Several researchers go further, arguing that early experience is not erased at all but transmuted: it survives as procedural competence, emotional disposition and tacit expectation, even when no episodic trace remains to be summoned.

The question also bears on more practical concerns. Clinicians and courts have sometimes been asked to weigh claims of memories reaching back to the first year of life. Given what is now known about the immaturity of the systems that support autobiographical recall, such claims warrant considerable caution – not because people are being dishonest, but because memory is reconstructive, and later knowledge can quietly furnish an image with details it never originally possessed.

None of this consigns our first years to irrelevance. Though inaccessible to recollection, they lay down the scaffolding of competence, temperament and attachment on which later life is built. We may have lost the episodes, but we are, in no small part, their product.

text: Some of the most important [[discoveries|discovery]] in history happened by accident. Scientists were looking for one thing – and found something different.

In 1928, a Scottish scientist called Alexander Fleming went on holiday. He left some dishes with bacteria in his laboratory. When he came back, he saw something strange. A blue-green mould was growing on one dish, and around the mould, the bacteria were dead. This mould gave us penicillin, the first antibiotic. It has saved millions of lives.

In 1945, an American engineer was working with a machine that made radio waves. He [[noticed|notice]] that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. This gave him an idea, and soon he invented the microwave oven.

Even the yellow sticky notes on your fridge were an accident. A scientist was trying to make a very strong glue, but his glue was weak. Years later, a [[colleague]] used it to make notes that stick and can be moved again and again.

But these discoveries were not only [[luck]]. Fleming, for example, didn't throw the dish away. He was [[curious]] and asked: “Why did this happen?” A famous French scientist, Louis Pasteur, said: “Chance favours the prepared mind.”

text: We often imagine scientists following a careful plan, testing one idea after another until they reach their goal. In reality, many great discoveries began with an accident – a mistake, a dirty dish or a [[strange]] result that nobody expected. The word for this kind of happy accident is “[[serendipity]]”.

The most famous example is penicillin. In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a summer holiday to find that mould had grown on one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mould, the bacteria had been killed. Fleming [[identified|identify]] the substance responsible and called it penicillin. However, it was another twelve years before scientists in Oxford worked out how to produce it in large amounts. During the Second World War, it saved the lives of thousands of soldiers, and antibiotics have since saved many millions more.

Other examples are just as surprising. In 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen noticed that a screen in his laboratory was glowing even though his equipment was covered. He had discovered X-rays, and within months doctors were using them to see inside the human body. In 1945, the engineer Percy Spencer was testing radar equipment when a chocolate bar in his pocket melted. Curious, he tried putting popcorn near the machine – and the microwave oven was born.

Even failure can be useful. In 1968, a chemist at the company 3M tried to make a super-strong glue but produced a weak one that could be removed easily. Nobody knew what to do with it until a colleague, tired of losing the paper bookmarks in his songbook, realised it would make perfect [[removable]] notes.

Still, luck alone is not enough. Many people must have seen mould on a dish or felt a strange warmth from a machine without thinking more about it. What made the difference was a scientist who [[paid|pay]] attention, asked “why?” and had the knowledge to understand the answer. As Louis Pasteur put it, “Chance favours the prepared mind.” Good science, it seems, needs both careful planning and an open mind that welcomes the [[unexpected]].

text: Textbooks tend to present science as an orderly march: a hypothesis is proposed, an experiment designed, a result obtained. The real history of discovery is messier. A remarkable number of [[breakthroughs|breakthrough]] began with something nobody was looking for – a [[contaminated|contaminate]] sample, a faulty instrument, an experiment that went wrong. The English writer Horace Walpole coined a word for such fortunate accidents in 1754: serendipity.

Penicillin is the classic case. In September 1928, Alexander Fleming returned to his London laboratory after a holiday and noticed that one of his culture plates of bacteria had been contaminated by a mould. Around it, the bacteria had died. Rather than throwing the plate away, Fleming investigated, identifying a substance produced by the mould that killed many types of bacteria. Yet his discovery languished for a decade. Only in the early 1940s did a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain find ways to purify and mass-produce the drug, in time for it to transform the treatment of wounded soldiers. The three men shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

Physics has its own [[equivalents|equivalent]]. In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen was experimenting with electrical discharges in a covered glass tube when he noticed a nearby screen glowing. Some invisible form of radiation was passing through the cover. Within weeks he had photographed the bones of his wife's hand, and X-rays rapidly entered medicine. Seventy years later, two American radio astronomers, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, were frustrated by a [[persistent]] background hiss in their antenna. They even cleaned out pigeon droppings in case they were the cause. The noise turned out to be the faint afterglow of the Big Bang – powerful evidence for the theory and the basis of another Nobel Prize.

Commercial products, too, have emerged from accidents. The microwave oven followed an engineer's discovery that radar equipment had melted a chocolate bar in his pocket, and the sticky notes found in offices everywhere began as a glue that was too weak for its intended purpose.

It would be easy to conclude that great science is mostly luck. But that misses the crucial point. Mould must have [[spoiled|spoil]] countless experiments before 1928; Fleming's contribution was to recognise its significance. Louis Pasteur captured the idea memorably: “Chance favours the prepared mind.” Serendipity depends on observers with enough knowledge to see that something is [[anomalous]] and enough curiosity to follow it up. Some research leaders argue that modern science, with its tight funding and pressure for predictable results, leaves too little room for such open-ended exploration – and may be missing discoveries as a result.

text: Scientific papers tell tidy stories. A question is posed, a method devised, a result reported, a conclusion drawn. The narrative is a useful convention, but it frequently obscures how discoveries actually happen. A striking proportion of [[landmark]] findings began not with a hypothesis but with an anomaly – a contaminated culture, an unexplained signal, an experiment that failed in an interesting way. In 1754 the writer Horace Walpole, inspired by a Persian fairy tale about three princes who kept making discoveries “by accidents and [[sagacity]]”, coined a word for the phenomenon: serendipity.

Penicillin remains the [[paradigmatic]] example. Returning to his London laboratory in September 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a culture plate of staphylococcus bacteria had been invaded by a mould, and that the bacterial colonies surrounding it had dissolved. Many researchers would have discarded the plate as spoiled. Fleming instead isolated the active substance and documented its antibacterial effect. Yet the discovery lay largely [[dormant]] for over a decade, since penicillin proved difficult to purify and Fleming lacked the resources to pursue it. It was the Oxford team of Howard Florey and Ernst Chain who, from 1939, developed methods for extraction and large-scale production, just in time for the drug to transform military medicine in the Second World War. The Nobel Prize of 1945 was shared among all three – a reminder that serendipity typically supplies a beginning rather than a finished achievement.

Physics offers equally [[instructive]] cases. In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen, investigating cathode rays in a tube wrapped in black card, saw a fluorescent screen across the room begin to glow. Recognising that an unknown form of radiation was penetrating the card, he spent weeks characterising it and soon produced an image of the bones in his wife's hand. Within a year, X-rays were being used in hospitals. In 1964, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, radio astronomers at Bell Laboratories, were plagued by a faint, uniform hiss in their antenna that persisted whichever direction they pointed it. Having ruled out every source they could think of – including pigeons nesting in the horn – they learned that theorists nearby had predicted precisely such a signal as the residual radiation of the Big Bang. Their [[inadvertent]] detection of the cosmic microwave background earned them a Nobel Prize.

Industry has its own folklore of happy accidents. Percy Spencer's observation that a radar magnetron had melted the chocolate in his pocket led to the microwave oven; a failed attempt at a super-strong adhesive at 3M eventually became the Post-it note, once a colleague grasped that weak, repositionable glue was a feature rather than a flaw. Some pharmaceutical successes have similar origins: drugs developed for one condition have repeatedly turned out to be more effective for another.

None of this [[diminishes|diminish]] the role of skill. Mould must have ruined innumerable experiments before Fleming's, and countless engineers must have stood beside radar sets; what distinguished the discoverers was the capacity to recognise significance in the unexpected. Pasteur's dictum – “chance favours the prepared mind” – remains the best summary. This has implications for how research is organised. Critics argue that funding systems which reward predictable, incremental outputs and penalise apparent failure may be squeezing out the open-ended inquiry in which serendipity flourishes. Planning, in short, is indispensable to science; but so, paradoxically, is leaving room for what cannot be planned.

text: The published record of science is an exercise in retrospective tidiness. Papers proceed from question to method to result to conclusion, as though discovery were a matter of executing a plan. The convention serves clarity, but it [[occludes|occlude]] a truth familiar to practising scientists: that a remarkable share of consequential findings originated not in a hypothesis but in an anomaly – a contaminated culture, an inexplicable signal, an experiment that failed in an illuminating way. The term for such [[felicitous]] accidents was coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, after a Persian tale of three princes forever discovering, “by accidents and sagacity, of things which they were not in quest of”. Serendipity, as Walpole's formulation makes clear, was never meant to denote luck alone.

Penicillin is the canonical case, and its full history is more instructive than the legend. In September 1928 Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find a staphylococcus culture plate colonised by a stray mould, around which the bacterial colonies had lysed. Fleming did not discard it as spoiled; he isolated the agent responsible and characterised its antibacterial action. But the discovery then lay [[fallow]] for over a decade, partly because the compound proved [[recalcitrant]] to purification and partly because Fleming, lacking chemical expertise and resources, did not press its therapeutic potential. It fell to Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford, from 1939, to devise methods of extraction and to persuade American manufacturers to scale up production – just in time for penicillin to revolutionise the treatment of battlefield infections. That all three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize is a useful corrective to the myth of the solitary genius struck by fortune: the accident supplied a beginning, but the achievement required years of deliberate, unglamorous labour.

Physics furnishes parallel episodes. In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen, investigating cathode rays in a tube shrouded in black card, observed a fluorescent screen glimmering across his darkened laboratory. Grasping that some unknown, penetrating radiation was at work, he devoted weeks of [[methodical]] experiment to establishing its properties before publishing – including the now-iconic image of his wife's hand. Seven decades later, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Laboratories were confounded by a faint, isotropic hiss in a horn antenna intended for satellite communication. Having exhausted every terrestrial explanation, down to the evicting of nesting pigeons, they learned that physicists at nearby Princeton had predicted exactly such a residue from the hot early universe. Their accidental detection of the cosmic microwave background supplied decisive evidence for the Big Bang and, in due course, a Nobel Prize.

Technology and medicine abound in comparable stories. Percy Spencer's realisation that a radar magnetron had melted a confectionery bar in his pocket led to the microwave oven; a 3M chemist's failed quest for a super-strong adhesive became the Post-it note once a colleague perceived that weakness and repositionability could be virtues. In pharmacology, drug repurposing – the discovery that a compound developed for one indication works better for another – has become sufficiently common to constitute a research strategy in its own right.

What unites these cases is not chance but the reception of chance. Moulds must have ruined innumerable cultures before 1928; generations of technicians must have stood near radar sets. Discovery required observers [[steeped|steep]] enough in their field to recognise that something did not fit, and curious enough to pursue it at the cost of their original plans. Pasteur's aphorism that “chance favours the prepared mind” has endured because it captures this conjunction exactly.

The point has acquired institutional urgency. Critics of contemporary research funding argue that grant systems built around predefined milestones, short timescales and an aversion to apparent failure select against precisely the [[latitude]] in which serendipity operates. Some funders have responded by setting aside resources for exploratory, high-risk work. The paradox is that science must be planned in order to be productive, yet it may be most productive when it leaves room for what no plan could have anticipated.

text: Do you remember the [[price]] of a loaf of bread five years ago? It was probably cheaper than today. When prices go up over time, economists call it inflation.

A little inflation is normal. Many [[governments|government]] want prices to rise by about two per cent a year. But in 2022, prices in many countries went up very fast. In Britain and the USA, inflation was about ten per cent. Food and energy became much more [[expensive]].

Why did this happen? After the COVID-19 pandemic, people wanted to buy a lot of things again, but factories and ships could not make and move everything fast enough. Then the war in Ukraine made gas and oil more expensive. When energy costs more, almost everything costs more.
Inflation is hard for poor families. They spend a big part of their money on food, heating and [[rent]]. If prices go up and their [[wages|wage]] don't, they can buy less.

Sometimes companies have a clever trick. They don't change the price, but they make the packet smaller. A chocolate bar costs the same, but it is a little lighter. People call this “shrinkflation”. So next time you go shopping, check the size – not just the price!

text: If you have ever heard older people say, “When I was young, a cinema ticket cost almost nothing,” you have heard someone describe inflation. Inflation is the general rise in prices over time, which means that the same amount of money buys less and less. It is usually measured by checking the prices of a typical “[[basket]]” of goods and services, from bread and petrol to haircuts and rent.

A small amount of inflation is considered healthy. Most central banks, such as the Bank of England and the US Federal Reserve, try to keep it at around two per cent a year. When prices rise slowly and [[predictably|predictable]], people and businesses can plan for the future.

In 2022, however, inflation reached levels not seen for forty years in many rich countries – over ten per cent in Britain and around nine per cent in the United States. There were several causes. After the pandemic, demand for goods [[recovered|recover]] quickly while factories and shipping were still disrupted. Then Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed up the price of gas, oil and wheat. Because energy is needed to make and transport almost everything, its higher price spread through the whole economy.

To fight inflation, central banks usually raise interest rates. This makes borrowing more expensive, so people and companies spend less, and prices rise more slowly. But higher rates also hurt families with [[mortgages|mortgage]] and can slow down the economy.

Inflation does not affect everyone [[equally]]. Poorer households spend a larger share of their income on food and energy, so they suffer most when these prices jump. People with savings lose too, because their money is worth less. Some people, however, gain: those with large fixed-rate debts find them easier to pay back. In the most extreme cases, called hyperinflation – as in Germany in 1923 or Zimbabwe in 2008 – prices can double in days, and money becomes almost [[worthless]].

text: Inflation is one of those economic terms that everyone has heard of and few can define precisely. Put simply, it is the rate at which the general level of prices rises over time, [[eroding|erode]] the purchasing power of money. Statistical offices measure it by tracking the cost of a representative “basket” of hundreds of goods and services – food, fuel, clothing, rent, haircuts, streaming subscriptions – and comparing it with the same basket a year earlier.

Modest, stable inflation is generally regarded as harmless, even [[desirable]]. Most major central banks, including the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, aim for around two per cent a year. Economists favour a small positive figure over zero partly because falling prices, or deflation, can be dangerous: if consumers expect goods to be cheaper next month, they [[postpone]] purchases, which can push an economy into a downward spiral.

From 2021, however, inflation surged across much of the world, peaking in 2022 at rates not seen since the early 1980s: around nine per cent in the United States and over ten per cent in the United Kingdom and the eurozone. Economists distinguish between “demand-pull” inflation, when spending outpaces the economy's capacity to produce, and “cost-push” inflation, when rising production costs are passed on to consumers. The post-pandemic surge involved both. As economies reopened, pent-up demand – supported by government relief payments – collided with factory closures and shipping bottlenecks. Then Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices for natural gas, oil, wheat and fertiliser soaring.

Central banks responded in the traditional way, raising interest rates at the fastest pace in decades. Higher rates make borrowing costlier and saving more attractive, cooling demand. The policy is effective but [[blunt]]: it works partly by slowing the economy and can increase unemployment, and it hits mortgage holders and indebted businesses especially hard.

The burden of inflation is unevenly [[distributed|distribute]]. Low-income households devote a larger share of their budgets to food and energy, precisely the items whose prices rose fastest in 2022, so their personal inflation rate was often well above the official average. Savers lose as the real value of their deposits falls, while borrowers with fixed-rate loans may benefit as their debts shrink in real terms. Firms have also found subtler ways to raise prices, such as “shrinkflation” – reducing the size of a product while keeping its price unchanged.

At its most extreme, inflation becomes hyperinflation, as in Weimar Germany in 1923 or Zimbabwe in 2008, when prices doubled in days and savings were wiped out. Such episodes are rare, but they explain why central bankers treat even moderate inflation with such [[vigilance]]: once people expect prices to keep rising, those expectations can become self-fulfilling.

text: Few economic concepts touch daily life as directly as inflation, yet few are as widely misunderstood. Formally, inflation is the sustained rise in the general price level, and with it the [[attrition]] of money's purchasing power. Statistical agencies estimate it by pricing a representative basket of goods and services – from bread and petrol to rents, haircuts and streaming subscriptions – and tracking how the cost of that basket changes from year to year. The resulting index is an average, and like all averages it conceals as much as it reveals.

Policymakers do not, as is often assumed, aim for zero inflation. The major central banks target roughly two per cent, on the grounds that a modest, predictable rate gives them room to cut interest rates in a downturn and guards against deflation, whose [[insidious]] dynamics – consumers delaying purchases in expectation of lower prices, firms cutting output and wages in response – can entrench economic stagnation, as Japan discovered in the 1990s.

The inflationary surge of 2021–23 was the most severe in four decades across much of the developed world, peaking at around nine per cent in the United States and above ten per cent in the United Kingdom and the eurozone. Its causes illustrate the textbook distinction between demand-pull pressures, in which aggregate spending outruns productive capacity, and cost-push pressures, in which rising input costs are transmitted to consumer prices. As economies reopened after the pandemic, demand buoyed by government support and accumulated savings collided with snarled supply chains. Russia's invasion of Ukraine then delivered a classic supply shock, sending the prices of gas, oil, grain and fertiliser sharply higher. Economists continue to debate how much additional inflation came from firms expanding their profit margins – a phenomenon some dubbed “greedflation” – though the evidence suggests its importance varied considerably by sector and country.

Central banks responded with the most rapid tightening of monetary policy in a generation. Raising interest rates restrains inflation by making credit more expensive and saving more rewarding, thereby [[dampening|dampen]] demand. The instrument is powerful but imprecise. It acts with long and variable lags, it cannot increase the supply of gas or grain, and it operates in part by weakening labour markets – raising the spectre of a recession engineered to tame prices.

The costs of inflation are distributed [[regressively]]. Lower-income households devote a disproportionate share of their budgets to food and energy, whose prices rose fastest, so the inflation they experienced frequently exceeded the headline rate. Savers holding cash see its real value [[dwindle]], while borrowers on fixed-rate loans enjoy a quiet [[windfall]] as their debts shrink in real terms. Firms, meanwhile, have resorted to less visible forms of price increase, such as shrinkflation – reducing package sizes while holding prices constant – which official statistics capture only imperfectly.

The ultimate fear underlying central bankers' [[vigilance]] is the de-anchoring of expectations. If workers and firms come to believe that high inflation will persist, they build it into wage demands and price-setting, and the belief becomes self-fulfilling. Hyperinflations such as those in Weimar Germany in 1923 or Zimbabwe in 2008 are extreme and rare, but they demonstrate how swiftly confidence in money, once lost, can collapse.

text: Inflation is at once the most intimate and the most misunderstood of macroeconomic phenomena. Everyone experiences it at the supermarket checkout; comparatively few could say precisely what it is. Technically, it denotes a persistent rise in the general level of prices and, [[concomitantly|concomitant]], a decline in the purchasing power of money. Statistical agencies approximate it by pricing a basket of several hundred representative goods and services, weighted according to household spending patterns, and recording the year-on-year change. The headline figure is thus an average of averages – a useful abstraction that no actual household experiences.

Contrary to popular assumption, central banks do not seek price stability in the literal sense of zero inflation. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England target around two per cent, a figure that provides a buffer against deflation and leaves room to cut nominal interest rates when the economy falters. Deflation is feared for good reason. When consumers anticipate falling prices they [[defer]] purchases, firms respond by curtailing output and wages, and the resulting contraction validates the original expectation – a self-reinforcing spiral that contributed to Japan's protracted stagnation from the 1990s onward.

The inflation of 2021–23, the most acute in the developed world since the early 1980s, offered a vivid tutorial in the discipline's categories. Demand-pull pressures – aggregate spending outstripping productive capacity – arose as economies reopened with households flush from fiscal transfers and enforced saving. Cost-push pressures followed from snarled supply chains and, after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a classic supply shock that sent the prices of natural gas, oil, grain and fertiliser [[spiralling|spiral]]. A further, more contentious mechanism concerned corporate pricing power: some economists argued that firms in concentrated industries used the general climate of rising costs as cover to widen their margins, a dynamic popularly labelled “greedflation”. The empirical record suggests the effect was real in certain sectors and countries but insufficient on its own to account for the episode.

Monetary authorities responded with the swiftest tightening in a generation. Higher policy rates suppress inflation by raising the cost of credit and the return on saving, thereby damping consumption and investment. Yet the instrument is notoriously blunt. Its effects arrive with long and variable lags; it can do nothing to conjure additional gas or grain; and it works in part by loosening labour markets, which is to say by making some people unemployed. Critics accordingly accused central banks of first underestimating inflation as “transitory” and then risking an [[overcorrection]] that would inflict recession to remedy a problem largely originating on the supply side.

Inflation's burden is regressive in its incidence. Poorer households spend disproportionately on food and energy, the categories that rose fastest, so the inflation they actually faced often exceeded the published rate by a substantial margin. Holders of cash and low-yielding deposits suffer an invisible [[confiscation]] as real values erode, whereas debtors with fixed-rate obligations – including, not least, heavily indebted governments – enjoy a corresponding [[windfall]]. Meanwhile, firms' recourse to shrinkflation, quietly reducing quantities while holding sticker prices constant, complicates measurement and corrodes consumer trust.

Underlying all of this is the question of expectations, which central bankers watch with something approaching [[obsession]]. Inflation is in part a psychological phenomenon: if workers and firms come to expect persistent price rises, they incorporate that expectation into wage claims and pricing decisions, and the anticipation becomes self-fulfilling. The hyperinflations of Weimar Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in 2008, when prices doubled within days and savings were obliterated, are extreme cases. But they demonstrate a principle that applies at any scale: money is a social convention sustained by confidence, and confidence, once forfeited, is far harder to restore than to lose.

text: Behind many famous companies is a surprisingly modest beginning. Apple was founded in a family garage in California. Spanx, the clothing brand, began with 5,000 dollars of its founder's savings and a [[prototype]] she made at home. Airbnb started in 2007 when two designers in San Francisco, unable to afford their rent, put air mattresses on their living-room floor and rented them to visitors attending a conference.

Stories like these make [[entrepreneurship]] look easy, but they hide an important truth: most new businesses do not survive for long. In the United States, around one in five new firms closes within its first year, and roughly half have closed after five years. Because we mostly hear about the successes, it is easy to [[underestimate]] the risks – a mistake psychologists call survivorship bias.

Why do so many new businesses fail? Research and founders' own accounts point to a few common reasons: there is not enough demand for the product, the money runs out, or the business is not competitive enough. Interestingly, a bad product is less often the problem than a product nobody really needs.

This is why many advisers now recommend starting small. Instead of spending a year building the perfect product, founders create a simple version – sometimes called a “minimum viable product” – and test it with real customers. They watch what people actually do, not just what they say, and [[adapt]] quickly. Airbnb's founders, for example, visited their first hosts and took better photos of their homes, and bookings went up.

Who becomes a successful entrepreneur? The [[stereotype]] is a twenty-something in a hoodie, but a large American study found that the average age of founders of the fastest-growing new companies was about forty-five. Experience, contacts and knowledge of an industry seem to matter. Above all, successful founders tend to be [[persistent]]: they treat failures as information rather than as the end of the story.

text: Business folklore loves a humble origin. Apple was assembled in a suburban garage; the shapewear brand Spanx was launched with 5,000 dollars of its founder's savings and a prototype cut from a pair of tights; Airbnb began when two struggling designers in San Francisco inflated air mattresses on their floor and rented them to delegates at a sold-out design conference. Such stories are inspiring, and they [[reinforce]] a powerful cultural message: with a good idea and enough determination, anyone can turn a kitchen-table project into a company.

The statistics tell a more sobering story. Data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics show that roughly 20 per cent of new businesses close within their first year and about half within five years. Because failed [[ventures|venture]] rarely make headlines, the public sees a [[distorted]] sample in which the winners are vastly over-represented – a phenomenon known as survivorship bias. Studying only successful founders to learn the secrets of success is a little like interviewing lottery winners to discover the best way to choose numbers.

When researchers and investors examine why start-ups fail, a few causes recur. The most frequently cited is the absence of a real market need: the product works, but not enough people want to pay for it. Running out of cash, being outcompeted and building the wrong team follow close behind. These patterns have shaped the “lean start-up” approach popularised by the entrepreneur Eric Ries, which urges founders to launch a minimum viable product – the simplest version that can be tested on real customers – and to measure how people actually behave before investing heavily. Airbnb's early growth stalled until its founders flew to New York, met their hosts and discovered that poor photographs were putting guests off; professional photos quickly lifted bookings.

Popular images of the entrepreneur are also [[misleading]]. The [[archetype]] is a college dropout in a hoodie, yet a large study of US firms by economists including Pierre Azoulay found that the average founder of the fastest-growing new companies was about forty-five years old. Middle-aged founders bring industry knowledge, professional networks and often savings – advantages that seem to outweigh youthful energy.

Access to these advantages is not evenly spread. Women and ethnic minority founders receive a small fraction of venture capital, and people without savings or family support can find it far harder to absorb the risk of failure. Some economists argue that stronger social safety nets actually encourage entrepreneurship, by making failure less [[catastrophic]].

None of this means that starting a business is unwise. It means that the kitchen table is a beginning, not a guarantee – and that the founders who succeed are often those who test their assumptions early, listen carefully and treat each setback as data rather than defeat.

text: Few genres of modern storytelling are as [[formulaic]] as the start-up origin myth. A founder, usually young and underfunded, spots an opportunity others have missed; a garage, dormitory or kitchen table serves as headquarters; setbacks are overcome through grit and ingenuity; and a global company eventually emerges. Apple's suburban garage, Spanx's 5,000-dollar beginning with a prototype snipped from a pair of tights, and Airbnb's air mattresses rented to conference delegates in San Francisco have all become set pieces in this genre. The stories are true, as far as they go. The difficulty lies in what they leave out.

What they omit, above all, is the far larger population of ventures that fail. In the United States, official data indicate that around a fifth of new establishments close within their first year and roughly half within five. Because unsuccessful firms leave few traces in the media, our impression of entrepreneurship is shaped by a profoundly [[skewed]] sample – the survivorship bias that leads observers to attribute success to traits that may be just as common among those who failed. Persistence, risk-taking and self-belief are celebrated in successful founders, yet they are presumably also abundant in the many whose businesses quietly folded.

Systematic studies of failure point to a recurring set of causes. Analyses of start-up post-mortems consistently rank the absence of genuine market demand at or near the top: firms build products that work technically but address problems customers do not care enough about to pay to solve. Cash-flow crises, stronger competitors and dysfunctional founding teams follow. These findings underpin the “lean start-up” methodology articulated by Eric Ries, which advocates releasing a minimum viable product, measuring real customer behaviour and [[iterating|iterate]] rapidly – “[[pivoting|pivot]]” if necessary – rather than perfecting a product in isolation. Airbnb's own trajectory illustrates the approach: when growth stagnated, the founders visited New York hosts in person, concluded that amateurish photographs were deterring bookings, and photographed the properties themselves, with an immediate effect on revenue.

Received wisdom about who succeeds also [[warrants|warrant]] revision. The archetypal founder is a twenty-something dropout, yet research by Pierre Azoulay and colleagues, drawing on data covering millions of US firms, found that the mean age of founders of the fastest-growing new companies was about forty-five, and that founders in their fifties were more likely than those in their twenties to build a highly successful firm. Prior industry experience appears to be a particularly strong predictor – a finding that sits awkwardly with the cult of youthful disruption.

Opportunity, moreover, is unevenly distributed. Women-led and minority-led start-ups receive a strikingly small share of venture capital, and would-be founders without savings or family wealth face a starker [[trade-off]] between a stable salary and an uncertain venture. Some economists contend that generous social insurance – unemployment benefits, health coverage not tied to employment – can actually stimulate entrepreneurship by cushioning the downside of failure and thereby widening the pool of people able to take the risk.

None of this is an argument against starting a business. It is an argument for a less romantic and more empirical approach: one that treats the kitchen table as a laboratory rather than a launch pad, regards early failures as evidence, and recognises that the [[determinants|determinant]] of success include not only individual talent but also experience, timing, networks and the institutions that make risk bearable.

text: Entrepreneurial culture has its own [[hagiography]]. The canonical narrative runs as follows: an unlikely founder, short of money but long on vision, glimpses an opportunity invisible to incumbents; a garage, dorm room or kitchen table becomes the improvised headquarters; adversity is vanquished by grit; and a global enterprise rises from humble beginnings. Apple's suburban garage, the 5,000 dollars of savings and home-made prototype that launched Spanx, and the air mattresses Airbnb's founders rented to delegates at an oversubscribed San Francisco conference have all been canonised in this tradition. The anecdotes are accurate. What is misleading is the inference drawn from them.

The missing evidence is the [[graveyard]] of ventures that never made it. US data indicate that roughly a fifth of new establishments close within twelve months and around half within five years. Since failures generate few headlines, public perception is formed from a radically unrepresentative sample – the survivorship bias that tempts commentators to credit success to qualities such as audacity, [[tenacity]] and self-belief, without asking how many failed founders possessed them in equal measure. Learning about entrepreneurship from billionaires alone, one researcher has quipped, is like learning about the safety of skydiving exclusively from people who landed.

Systematic post-mortems of failed start-ups reveal [[recurrent]] causes. Chief among them is the absence of genuine demand: products that function perfectly but solve problems customers do not regard as worth paying to solve. Cash-flow crises, superior competitors and fractious founding teams follow. It was partly in response to such findings that Eric Ries articulated the “lean start-up” doctrine, which counsels founders to release a minimum viable product, test hypotheses against observed customer behaviour rather than stated intentions, and iterate – or pivot – before capital is exhausted. Airbnb's early history is a case in point: when growth flatlined, the founders travelled to New York, diagnosed amateurish photography as the obstacle, photographed hosts' homes themselves and watched revenue rise almost at once.

Conventional assumptions about who succeeds are equally ripe for revision. The cultural archetype is the precocious dropout, but research by Pierre Azoulay and colleagues, drawing on administrative data covering millions of American firms, found that the mean age of founders of the fastest-growing new companies was about forty-five, and that a fifty-year-old founder was considerably more likely than a thirty-year-old to build a firm in the top tier of growth. Accumulated industry expertise – knowledge of customers, suppliers and regulations – emerged as a potent predictor, an inconvenient finding for a mythology that [[fetishises|fetishise]] youthful disruption.

Nor is the opportunity to fail affordably evenly distributed. Start-ups led by women or by founders from ethnic minorities receive a strikingly small share of venture capital, and aspiring entrepreneurs without personal wealth confront a far starker choice between a secure income and a speculative venture. Some economists accordingly argue that robust social insurance – unemployment benefits, healthcare decoupled from employment, [[forgiving]] bankruptcy laws – does not stifle enterprise but enables it, by truncating the downside of failure and thereby broadening the pool of people able to take the plunge. On this view, the welfare state and the entrepreneurial economy are less antagonists than [[complements|complement]].

None of this is a counsel of despair. It is a plea for epistemic humility: for treating the kitchen table as a laboratory rather than a launch pad, early failure as data rather than verdict, and success as the product not only of individual brilliance but of experience, timing, networks and the institutional scaffolding that renders risk survivable. The garage myth is a good story. It is a poor guide to practice.

text: In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that by 2030 his grandchildren's generation would work just fifteen hours a week. Technology would make us so [[productive]] that long hours would no longer be necessary. His prediction was wrong – most full-time workers still work around forty hours – but the idea of working less has come back in the form of the four-day week.

The most popular model is called “100-80-100”: workers get 100 per cent of their pay for working 80 per cent of their time, in exchange for keeping 100 per cent of their productivity. Between 2015 and 2019, public sector organisations in Iceland tested shorter hours with around 2,500 workers. Researchers found that productivity stayed the same or improved in most workplaces, while wellbeing rose. Since then, most Icelandic workers have gained the right to shorter hours.

In 2022, the largest trial so far took place in Britain, involving 61 companies and nearly 3,000 employees for six months. The results were [[encouraging]]. Most companies reported that [[revenue]] stayed roughly the same, the number of sick days fell, and fewer people left their jobs. At the end, 56 of the 61 companies decided to continue, many of them permanently.

How is this possible? Many firms [[cut out]] wasted time: long meetings became short ones, and staff were encouraged to focus without constant interruptions. Some experts mention “Parkinson's law” – the idea that work expands to fill the time available. Give people less time, and they often find ways to finish the same tasks.

Critics, however, raise [[concerns|concern]]. The companies in the trials chose to take part, so they may have been especially suited to the idea. In hospitals, care homes or shops, where someone must always be present, a four-day week can mean hiring more staff. Some workers also find that squeezing five days of work into four is more [[stressful]], not less. The four-day week may not suit everyone, but it has started a serious debate about how much we really need to work.

text: In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes made one of the most famous predictions in his field. Technological progress, he argued, would make societies so wealthy that within a century his grandchildren's generation would need to work only fifteen hours a week; the great challenge would be how to fill their [[leisure]]. Productivity did rise roughly as he expected. Working hours, however, did not fall nearly as far: in most rich countries, the standard full-time week has been stuck at around forty hours for decades.

The four-day week is the latest attempt to [[revisit]] Keynes's vision. Its most influential version, promoted by the campaign group 4 Day Week Global, follows a “100-80-100” principle: employees receive full pay for 80 per cent of their previous hours, on condition that they maintain full productivity. Crucially, this is different from a “compressed” week, in which the same total hours are squeezed into four longer days.

Evidence has accumulated quickly. Between 2015 and 2019, Reykjavík City Council and Iceland's national government trialled shorter hours with about 2,500 public employees – roughly one per cent of the country's workforce. Researchers reported that productivity and service provision were maintained or improved in the majority of workplaces, while measures of stress and [[burnout]] declined. Subsequent union agreements gave a large majority of Icelandic workers the right to shorter hours.

In 2022 Britain hosted the largest coordinated trial so far: 61 organisations and almost 3,000 employees, from marketing agencies to a fish-and-chip shop, adopted a four-day week for six months. Revenue was broadly unchanged over the period, sick days fell by roughly two-thirds and the number of staff resigning dropped by more than half. Fifty-six of the 61 firms chose to continue, and 18 made the change permanent.

Supporters argue that the gains come from [[eliminating|eliminate]] inefficiency rather than from working harder. Firms in the trials shortened meetings, introduced periods of uninterrupted “deep work” and cut unnecessary emails. Parkinson's law – the observation that work expands to fill the time available for its completion – may also work in reverse.

Sceptics point to important [[caveats|caveat]]. Companies volunteered for the trials, so they were probably more enthusiastic and better suited than the average employer, and results were largely self-reported. In sectors where staff must be physically present, such as healthcare, retail or transport, reducing hours without reducing service requires hiring more people – a significant cost. Some employees also found that cramming five days' work into four increased pressure rather than relieving it.

The debate is far from settled. Yet the trials have [[unsettled|unsettle]] a long-held assumption: that hours worked are a reliable measure of work done. For many office jobs, at least, the evidence suggests they are not.
