text: Few values are more deeply [[embedded]] in consumer societies than choice. We are offered tens of thousands of supermarket products, a near-infinite catalogue of streaming content and, increasingly, responsibility for complex decisions once made on our behalf – from pension investments to energy tariffs. The underlying premise is that more options allow each individual to find the best fit for their preferences. Psychological research over the past quarter-century has complicated that premise, suggesting that under some conditions abundant choice can impair decision-making and diminish satisfaction.

The finding that crystallised the debate was published in 2000 by Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper. At an upmarket grocery store in California, a tasting booth displayed either six or twenty-four varieties of jam. The larger [[assortment]] was more [[enticing|entice]] – 60 per cent of passing shoppers stopped, versus 40 per cent for the smaller one – but only around 3 per cent of those who stopped went on to buy, against roughly 30 per cent at the limited display. A follow-up laboratory study found that students offered a larger selection of chocolates enjoyed the one they chose less and were more likely to regret their choice. Iyengar later reported that, in American retirement plans, each additional ten funds was associated with a decline of roughly two percentage points in employee participation, at a real financial cost to those who opted out.

Barry Schwartz's The Paradox of Choice turned these findings into an influential critique of consumer culture. Expanding the choice set, he argued, raises the cognitive cost of deciding, inflates expectations and multiplies opportunities for regret and self-blame, since a disappointing outcome can no longer be attributed to circumstance. Schwartz drew on Herbert Simon's distinction between maximising – exhaustively searching for the optimal option – and “satisficing”, Simon's blend of satisfying and sufficing, which means accepting the first option that meets one's criteria. In a study of graduating university students, those with a maximising disposition obtained starting salaries roughly 20 per cent higher than satisficers, yet felt worse about their jobs: more pessimistic, more stressed and less satisfied.

The phenomenon has proved less universal than early accounts implied. A 2010 meta-analysis by Benjamin Scheibehenne and colleagues found that the mean effect of choice overload across studies was close to zero, though results varied widely. A later meta-analysis by Alexander Chernev and colleagues helped to explain the [[discrepancy]] by identifying [[moderating|moderate]] factors: overload is most likely when the options are complex, when they are difficult to compare, when decision-makers lack well-defined preferences and when the goal is to minimise effort. Where people know what they want, or where options are clearly organised, larger assortments can be beneficial.

The practical implications are correspondingly [[nuanced]]. For designers of choice environments – governments, employers, retailers – thoughtful defaults, curated selections and clear categorisation can reduce overload without removing freedom. For individuals, the research suggests a strategy of selective maximising: investing effort in decisions that matter and deliberately satisficing elsewhere. The point is not that choice is bad, but that unlimited choice is not [[synonymous]] with well-being.

text: Choice occupies a near-sacred place in the self-understanding of liberal consumer societies. Shoppers navigate supermarkets stocking tens of thousands of lines, viewers scroll through streaming libraries that would outlast several lifetimes, and citizens are increasingly made responsible for intricate decisions – pension allocations, energy tariffs, school places – once taken on their behalf. The animating premise is that an expanded menu allows each person to match outcomes more precisely to idiosyncratic preferences. Behavioural research of the past quarter-century has [[problematised|problematise]] that premise, without overturning it.

The study that gave the idea its popular currency was Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper's experiment of 2000. Customers at an upmarket Californian grocer encountered a tasting booth displaying either six or twenty-four varieties of jam. The larger array proved more alluring – 60 per cent of passers-by paused, against 40 per cent – yet only some 3 per cent of those who paused went on to purchase, compared with roughly 30 per cent at the modest display. Companion studies found that participants choosing from a larger set of chocolates savoured their selection less and regretted it more, and Iyengar's subsequent analysis of American retirement plans suggested that each further ten funds offered was associated with a fall of roughly two percentage points in participation – a choice not to choose that carried real financial costs.

Barry Schwartz's The Paradox of Choice transmuted these findings into a broader [[indictment]] of consumer culture. An expanded choice set, he argued, raises the cognitive cost of deliberation, escalates expectations and multiplies the occasions for counterfactual regret; and because a poor outcome can no longer be blamed on a lack of alternatives, disappointment [[curdles|curdle]] into self-reproach. Schwartz enlisted Herbert Simon's venerable distinction between maximising – the exhaustive pursuit of the optimal – and satisficing, Simon's [[portmanteau]] of satisfying and sufficing, which denotes the acceptance of the first option that clears a threshold of adequacy. In one longitudinal study of graduating students, maximisers secured starting salaries around a fifth higher than satisficers yet reported greater pessimism, stress and dissatisfaction with the posts they accepted: objectively better off, subjectively worse.

As so often in psychology, the original effect has proved more [[contingent]] than its popularisers implied. A 2010 meta-analysis led by Benjamin Scheibehenne, aggregating fifty experiments, estimated a mean effect of choice overload statistically indistinguishable from zero, accompanied by striking heterogeneity – some studies showing large effects, others the reverse. Rather than discarding the phenomenon, a subsequent meta-analysis by Alexander Chernev and colleagues sought to explain that variance, identifying moderators under which overload reliably emerges: complex choice sets, options that are difficult to compare, the absence of articulated preferences and a goal of minimising decisional effort. Where preferences are clear or alternatives well organised, larger assortments may be positively advantageous, allowing people to find a closer match.

The prescriptive upshot is accordingly calibrated rather than [[categorical]]. For the architects of choice environments – regulators, employers, retailers, platform designers – the evidence favours well-chosen defaults, curated subsets and transparent categorisation, measures that can ease the burden of deliberation without curtailing liberty. There is, admittedly, a tension here: defaults chosen by others raise legitimate questions about whose interests they serve, and the line between helpful curation and [[paternalism]] is contested. For individuals, the research recommends a policy of selective maximising – reserving exhaustive search for consequential decisions and cultivating deliberate satisficing elsewhere.

The deeper lesson is conceptual. Freedom of choice is valuable, but it is not reducible to the number of options on a menu; and a culture that equates the two may produce, paradoxically, people who feel less free.

text: Every spring, families across Central Asia, Iran and the Caucasus celebrate Navruz, the Persian New Year. In Uzbekistan, women stay up all night stirring huge pots of sumalak, a sweet paste made from sprouted wheat, while they sing and tell stories. In 2009 UNESCO added Navruz to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. But in a world of smartphones and fast food, why do such old [[customs|custom]] survive?

One answer is that traditions connect us to other people. Sharing the same actions at the same time creates a strong feeling of [[belonging]]. In a study in a Spanish village, scientists measured the heart rates of people walking across hot coals during a festival and of the friends and family watching them (the [[spectators|spectator]]). The heartbeats of performers and spectators began to rise and fall together – a sign of how closely the ritual [[linked|link]] them.

Rituals also help us deal with [[uncertainty]]. Researchers at Harvard found that people who performed a short ritual before a stressful task, such as singing in public, felt less anxious and performed better than those who didn't – even when the ritual was invented for the experiment. Rituals after a loss, such as funerals, seem to help people feel more in control of their grief.

Interestingly, not all traditions are ancient. In the 1980s, the historians Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger described “invented traditions” – customs that look very old but were created quite recently, often to build national identity. Many of the tartan patterns linked to particular Scottish clans, for example, date from the nineteenth century.

Traditions are not frozen. They [[adapt]] to new conditions: families now share holiday greetings by video, and young people add their own music to old celebrations. What seems to matter is not that a custom is truly ancient, but that it gives people a shared story and a sense of who they are.

text: Each March, households from the Balkans to western China mark Navruz, the ancient Persian New Year that coincides with the spring equinox. In Uzbekistan, women gather around enormous cauldrons of sumalak, taking turns to stir the sprouted-wheat paste through the night while singing and sharing stories; in Iran, families lay a table with seven symbolic items whose names begin with the letter “s”. Navruz has survived empires, revolutions and decades of official [[discouragement|discourage]], and in 2009 UNESCO inscribed it on its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity. Its persistence raises a broader question: in societies transformed by technology and mobility, why do people cling so [[tenaciously]] to old customs?

Anthropologists emphasise social [[cohesion]]. Collective rituals – synchronised movement, shared food, common songs – appear to strengthen group bonds. In a striking study at a fire-walking festival in the Spanish village of San Pedro Manrique, researchers led by Dimitris Xygalatas fitted heart-rate monitors to fire-walkers and spectators. The heart rhythms of performers and their relatives in the crowd became closely aligned, while those of unrelated visitors did not. The ritual, in a measurable sense, made people's bodies move in step.

Psychologists have added an individual dimension. Experiments by Francesca Gino and Michael Norton at Harvard found that performing even an arbitrary ritual – a few prescribed gestures before singing in front of strangers – reduced anxiety and improved performance. Other studies suggest that mourning rituals help bereaved people regain a sense of control. Rituals, it seems, [[impose|impose]] order on situations that feel uncertain or overwhelming.

Yet the authority of tradition often rests on an illusion of great age. In their influential book The Invention of Tradition, the historians Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger showed that many customs presented as ancient were in fact created in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, frequently to legitimise new nations or institutions. The association of particular tartans with particular Scottish clans, for instance, owes much to Victorian enthusiasm and commercial weavers. Such origins do not make traditions fake; they show that people have always [[fashioned|fashion]] customs to meet present needs.

This flexibility is the key to survival. Traditions that refuse to change risk becoming museum pieces, while those that adapt – incorporating new music, new media and new participants – remain alive. Diaspora communities hold Navruz celebrations in city parks thousands of miles from home, and relatives separated by migration gather around a shared screen. The [[outward]] form shifts; the underlying function – binding people together and giving them a sense of continuity – endures.

text: Every March, at the vernal equinox, a festival older than most of the world's religions unfolds across a vast arc of territory from the Balkans to Xinjiang. Navruz – literally “new day” in Persian – is marked in Uzbekistan by women who keep [[vigil]] over immense cauldrons of sumalak, taking turns to stir the sprouted-wheat mixture through the night amid song and storytelling; in Iran, by the haft-sin table of seven symbolic items; in Afghanistan and Azerbaijan, by its own constellation of customs. The festival has outlasted empires and survived periods of official hostility, and since 2009 it has featured on UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity. Its [[resilience]] invites a broader inquiry: why, in societies reshaped by urbanisation, migration and digital technology, do people remain so attached to ritual?

Anthropologists have long located the answer in social cohesion – the capacity of shared ritual to bind individuals into a group. Recent fieldwork has given this idea unusual empirical precision. At an annual fire-walking ceremony in San Pedro Manrique, a Spanish village, a team led by the anthropologist Dimitris Xygalatas recorded the heart rates of fire-walkers and onlookers. The physiological arousal of performers and of spectators who were related to them rose and fell in close synchrony, whereas that of unrelated observers did not – suggesting that collective ritual can align people's bodily states as well as their sentiments.

Experimental psychology has [[illuminated|illuminate]] the individual functions of ritual. In studies by Francesca Gino, Michael Norton and colleagues, participants who performed a brief, entirely arbitrary sequence of actions before a nerve-racking task – singing a song in front of a stranger, for instance – reported lower anxiety and performed measurably better than those who did not. Related research suggests that rituals after loss help mourners recover a sense of control. The very formality of ritual, its fixed and repeated structure, appears to impose order on experiences that would otherwise feel chaotic.

Tradition's authority, however, often depends on a perception of antiquity that does not withstand historical scrutiny. In The Invention of Tradition, published in 1983, the historians Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger argued that many customs presented as timeless were [[fabricated|fabricate]] in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, frequently to lend legitimacy to emerging nation-states and institutions. Their best-known example is the Scottish Highland tradition, whose association of specific tartans with specific clans owes more to Victorian romanticism and the marketing of textile manufacturers than to medieval practice. The point is not that invented traditions are fraudulent but that the past is continually [[repurposed|repurpose]] to serve present needs.

That adaptability is precisely what keeps tradition alive. Customs that harden into fixed performances risk becoming heritage displays rather than lived practice, whereas those that absorb new music, technologies and participants retain their [[vitality]]. Diaspora communities now celebrate Navruz in public parks in Berlin and Toronto, and families scattered by migration share the festival across video calls. The outward forms are fluid; the underlying functions – affirming belonging, marking time and offering continuity in a changing world – are remarkably [[constant]].

text: At the vernal equinox each year, a festival of [[venerable]] antiquity unfolds across a broad swathe of Eurasia, from the Balkans through Iran and the Caucasus to the Fergana Valley and Xinjiang. Navruz, the Persian “new day”, predates Islam and Christianity alike, and its local idioms are richly various: Uzbek women keep an all-night vigil over cauldrons of sumalak, stirring the sprouted-wheat paste in shifts to the accompaniment of song; Iranian households arrange the haft-sin, seven emblematic objects whose names begin with the same letter. The festival has weathered conquest, revolution and stretches of official disapproval, and in 2009 UNESCO enrolled it among humanity's intangible cultural heritage. Its endurance poses a question that modernisation theory once seemed to have answered: why, amid urbanisation, mass migration and digital saturation, does ritual not wither away?

The classic sociological answer, associated with Émile Durkheim, is that collective ritual generates and renews social solidarity – what he called “collective [[effervescence]]”. Contemporary research has lent this intuition a quantitative edge. At the fire-walking festival of San Pedro Manrique in Spain, the anthropologist Dimitris Xygalatas and colleagues monitored the heart rates of fire-walkers and spectators and found that the arousal of performers and their relatives in the crowd fluctuated in close synchrony, while that of unrelated onlookers did not. Ritual, on this evidence, does more than express a bond; it [[enacts]] one physiologically.

Experimental psychology has supplied complementary insight into ritual's private uses. In work by Francesca Gino, Michael Norton and their collaborators, participants who executed a short and wholly arbitrary series of gestures before an anxiety-provoking task – singing before a stranger, solving maths problems under evaluation – reported less anxiety and performed better than controls. Parallel studies of mourning practices suggest that ritualised responses to loss restore a sense of agency to the bereaved. The stipulated, repetitive form of ritual seems to confer a measure of predictability on circumstances that are intrinsically unpredictable.

The prestige of tradition frequently rests, however, on a claim to antiquity that history cannot sustain. Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger's The Invention of Tradition (1983) documented how many apparently immemorial customs were [[confected|confect]] in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, often to furnish emergent nation-states and institutions with a [[usable]] past. Hugh Trevor-Roper's contribution on the Scottish Highlands showed that the association of particular tartans with particular clans owed more to Victorian romanticism, a royal visit and enterprising textile manufacturers than to medieval clan practice. To call such traditions “invented” is not to call them spurious. It is to recognise that every present reworks the past it inherits, and that authenticity is less a property of origins than of continued, meaningful practice.

The same holds for Navruz itself. Under Soviet rule the festival was at times discouraged as a religious or nationalist survival, yet it persisted in private kitchens and village courtyards, only to be rehabilitated after independence as a national holiday and an emblem of statehood. Its trajectory illustrates a recurrent pattern: traditions suppressed by one regime are frequently revived, and often reshaped, by the next, acquiring new political meanings while retaining much of their domestic texture.

It is precisely this [[malleability]] that sustains tradition. Customs ossified into fixed performances drift towards the condition of heritage spectacle, preserved for tourists rather than lived by participants; those that absorb new music, media and members retain their vigour. Navruz is now celebrated in the parks of Berlin and Toronto, and families dispersed by migration convene around a shared screen to watch the sumalak simmer. The forms are [[protean]]; the functions – affirming belonging, punctuating time and offering continuity amid upheaval – are strikingly stable. Modernity, it turns out, did not abolish the need that ritual meets. If anything, by multiplying uncertainty and dissolving older communities, it may have intensified it.

text: Your postcode is the short code at the end of your address. It tells the post office where you live. But in many countries, it can also tell us something surprising: how long you will probably live.

In England, men in the [[poorest|poor]] areas live about ten years less than men in the richest areas. In some cities, two places only a few kilometres apart have very different lives. People in one area are healthier, earn more and go to better schools.
Why? Poorer areas often have more [[pollution]], fewer parks and more fast-food shops. Jobs there may be harder and pay less. People have more stress and less money for healthy food.

Where children grow up is very important. In the USA, some poor families [[moved|move]] to better areas with help from the government. Years later, the children who moved when they were young earned more money as adults than children who stayed.

This is called the “postcode lottery”: your [[chances|chance]] in life depend partly on luck – where you were born. But many people think governments can change this with better schools, homes and [[hospitals|hospital]] in poorer areas.

text: People often say that the most important day of your life is the day you were born – but the place may matter almost as much. In many countries, health, income and education are closely linked to where people live. Some call this the “postcode lottery”.

The [[differences|difference]] can be shocking. In England, official figures show that men in the most deprived areas can expect to live almost ten years less than men in the least deprived areas, and they spend far more of their lives in poor health. In 2008, a World Health Organization report found that a boy born in Calton, a poor area of Glasgow, could expect to live 28 years less than a boy born in Lenzie, a [[wealthy]] suburb just a few miles away.

Why do these gaps exist? The answer is not only about doctors and hospitals. Experts talk about the “social determinants of health” – the conditions in which people are born, grow up, work and age. Poorer neighbourhoods tend to have worse housing, more air pollution, fewer green spaces and more shops selling cheap, unhealthy food. People there are more likely to do physically hard or [[insecure]] jobs, and long-term money worries create [[stress]] that damages health.

The effects begin early. In the United States, the economist Raj Chetty studied families who received help to move from very poor neighbourhoods to better ones. Children who moved before the age of thirteen went on to earn significantly more as adults and were more likely to go to college. Children who moved as teenagers benefited less, which suggests that the number of years spent in a neighbourhood [[matters|matter]].

None of this means that a postcode decides everything. But it shows that inequality is not only about individual choices. Many researchers argue that improving schools, housing, transport and local services in poorer areas is one of the most effective ways to give every child a [[fairer]] start.

text: In 2008, a report for the World Health Organization contained a statistic that quickly became [[notorious]]. A boy born in Calton, a deprived district in the east end of Glasgow, could expect to live to around 54; a boy born in Lenzie, a [[prosperous]] commuter suburb a few miles away, could expect to reach 82. The 28-year gap was extreme, but the pattern it illustrated is found throughout the developed world: where people live is closely tied to how long, and how healthily, they live. In Britain the phenomenon is often called the “postcode lottery”.

National figures are less dramatic but still [[stark]]. In England, the Office for National Statistics reports that men in the most deprived tenth of neighbourhoods live almost a decade less than men in the least deprived tenth, and the gap in healthy life expectancy – years lived in good health – is nearly two decades. In London, researchers have mapped how life expectancy falls by up to a year for every couple of stops travelled east along certain Underground lines, from wealthy central districts to poorer outer boroughs.

The chair of the WHO commission, the epidemiologist Michael Marmot, has argued that such inequalities are not primarily the product of medical care or individual lifestyle choices but of the “social determinants of health”: the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age. Deprived areas tend to combine poorer housing, higher air pollution, fewer green spaces, more fast-food outlets, higher crime and less secure employment. Chronic financial insecurity produces stress that is linked to heart disease, depression and other illnesses. Health behaviours such as smoking matter, but they are themselves shaped by circumstances.

Neighbourhood effects also influence opportunity. Research led by the economist Raj Chetty used data on millions of Americans to show that children's chances of earning more than their parents vary [[dramatically]] between, and even within, cities. Re-examining a 1990s experiment called Moving to Opportunity, in which some low-income families were given vouchers to move to lower-poverty areas, Chetty's team found that children who moved before the age of thirteen earned roughly 31 per cent more as adults than similar children who stayed. Each extra year spent in a better neighbourhood seemed to add to the benefit.

These findings [[challenge]] the idea that outcomes depend simply on individual effort. They have also shaped policy debates. Marmot has proposed “proportionate universalism”: services available to everyone, but with resources and intensity increasing in proportion to need. Critics question how much governments can achieve, and point out that improving an area can raise rents and push poorer residents out. Yet the evidence that place shapes life chances is now difficult to [[dismiss]].

text: Few statistics in public health have travelled as far as the one published in 2008 by the World Health Organization's Commission on Social Determinants of Health. A boy born in Calton, in Glasgow's deprived East End, could expect to live to about 54; one born in Lenzie, an [[affluent]] suburb a short train ride away, to around 82. The 28-year gap was an [[outlier]], and life expectancy in Calton has since been recalculated, but it crystallised a pattern found across rich societies: place is a powerful predictor of how long people live and how much of that life is spent in good health.

At a national level the differences are less extreme but no less [[consequential]]. In England, official data show that men in the most deprived tenth of areas live nearly ten years less than those in the least deprived tenth, and the gap in healthy life expectancy approaches twenty years. Mapping exercises have made the [[gradient]] visible: along some London Underground routes, average life expectancy falls by roughly a year with every two or three stations travelled from affluent central districts into poorer outer neighbourhoods. Crucially, the relationship is not confined to the very poor. Health improves step by step with every increase in social position – what researchers call the social gradient in health.

Michael Marmot, who chaired the WHO commission, has argued that such disparities cannot be explained primarily by access to doctors or by individual choices about diet and smoking. They reflect the “causes of the causes”: the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, and the distribution of money, power and resources that shapes those conditions. Deprived neighbourhoods concentrate disadvantages – damp or overcrowded housing, polluted air, scarce green space, an abundance of cheap calorie-dense food, insecure work and higher crime. Persistent insecurity and lack of control over one's circumstances generate chronic stress, which has measurable effects on cardiovascular and mental health.

Place also shapes economic opportunity. Using anonymised tax records for tens of millions of Americans, Raj Chetty and colleagues have mapped striking variation in intergenerational mobility – the likelihood that children from low-income families will out-earn their parents – not only between regions but between neighbouring districts. Their re-analysis of the 1990s Moving to Opportunity experiment, which randomly offered some low-income families housing vouchers to relocate to lower-poverty neighbourhoods, found that children who moved before adolescence earned around 31 per cent more as adults and were more likely to attend college. The gains appeared to [[accumulate]] with each additional year of childhood spent in the better area, implying a causal effect of neighbourhood rather than mere selection.

These findings [[complicate]] narratives that attribute life outcomes chiefly to individual effort, and they have informed policy. Marmot advocates “proportionate universalism”: universal provision, with the scale and intensity of support rising in line with disadvantage. Sceptics caution that area-based regeneration can trigger gentrification, raising rents and displacing the very residents it was meant to help, and that some gaps reflect who moves where as well as what places do to people. Even so, the weight of evidence makes it hard to sustain the view that geography is merely a [[backdrop]] to individual lives. It is, to a considerable degree, part of their script.

text: Some statistics acquire a life of their own. In 2008 the World Health Organization's Commission on Social Determinants of Health reported that a boy born in Calton, in Glasgow's post-industrial East End, could expect to live to roughly 54, while one born in Lenzie, a leafy dormitory suburb a few miles north, could anticipate around 82. The figure was something of an [[aberration]] – later recalculations narrowed it – but it served as a vivid emblem of a pattern that pervades affluent societies: the map of where people live is, to a disconcerting degree, a map of how long they will live and how much of that time will be spent in good health.

National data are less lurid but scarcely more comforting. In England, men in the most deprived decile of neighbourhoods die nearly a decade earlier on average than those in the least deprived, and the disparity in healthy life expectancy approaches two decades. Researchers have rendered the gradient almost tangible by tracing how average life expectancy declines, station by station, along certain London Underground lines as they run from prosperous central districts towards poorer outer boroughs. Most significantly, the relationship is graded rather than binary: health worsens incrementally at every step down the social ladder, not merely at its foot. This “social gradient” implies that the problem cannot be confined to a residual underclass; it runs through the entire social structure.

The epidemiologist Michael Marmot, who chaired the WHO commission, has argued that these inequalities are not chiefly attributable to deficiencies in medical care or to [[feckless]] individual choices, but to what he terms “the causes of the causes”: the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, and the distribution of power, money and resources that structures them. Disadvantaged neighbourhoods tend to concentrate adversities – damp and overcrowded housing, polluted air, a [[dearth]] of green space, a [[surfeit]] of cheap, energy-dense food, precarious work and higher exposure to crime. Marmot places particular weight on control: chronic insecurity and a lack of autonomy over one's circumstances generate sustained physiological stress with measurable cardiovascular, metabolic and psychiatric consequences. Smoking and poor diet are real risks, but they cluster where hardship clusters.

Place shapes opportunity no less than health. Drawing on de-identified tax records for tens of millions of Americans, Raj Chetty and his collaborators have charted pronounced variation in intergenerational mobility – the chance that a child born into a low-income family will rise up the income distribution – between cities and even between adjacent neighbourhoods. Their re-examination of the Moving to Opportunity experiment of the 1990s, which assigned housing vouchers by lottery to some low-income families, enabling them to move to less impoverished areas, found that children who moved before their teens earned roughly 31 per cent more in adulthood and were more likely to attend college. Because the benefit rose with each additional year of exposure, the researchers concluded that neighbourhoods exert genuine causal effects rather than merely sorting families who would have prospered anyway.

Such evidence [[unsettles|unsettle]] the meritocratic narrative in which outcomes faithfully reflect effort and talent. It has also informed policy. Marmot advocates “proportionate universalism” – services available to all, with their scale and intensity calibrated to need. Critics raise legitimate objections: area-based regeneration can precipitate gentrification, inflating rents and displacing precisely the residents it was meant to benefit; and part of the geographical gradient reflects selective migration, as healthier and wealthier people move out of struggling places. Yet these qualifications refine rather than refute the central finding. Geography is not merely the stage on which individual lives are played out; it is one of the [[playwrights|playwright]].

The phrase “postcode lottery” is in one respect [[apt]] and in another misleading. It is apt because no child chooses where they are born. It is misleading because, unlike a lottery, the distribution of these outcomes is not random. It is the cumulative result of decisions – about housing, transport, schooling and investment – that societies make, and can therefore unmake.

text: If a business meeting in Zurich is planned for 9.00, people will usually be seated by 8.58. If a family dinner in Rio de Janeiro is planned for 8.00, guests may arrive at 9.00 – and nobody will think they are late. Ideas about time, it turns out, are not universal. They are part of culture.

The American anthropologist Edward T. Hall described two [[attitudes|attitude]] to time. In “monochronic” cultures, such as Germany, Switzerland or the United States, time is seen as a line divided into units. People do one thing at a time, follow schedules carefully and see [[punctuality]] as a sign of respect. In “polychronic” cultures, common in much of Latin America, the Middle East and Africa, people do several things at once, and relationships are more important than [[strict]] timetables. If a conversation with a friend is important, it is fine to arrive late for the next appointment.

In the 1990s, the psychologist Robert Levine compared the “pace of life” in thirty-one countries. His team measured how quickly people walked a short distance in city centres, how long it took to buy a stamp at a post office and how [[accurate]] public clocks were. Switzerland came first, followed by Ireland and Germany; Mexico, Brazil and Indonesia were among the slowest. In another study, Brazilian students said someone was late for a lunch appointment after about 33 minutes, while American students said so after about 19.

These differences can cause real [[conflict]]. A German manager may see a Mexican colleague's lateness as disrespect, while the colleague may see the manager's rush to start the meeting as cold and unfriendly. Neither is right or wrong; they simply follow different rules.

In a world of global business and international friendships, it helps to be [[aware]] of these hidden rules. Asking “When should I really arrive?” is not a strange question. It shows that you understand that “on time” can mean different things in different places.

text: Arrive at a business meeting in Zurich two minutes late and you may be greeted with a polite but unmistakable glance at the clock. Arrive at a family celebration in Rio de Janeiro at the time printed on the invitation and you may find the hosts still getting dressed. Few aspects of culture are as invisible – or as [[revealing]] – as attitudes to time.

The anthropologist Edward T. Hall, writing in the 1950s, introduced a distinction that is still widely used. In monochronic cultures, time is treated as a resource that can be saved, spent or wasted. People prefer to do one thing at a time, value schedules and deadlines, and regard punctuality as a mark of reliability and respect. Northern Europe and North America are typical examples. In polychronic cultures, which Hall associated with much of the Mediterranean, Latin America, the Middle East and Africa, people juggle several activities at once, plans are more [[fluid]], and maintaining relationships takes [[priority]] over sticking to the clock. Interrupting a conversation with a friend to rush to an appointment may seem far ruder than arriving late.

The psychologist Robert Levine put such ideas to an empirical test. In the 1990s, his researchers in thirty-one countries recorded how long it took pedestrians to walk sixty feet on a city pavement, how long post office clerks took to sell a stamp, and how accurate the clocks in bank windows were. Switzerland topped the ranking, with Ireland, Germany and Japan close behind; Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico were at the bottom. Levine found that faster countries tended to be wealthier, colder and more individualistic – and also had higher rates of heart disease.

Definitions of lateness [[vary]] too. When Levine taught in Brazil, he asked students how late someone could be for a lunch appointment before being considered late; the average answer was about 33 minutes, compared with about 19 among students in California. Brazilians were also more likely to see a person who was always late as relaxed and successful rather than disrespectful.

In a globalised world, these differences regularly cause [[friction]]. The business writer Erin Meyer, who studies international teams, describes scheduling as a scale running from “linear time” to “flexible time”, and notes that people often judge others' behaviour by the standards of their own culture without realising it. A German manager may read a Brazilian colleague's late arrival as unreliability; the colleague may read the manager's insistence on an exact start as coldness.

No approach is objectively correct. Monochronic cultures may be efficient at coordinating complex projects; polychronic cultures may be better at nurturing relationships and adapting to the unexpected. The practical lesson is simple: ask. Clarifying whether “eight o'clock” means eight o'clock is not naive; it is a sign of cultural [[intelligence]].

text: Few cultural assumptions are so deeply internalised that we fail to notice them until they are violated. Attitudes to time are among the most powerful of these. Turn up three minutes late to a meeting in Zurich and you may be met with a pointed glance at a watch; turn up punctually to a dinner party in Rio de Janeiro and you may find your hosts mid-shower. Each reaction feels natural to those involved, and each can seem [[baffling]] – or offensive – to an outsider.

In The Silent Language, published in 1959, the anthropologist Edward T. Hall proposed a [[dichotomy]] that has shaped thinking about intercultural communication ever since. Monochronic cultures conceive of time as linear and segmented, a scarce commodity to be scheduled, saved and spent. They favour sequential attention to tasks, adherence to plans and punctuality as a moral signal of reliability. Polychronic cultures treat time as more [[elastic]] and cyclical; people attend to multiple activities and relationships simultaneously, schedules are provisional, and the obligations of personal relationships routinely [[override]] those of the clock. Hall located northern Europe and Anglo-America at the monochronic end, and much of southern Europe, Latin America, the Arab world and sub-Saharan Africa at the polychronic end, while stressing that individuals and contexts vary considerably within any society.

The psychologist Robert Levine sought to measure such differences rather than merely describe them. In a study of thirty-one countries published in 1999, his researchers timed pedestrians walking sixty feet along uncrowded pavements, recorded how long post office clerks took to complete a standard stamp purchase, and checked the accuracy of public clocks. Switzerland emerged as the fastest country, followed by Ireland, Germany and Japan; Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico were the slowest. A faster pace of life correlated with economic vitality, a colder climate and individualistic values – and, less happily, with higher rates of coronary heart disease. Earlier, while teaching in Brazil, Levine had been struck by how differently his students defined lateness: they allowed roughly 33 minutes' grace for a lunch appointment, compared with about 19 among Californian students, and they were more inclined to [[associate]] chronic lateness with success than with disrespect.

In multinational organisations, these divergent [[norms|norm]] are a persistent source of misunderstanding. The management scholar Erin Meyer places cultures on a scheduling scale from “linear time” to “flexible time” and observes that the problem is rarely the difference itself but the tendency to interpret others' behaviour through one's own norms. A Swiss manager may [[construe]] a Brazilian colleague's late arrival as unreliability, while the colleague perceives the manager's insistence on an exact start as rigid and impersonal.

Neither orientation is intrinsically superior. Monochronic norms facilitate coordination in large, complex enterprises; polychronic norms foster relationships, improvisation and responsiveness to the unexpected. The most useful skill is metacognitive: recognising that one's own sense of what counts as “on time” is a cultural convention rather than a universal law – and having the humility to ask.

text: Some of the most consequential features of a culture are those its members never think to articulate. Conceptions of time belong to this category. A three-minute delay in Zurich may earn a reproving glance at a wristwatch; arriving at the appointed hour for a dinner in Rio de Janeiro may mean encountering one's hosts still in a bathrobe. To insiders, each response is simply common sense. To outsiders, each can appear inexplicable, even insulting – a reminder that the temporal order we inhabit is no less a social construction than the language we speak.

Edward T. Hall's The Silent Language (1959) offered an enduring, if schematic, framework for these differences. Monochronic cultures, in Hall's account, apprehend time as linear, divisible and scarce – a commodity to be budgeted and not squandered. They privilege sequential attention to tasks, fidelity to schedules and punctuality as an index of trustworthiness. Polychronic cultures construe time as more elastic and recursive; their members attend to several activities and interlocutors at once, treat schedules as provisional and accord personal obligations [[precedence]] over appointments. Hall situated northern Europe and Anglo-America towards the monochronic pole and much of the Mediterranean, Latin America, the Arab world and sub-Saharan Africa towards the polychronic one – while cautioning, as his popularisers often did not, that the distinction describes tendencies rather than [[immutable]] national characters, and that urban professionals in polychronic societies may be scrupulously punctual at work while remaining relaxed at home.

Robert Levine's comparative research lent these generalisations quantitative texture. His team's 1999 study of thirty-one countries combined three indicators – the time taken by pedestrians to cover sixty feet on uncrowded downtown pavements, the speed with which postal clerks completed a standardised stamp purchase, and the accuracy of public clocks. Switzerland headed the index, with Ireland, Germany and Japan in close pursuit; Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico occupied the other extreme. A brisk tempo correlated with economic productivity, a cool climate and individualism – but also with elevated mortality from coronary heart disease, a [[sobering]] coda to any celebration of efficiency. Levine's earlier experience as a visiting professor in Brazil, where students tolerated some 33 minutes' delay for a lunch appointment against roughly 19 among their Californian counterparts, and where habitual lateness was more readily read as a marker of status than of disrespect, had first alerted him to the depth of the divergence.

In multinational workplaces these [[tacit]] norms are a perennial source of [[attribution]] error – the tendency to explain others' conduct by reference to their character rather than their context. The management scholar Erin Meyer arrays cultures along a continuum from “linear time” to “flexible time” and argues that friction arises less from difference than from misinterpretation: a Swiss executive may impute unreliability to a Brazilian colleague's late arrival, while the colleague discerns in the executive's insistence on an exact start an impersonal rigidity that sits ill with the building of trust.

It would be [[parochial]] to rank these orientations. Monochronic norms lend themselves to the coordination of large, interdependent enterprises; polychronic norms excel at sustaining relationships and responding [[nimbly]] to contingency. Moreover, globalisation and digital calendars are blurring the poles: polychronic cities are increasingly governed by the clock at work, while monochronic workplaces experiment with flexible hours. What remains indispensable is a kind of metacognitive humility – the recognition that one's intuition of what “on time” means is a convention absorbed in childhood rather than a law of nature, and that the simplest remedy for temporal misunderstanding is also the least glamorous: asking.

text: For most of human history, populations looked like pyramids: many children at the bottom and few old people at the top. That shape is changing. Around the world, people are living longer and having fewer children, and the result is a population that is getting older every year.

The rise in life expectancy is one of humanity's greatest [[achievements|achievement]]. In 1950, the average person could expect to live to about forty-six; today the figure is over seventy. Better nutrition, vaccines, clean water and medical care have saved millions of lives.

At the same time, birth rates have fallen sharply. For a population to stay the same size without migration, each woman needs to have around 2.1 children on average – the so-called replacement level. Many countries are now far below it. South Korea's rate has fallen below one child per woman, the lowest in the world. Reasons include the high cost of housing and education, long working hours, and the [[difficulty]] women face in combining careers and family.

An older population creates economic challenges. When there are fewer people of working age and more retirees, governments collect less tax but spend more on [[pensions|pension]] and healthcare. Many countries have raised the [[retirement]] age; in 2023, France's decision to raise it from 62 to 64 led to months of protests. Some governments encourage immigration, while others invest in technology to support older people.

Not every country is ageing at the same speed. Much of Africa and parts of Central Asia still have young, fast-growing populations, which brings its own challenges, such as creating enough jobs. And older people are not just a cost. Many work, [[volunteer]], care for grandchildren and spend money in the so-called “silver economy”. An ageing world is not necessarily a declining one – but it will need to [[rethink]] how work, family and care are organised.

text: Demographers sometimes describe the twenty-first century as the century of ageing. For most of history, human populations were shaped like pyramids, with large numbers of children at the base and a narrow tip of older people. Across much of the world that pyramid is turning into something closer to a column – and in some countries, an [[inverted]] pyramid. The United Nations projects that by 2050 roughly one person in six worldwide will be over sixty-five, up from one in eleven in 2019.

Two forces drive this transformation. The first is a dramatic increase in [[longevity]]. Global life expectancy at birth has risen from around forty-six in 1950 to over seventy today, thanks to falling child mortality, vaccination, better nutrition and advances in medicine – an [[unprecedented]] achievement. The second is the collapse in fertility. A total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to keep a population stable without migration. The global average has fallen to roughly 2.3, and in many countries it is far lower: in Italy and Spain around 1.2, and in South Korea, the world's lowest, below 0.8. Economists and sociologists cite the rising cost of housing and childcare, longer periods of education, insecure employment and the persistent difficulty of [[reconciling|reconcile]] career and family, especially for women.

The economic implications are significant. As the working-age population shrinks relative to the number of retirees, the “old-age dependency ratio” rises, putting pressure on pension systems and public finances, which in many countries rely on current workers' contributions to pay current retirees. Health and long-term care costs grow too. Governments have responded in various ways: raising the retirement age – France's 2023 increase from 62 to 64 provoked mass protests – encouraging older people to keep working, offering incentives to have children, and admitting more immigrants. Results have been mixed; generous family policies in countries such as Hungary have had only modest effects on birth rates.

Yet ageing is not a universal story. Much of sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Central and South Asia still have young, rapidly growing populations, and by the end of the century Africa may be home to a large share of the world's young people. These countries face different challenges: providing education and jobs for millions of young people entering the labour market each year.

It is also a mistake to view older people simply as a [[burden]]. Many remain healthy and active far longer than previous generations, contributing through paid work, volunteering, caring for grandchildren and spending in the growing “silver economy”. The real question is whether societies can [[adapt]] – redesigning workplaces, pensions, housing and cities – quickly enough to turn longer lives into a benefit rather than a strain.

text: Demographers have taken to calling the twenty-first century the century of ageing, and the label is apt. For almost all of human history, age structures resembled pyramids: broad bases of children tapering to a narrow apex of the old. That geometry is being [[upended|upend]]. The United Nations projects that by 2050 roughly one person in six on the planet will be aged over sixty-five, compared with one in eleven in 2019, and that the number of people aged eighty or over will roughly triple. In several East Asian and southern European countries, the pyramid is already becoming inverted.

Two developments underlie this transformation. The first is a historic triumph: global life expectancy at birth has climbed from around forty-six in 1950 to above seventy today, propelled by plummeting infant and child mortality, mass vaccination, improved sanitation and nutrition, and advances in medical treatment. The second is the steep and, in many places, [[unanticipated|unanticipate]] decline in fertility. Replacement level – the rate at which a population sustains itself without migration – is around 2.1 births per woman. The global total fertility rate has slid to roughly 2.3, and more than half of all countries now fall below replacement. Italy and Spain hover around 1.2; South Korea, at under 0.8, has recorded the lowest rates ever measured in a nation not at war. Explanations range from the costs of housing, childcare and increasingly lengthy education to labour-market insecurity, demanding work cultures and the disproportionate burden of domestic labour that falls on women.

The fiscal consequences are considerable. Pay-as-you-go pension systems, in which today's workers fund today's retirees, come under strain as the old-age dependency ratio climbs, while spending on healthcare and long-term care rises with the number of the very old. Governments have deployed an assortment of responses. Raising statutory retirement ages is politically [[fraught]], as France discovered when its 2023 reform lifting the minimum age from 62 to 64 provoked months of strikes and demonstrations. Pro-natalist policies – generous parental leave, cash bonuses, tax breaks for large families – have generally produced only modest and often temporary increases in births, as Hungary's costly programme illustrates. Immigration can [[offset]] workforce decline, but it raises its own political controversies.

Ageing is, however, far from uniform. Much of sub-Saharan Africa retains high fertility and very young populations, as do parts of South and Central Asia, and Africa's share of the world's young people is set to grow substantially. For these countries the pressing task is not supporting retirees but educating and employing vast [[cohorts|cohort]] of young people – a potential “demographic dividend” if jobs can be created, or a source of instability if they cannot.

It is equally important to resist a narrative of [[inevitable]] decline. Today's older adults are, on average, healthier, better educated and more active than their predecessors, and they contribute substantially through work, volunteering, unpaid care and consumption. The central policy challenge is one of adaptation: redesigning pensions, workplaces, housing and urban environments so that longer lives become an opportunity rather than a [[liability]].

text: Demographers have begun, with some justification, to call the twenty-first century the century of ageing. Throughout nearly all of human history, the distribution of populations by age resembled a pyramid: a broad base of children, steadily narrowing towards a slender apex of the old. That geometry is now being [[inverted|invert]]. The United Nations projects that by mid-century roughly one person in six worldwide will be over sixty-five, as against one in eleven in 2019, and that the population aged eighty and above will approximately triple. In Japan, Italy and South Korea, the pyramid already resembles an urn, swollen in the middle and upper ranges and pinched at the base.

The transformation is the product of two distinct, if related, revolutions. The first is the [[conquest]] of premature death. Global life expectancy at birth has risen from around forty-six in 1950 to above seventy, reflecting precipitous declines in infant and child mortality, the diffusion of vaccines and antibiotics, sanitation, nutrition and the control of infectious disease – a collective achievement without historical parallel. The second is the collapse of fertility. Replacement-level fertility, the rate at which a population reproduces itself in the absence of migration, stands at about 2.1 births per woman. The global figure has fallen to around 2.3, more than half of all countries now sit below replacement, and some have descended to levels demographers once regarded as implausible: roughly 1.2 in Italy and Spain, and under 0.8 in South Korea, the lowest recorded in peacetime. The causes are overdetermined – the escalating costs of housing and childcare, ever-lengthening education, precarious early careers, gruelling work cultures and the persistence of an unequal domestic division of labour that penalises women who combine employment with motherhood.

The fiscal implications are [[formidable]]. Pay-as-you-go pension systems, which transfer resources from current workers to current retirees, are strained as the old-age dependency ratio rises, while expenditure on healthcare and long-term care climbs with the number of the very old. Policy responses have been various and, frequently, contentious. Raising statutory retirement ages is economically logical but politically combustible, as France's 2023 reform – lifting the minimum age from 62 to 64 – demonstrated through months of strikes. Pro-natalist measures, from extended parental leave to cash payments and tax exemptions for mothers of several children, have yielded effects that are modest, costly and often [[transient]]: Hungary has devoted a substantial share of GDP to family policy with only limited demographic return. Immigration can [[mitigate]] labour shortages, but its political salience has rarely been higher.

Ageing is, moreover, profoundly uneven. Much of sub-Saharan Africa, together with parts of South and Central Asia, retains high fertility and youthful age structures, and Africa's share of the world's young people is projected to rise sharply. For these societies the imperative is not financing retirement but absorbing successive cohorts of young adults into education and productive employment. Success could yield a “demographic dividend” of the kind that helped propel East Asia's growth; failure could breed unemployment and instability. The global demographic map is thus [[bifurcating|bifurcate]]: one half of the world grappling with too few young people, the other with too few jobs for them.

None of this warrants the apocalyptic tone that often attends discussions of ageing. Older adults today are, on average, healthier, better educated and more active than any previous generation of their age, and their contributions – through paid work, volunteering, informal care and consumption – are substantial and frequently uncounted. Indeed, some economists argue that conventional dependency ratios exaggerate the burden by assuming that everyone over sixty-five is economically inactive. The challenge is less demographic than institutional: whether pensions, labour markets, housing and cities can be redesigned with sufficient imagination to make longevity the dividend it ought to be rather than the [[predicament]] it is often portrayed as.

text: Watching the news, you might think that countries do nothing but argue. Yet behind the headlines, governments cooperate every day on thousands of issues, from air travel and postal services to fighting disease. Why do countries – even rivals – choose to work together?

One reason is that some problems simply cannot be solved by one country alone. In 1985, British scientists reported a huge “hole” in the ozone layer over Antarctica, caused by chemicals used in fridges and spray cans. Two years later, countries signed the Montreal Protocol to phase out these chemicals. Every member of the United Nations eventually [[joined|join]], and scientists now expect the ozone layer to recover over the coming decades. It is often called the most successful environmental agreement in history.

Another reason is [[mutual]] benefit. Trade agreements allow countries to sell what they produce best and buy what others produce more cheaply. Organisations such as the World Trade Organization set rules that make this trade more [[predictable]].

Cooperation can even happen between enemies. In 1959, at the height of the Cold War, the United States, the Soviet Union and ten other countries signed the Antarctic Treaty, agreeing that the continent would be used only for peaceful purposes and science. Decades later, American and Russian astronauts shared the International Space Station, even when relations on Earth were [[tense]].

Scientists who study cooperation have found that it is easier when countries expect to deal with each other again and again. In the 1980s, the political scientist Robert Axelrod ran a computer tournament to find the best strategy in a game where players could cooperate or cheat. The winner was a simple rule: cooperate first, then copy what the other player did last time. This suggests that trust is built step by step – and that [[reputation]] matters. Cooperation is never guaranteed, but it is more common, and more [[rational]], than the headlines suggest.

text: News coverage of international politics tends to focus on conflict: trade wars, diplomatic disputes, military tensions. Less visible, but far more common, is cooperation. Governments coordinate air traffic, share weather data, set technical standards for everything from telephone networks to shipping containers, and work together to track and contain [[outbreaks|outbreak]] of disease. Why do [[sovereign]] states, each pursuing its own interests, so often choose to collaborate?

The most straightforward answer is that many problems are transnational. Pollution, pandemics and financial crises ignore borders, and no country can solve them alone. The clearest success story is the protection of the ozone layer. After British Antarctic Survey scientists reported in 1985 that the stratospheric ozone over Antarctica was being severely depleted, governments moved with unusual speed. The 1987 Montreal Protocol committed signatories to phase out chlorofluorocarbons and related chemicals, and it later became the first UN treaty to be ratified by every member state. Scientists now project that the ozone layer will return to its 1980 condition over most of the world by around 2040 and over Antarctica by the 2060s.

A second explanation emphasises mutual gain. Economists have long argued that trade allows countries to specialise in what they do relatively well, making everyone better off. International institutions such as the World Trade Organization reduce the costs of cooperation by setting shared rules, monitoring [[compliance]] and providing ways to settle disputes.

Strikingly, cooperation can survive even deep [[hostility]]. In 1959, at the height of the Cold War, twelve countries including the United States and the Soviet Union signed the Antarctic Treaty, freezing territorial claims and reserving the continent for peaceful scientific research. Decades later, American and Russian astronauts continued to work side by side aboard the International Space Station despite worsening relations on the ground.

Game theory offers insight into why such cooperation is possible. In the “prisoner's dilemma”, two players each gain by cheating, yet both end up worse off than if they had cooperated. When the game is played only once, cheating is tempting. But in the 1980s the political scientist Robert Axelrod showed, through computer tournaments, that when the game is repeated, a simple strategy called “tit for tat” – cooperate first, then [[mirror]] the other side's previous move – performs remarkably well. Repetition creates a “shadow of the future”: the expectation of future interaction makes betrayal costly.

None of this means cooperation is easy. Agreements can collapse when powerful states withdraw, and problems such as climate change, where costs are immediate and benefits [[diffuse]], have proved far harder to solve than the ozone hole. But the record shows that, with the right incentives and institutions, rivals can and do find reasons to work together.

text: International politics is usually reported as a [[catalogue]] of quarrels. Yet the mundane reality of global affairs is one of pervasive cooperation. Governments jointly regulate civil aviation and shipping, allocate radio frequencies, harmonise technical standards, share meteorological and epidemiological data and coordinate responses to financial shocks. The puzzle, for scholars of international relations, is why this cooperation occurs at all in a system with no world government – an “[[anarchic]]” order, in the technical sense, in which each state is ultimately responsible for its own security and interests.

One answer lies in the nature of the problems themselves. Many of the most pressing challenges are transboundary: air and water pollution, pandemics, financial contagion and climate change respect no frontiers. The protection of the ozone layer remains the paradigmatic success. When scientists from the British Antarctic Survey reported in 1985 that springtime ozone over Antarctica had fallen dramatically, the finding [[galvanised|galvanise]] diplomats with remarkable speed. The Montreal Protocol, agreed in 1987 and repeatedly strengthened, committed states to phase out chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting substances; in 2009 it became the first treaty in UN history to achieve universal ratification. Assessments now project recovery of the ozone layer to 1980 levels over most of the globe by about 2040, and over Antarctica by the mid-2060s.

Liberal theorists of international relations stress the role of institutions in making such cooperation durable. By establishing rules, monitoring behaviour and offering mechanisms for resolving disputes, bodies such as the World Trade Organization reduce uncertainty and the costs of negotiating each issue afresh. Interdependence also raises the price of conflict: states that trade heavily with one another have strong incentives to keep relations stable.

Cooperation can persist even amid profound [[antagonism]]. The Antarctic Treaty of 1959, signed by twelve states including both Cold War superpowers, suspended territorial claims and dedicated the continent to peaceful science – an arrangement that endures today. The International Space Station, assembled from the late 1990s by the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada, kept operating through periods of sharply deteriorating relations, its crews [[interdependent|interdepend]] for survival in orbit.

Game theory helps to explain how self-interested actors sustain cooperation. In the classic prisoner's dilemma, each player is individually better off defecting, yet mutual defection leaves both worse off than mutual cooperation. Robert Axelrod's influential computer tournaments in the early 1980s showed that when the game is repeated indefinitely, [[reciprocal]] strategies such as “tit for tat” – begin by cooperating, then replicate the opponent's previous move – tend to prevail. The prospect of future encounters, what Axelrod called “the shadow of the future”, makes betrayal costly and reputation valuable.

None of this guarantees success. Agreements [[unravel|unravel]] when major powers withdraw or when the benefits of cheating are high. Climate change, in which the costs of action fall on present generations while benefits are spread across the world and into the future, has proved a far harder collective-action problem than ozone depletion. Yet the historical record suggests that cooperation is not a naive aspiration. Under the right conditions, it is the rational choice of states pursuing their own interests.

text: If one judged international affairs by the evening news, one might conclude that states do little but [[feud]]. The [[quotidian]] reality is otherwise. Behind the headlines, governments jointly administer the rules of civil aviation and maritime navigation, apportion the radio spectrum, harmonise technical standards, pool meteorological and epidemiological intelligence and coordinate their responses to financial crises. For theorists of international relations, this pervasive collaboration poses a genuine puzzle. The international system is “anarchic” – not chaotic, but lacking any authority above the state capable of enforcing agreements. Why, in such a system, should self-regarding governments bind themselves to one another at all?

Part of the answer lies in the character of the problems. A growing share of the hazards states confront are transboundary – atmospheric pollution, pandemic disease, financial contagion, climate change – and are therefore [[refractory]] to unilateral solution. The protection of the ozone layer remains the textbook case. In 1985 researchers from the British Antarctic Survey published evidence of a precipitous springtime decline in stratospheric ozone over Antarctica. Within two years governments had concluded the Montreal Protocol, committing themselves to phase out chlorofluorocarbons and related compounds; successive amendments tightened its terms, and in 2009 it became the first treaty in the history of the United Nations to secure universal ratification. Scientific assessments now anticipate a return to 1980 ozone levels across most latitudes by around 2040 and over Antarctica by the mid-2060s – a rare instance in which a global environmental threat was identified, negotiated and largely neutralised within a single working lifetime.

Liberal institutionalists argue that such outcomes depend on institutions that lower the transaction costs of cooperation: by codifying rules, monitoring compliance and furnishing procedures for settling disputes, organisations such as the World Trade Organization [[obviate]] the need to renegotiate each bargain from scratch and make defection more visible. Dense economic interdependence, meanwhile, raises the opportunity cost of conflict. Realists remain sceptical, contending that institutions merely reflect the distribution of power and that cooperation endures only so long as it suits the strongest states – a scepticism periodically vindicated when major powers abandon agreements they find inconvenient.

Cooperation has nonetheless proved capable of surviving acute [[enmity]]. The Antarctic Treaty, concluded in 1959 by twelve states including both Cold War superpowers, froze territorial claims and consecrated the continent to peaceful science; it remains in force. The International Space Station, assembled from 1998 by the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada, continued to function through repeated diplomatic crises, its crews bound by a mutual dependence that geopolitics could not easily sever.

Game theory supplies the most [[parsimonious]] explanation of how egoists come to cooperate. In the prisoner's dilemma, each party's dominant strategy is to defect, yet mutual defection yields an outcome both regard as inferior to mutual cooperation. Robert Axelrod's celebrated computer tournaments of the early 1980s demonstrated that in an indefinitely repeated game, conditionally cooperative strategies – most famously “tit for tat”, which opens with cooperation and thereafter reciprocates the opponent's last move – outperform more exploitative rivals. What sustains cooperation is “the shadow of the future”: the anticipation of continued interaction renders betrayal costly and reputation an asset worth protecting.

The limits are equally instructive. Cooperation is most fragile where the temptation to free-ride is greatest and the shadow of the future shortest. Climate change epitomises the difficulty: mitigation imposes [[concentrated]] costs on present generations, while its benefits are diffuse, delayed and shared by non-contributors – which helps to explain why it has proved immeasurably harder to resolve than the ozone problem. Yet the record of the past century suggests that cooperation is neither a utopian ideal nor an anomaly. Under conditions that can be identified and, to some extent, engineered, it is what rational states do.

text: Sugary drinks are one of the biggest sources of sugar in many people's diets, especially children's. A single can of cola can contain around 35 grams of sugar – more than the daily [[maximum]] that health organisations recommend for a young child. Because these drinks contain a lot of calories but don't make us feel full, doctors link them to obesity, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay.

To [[tackle]] the problem, more than fifty countries and cities have introduced taxes on sugary drinks. One of the first large examples was Mexico, which in 2014 added a tax of one peso per litre, raising prices by about ten per cent. A study found that purchases of taxed drinks fell by around six per cent in the first year, and by more among poorer households, while sales of bottled water rose.

The United Kingdom chose a different design. Its Soft Drinks Industry Levy, which started in 2018, charges manufacturers more for drinks with more sugar: drinks with over five grams per 100 millilitres pay a lower rate, and those with over eight grams pay a higher one. Companies had two years' warning, and many reformulated their products – cutting the sugar to avoid the tax. As a result, the amount of sugar sold in soft drinks fell by around a third, even though people kept buying similar [[quantities|quantity]] of drinks.

The taxes are [[controversial]]. Critics call them a “nanny state” policy and argue that adults should make their own choices. Others point out that the taxes are regressive: poorer people spend a larger share of their income on them. text: Sugar-sweetened beverages have become a favourite target of public health policy, and for understandable reasons. A standard can of cola contains around 35 grams of sugar, roughly the entire recommended daily limit for an adult and well above that for a child. Liquid calories appear to be poorly [[compensated|compensate]] for – people who drink them do not eat correspondingly less – and high consumption is associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes and dental decay. The World Health Organization now recommends taxes that raise the price of such drinks by at least 20 per cent.

Mexico, which had one of the world's highest rates of soft-drink consumption, became an influential test case in 2014, when it imposed an excise tax of one peso per litre, increasing prices by around ten per cent. Researchers who analysed household shopping data found that purchases of taxed drinks fell by about six per cent in the first year and twelve per cent by its final month, with the largest reductions among the poorest households. Purchases of untaxed drinks, mainly bottled water, rose.

The United Kingdom adopted a cleverer design. Rather than taxing consumers directly, its Soft Drinks Industry Levy, announced in 2016 and introduced in April 2018, charges producers according to sugar content: 18 pence per litre for drinks with more than five grams of sugar per 100 millilitres and 24 pence for those above eight grams. The two-year gap between announcement and implementation gave manufacturers an incentive to reformulate, and many did, lowering sugar content below the [[thresholds|threshold]]. Studies suggest that the total amount of sugar sold in soft drinks fell by around a third, while the volume of drinks sold barely changed. The tax, in other words, changed products rather than habits – arguably a more [[effective]] outcome.

Not every experiment has been as smooth. When Philadelphia taxed sweetened drinks in 2017, sales in the city dropped sharply, but a significant part of the fall was offset by residents buying drinks in neighbouring areas without the tax – a reminder that local taxes can be [[circumvented|circumvent]].

Opposition to such taxes comes from several directions. The drinks industry argues that they cost jobs and unfairly single out one product. Libertarian critics object to government “nannying”. Others note that the taxes are regressive, taking a larger share of income from poorer households. Supporters counter that the poor also bear the greatest burden of diet-related illness and therefore stand to gain most, especially if [[revenue]] is spent on them – the UK, for instance, earmarked funds for school sport and breakfast clubs.

The long-term effect on obesity remains [[contested]], since weight is influenced by many factors. But sugar taxes demonstrate that fiscal policy can shift both consumer behaviour and industry practice – and that the design of a tax can matter as much as its size.

text: Few consumer products have attracted as much attention from health policymakers as sugar-sweetened beverages. The case against them is [[cumulative]]. A standard can of cola contains roughly 35 grams of sugar – approximately the full daily allowance recommended for an adult and considerably more than that for a child. Liquid calories appear to be poorly registered by the body's appetite mechanisms, so that consumers do not offset them by eating less, and heavy consumption is associated with weight gain, type 2 diabetes and dental caries. Since 2016 the World Health Organization has advocated taxes that raise retail prices by at least a fifth.

Mexico supplied the first large-scale national test. In 2014 the government imposed an excise of one peso per litre, raising prices by roughly ten per cent in a country with some of the highest per capita consumption in the world. Analyses of household purchasing data found that purchases of taxed beverages fell by about six per cent over the first year, reaching a twelve per cent reduction by December, with the steepest declines among low-income households – precisely the group of greatest concern to public health researchers. Purchases of untaxed alternatives, chiefly bottled water, increased.

The United Kingdom's approach was more [[ingenious]]. Its Soft Drinks Industry Levy, announced in 2016 and implemented in April 2018, is levied on producers and importers rather than shoppers and is tiered by sugar concentration: 18 pence per litre above five grams per 100 millilitres, and 24 pence above eight grams. Crucially, the two-year interval between announcement and implementation allowed manufacturers to escape the levy altogether by reformulating, and many major brands did so, reducing sugar content below the thresholds. Evaluations indicate that the sugar sold in soft drinks fell by around a third between 2015 and 2019, while sales volumes were broadly maintained. The levy thus operated less by deterring consumers than by reshaping the food environment – arguably the more [[durable]] route to change.

Implementation has not always been straightforward. Philadelphia's 2017 tax of 1.5 cents per ounce, which also covered artificially sweetened drinks, produced a steep fall in sales within the city, but cross-border shopping in untaxed suburbs offset a substantial proportion of the reduction, illustrating the [[leakage]] to which local taxes are prone.

Opposition draws on economic, philosophical and distributive arguments. The beverage industry contends that the taxes destroy jobs and arbitrarily single out one product among many sources of sugar. Libertarians object on principle to what they regard as [[paternalistic]] interference in adult choices. Critics on the left point out that such taxes are regressive, absorbing a larger share of poorer households' income. Defenders respond that the health benefits are likewise [[progressive]], since diet-related disease is concentrated among the poor, and that the regressive effect can be neutralised by spending the revenue on those households – as the UK did by funding school sport and breakfast programmes.

Whether sugar taxes measurably reduce obesity over the long term is still [[debated]]; body weight reflects many interacting factors, and causal effects are difficult to isolate. What the evidence already shows is that fiscal policy can alter both consumer behaviour and corporate product design, and that a well-designed tax may achieve more through what companies do to avoid it than through the revenue it raises.
