text: Sugar-sweetened beverages occupy a peculiar place in the [[demonology]] of public health. They are not the only source of excess sugar in modern diets, but they are among the most concentrated and the least satiating. A standard can of cola delivers some 35 grams of sugar – roughly an adult's entire recommended daily allowance and far more than a child's – and the evidence suggests that calories consumed in liquid form escape the compensatory mechanisms of appetite, so that drinkers do not eat commensurately less. High consumption is associated with weight gain, type 2 diabetes and dental caries, and since 2016 the World Health Organization has urged governments to impose taxes raising retail prices by at least a fifth.

Mexico, among the world's heaviest consumers of soft drinks, provided the first national-scale experiment. Its 2014 excise of one peso per litre raised prices by around ten per cent. Analyses of household scanner data found that purchases of taxed beverages declined by roughly six per cent in the first year, reaching a twelve per cent reduction by the year's end, with the sharpest falls among the poorest households – the very population in which diet-related disease was most [[entrenched]]. Purchases of untaxed alternatives, predominantly bottled water, rose correspondingly.

The United Kingdom pursued a more sophisticated architecture. The Soft Drinks Industry Levy, announced in 2016 and in force from April 2018, falls on producers and importers rather than directly on consumers and is graduated by sugar density: 18 pence per litre for drinks exceeding five grams per 100 millilitres and 24 pence above eight grams. The [[decisive]] design feature was the two-year interval between announcement and implementation, which gave manufacturers a straightforward means of avoiding the levy entirely – reformulation. Major brands duly reduced sugar content below the thresholds, and evaluations suggest that the quantity of sugar sold through soft drinks fell by around a third between 2015 and 2019, while sales volumes held broadly steady. The levy succeeded, in effect, by altering the supply side of the market: it reshaped the products on the shelf rather than relying on consumers to resist them – an approach that exploits [[inertia]] rather than fighting it.

Less elegant designs have proved more [[porous]]. Philadelphia's 2017 levy of 1.5 cents per ounce, which also extended to artificially sweetened drinks, was followed by a steep fall in sales within city limits, but a substantial share of that fall was offset by residents shopping in untaxed suburbs – the cross-border leakage to which subnational taxes are structurally vulnerable.

The political economy of sugar taxes is fraught. The beverage industry contends that they destroy jobs and arbitrarily stigmatise one product among many. Libertarians object in principle to paternalistic interference with adult choice, a charge distilled in the epithet “nanny state”. From the left comes the objection that excise taxes are regressive, consuming a larger fraction of poorer households' budgets. Proponents reply that the health gains are correspondingly progressive, since the burden of diet-related disease falls disproportionately on the poor, and that regressivity can be reversed by [[hypothecating|hypothecate]] revenue to the households that pay it – the rationale behind the UK's allocation of levy receipts to school sport and breakfast programmes. Behavioural economists add that a tax which changes defaults is arguably less coercive than one that relies on repeatedly penalising individual purchases.

Whether these measures will produce detectable reductions in obesity remains genuinely [[moot]]: body weight is the product of countless interacting influences, and isolating the effect of a single fiscal instrument is methodologically formidable. What the accumulated evidence does establish is that taxation can modify not only individual consumption but corporate formulation, and that the most consequential effect of a well-designed levy may lie not in the revenue it collects but in the behaviour it induces among those determined not to pay it.

text: Many big rivers flow through more than one country. The Nile flows through eleven countries in Africa. In Central Asia, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya start in the mountains and flow through several countries before they reach the Aral Sea.

Everybody needs water – for drinking, for farms and for [[electricity]]. When one country uses a lot of river water, there is less for the countries further down the river. This can cause [[arguments|argument]].

The Aral Sea shows what can happen. Fifty years ago, it was one of the biggest lakes in the world. Then a lot of river water was used to grow cotton. Today, most of the sea has [[disappeared|disappear]], and old fishing boats lie in the desert.

Some people say that in the future, countries will fight wars about water. But scientists who studied river history found something surprising: countries [[agree]] about water much more often than they fight. India and Pakistan, for example, signed a water treaty in 1960, and it worked for many years.
Sharing a river is not easy. But when countries talk, share information and make fair rules, water can bring them [[closer|close]] together.

text: Rivers ignore borders. Around 300 river basins in the world are shared by two or more countries, and about 40 per cent of the world's population lives in them. When a river crosses a border, every country's use of water [[affects|affect]] its neighbours. A dam upstream can mean less water downstream; pollution in one country can poison fish in another.

Central Asia knows this well. The region's two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, rise in the mountains of Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan and flow through Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan. In the Soviet period, huge amounts of their water were diverted to [[irrigate]] cotton fields. As a result, the Aral Sea, once the world's fourth-largest lake, shrank to a small fraction of its former size, leaving a salty desert and destroying the local fishing industry. Today, countries upstream want water for hydroelectric power in winter, while those downstream need it for farms in summer – a classic source of [[tension]].

Similar debates exist elsewhere. On the Nile, Ethiopia built a giant dam to produce electricity, while Egypt, which depends on the river for almost all its fresh water, feared its supply would fall. Years of negotiations followed.

Many journalists have predicted “water wars”. However, researchers led by Aaron Wolf at Oregon State University studied thousands of events involving shared rivers over half a century and found that cooperation was far more common than conflict, and that no modern war had been fought mainly over water. Countries usually prefer to sign agreements, because fighting is expensive and rivers are hard to [[defend]].

The Indus Waters Treaty is a famous example. Signed by India and Pakistan in 1960 with help from the World Bank, it divided the rivers of the Indus system between the two countries and survived several wars between them. However, it has come under growing pressure in recent years, showing that even successful agreements need trust to [[survive]]. Climate change, which is shrinking glaciers and making rainfall less [[predictable]], will make good cooperation even more important.

text: Some 310 river basins cross international borders, together supplying water to around 40 per cent of the world's population. Along each of them, the choices of one country – to build a dam, divert water for irrigation or discharge pollution – [[ripple|ripple]] downstream to its neighbours. The geography of water creates [[asymmetries|asymmetry]] of power: upstream states control the flow, while downstream states depend on what is left.

Few regions illustrate the stakes better than Central Asia. The Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers originate in the high mountains of Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan before crossing the plains of Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan. From the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted vast quantities of their water into irrigation canals to grow cotton in the desert. The consequence was one of the twentieth century's worst environmental disasters: the Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake on Earth, shrank by roughly 90 per cent, leaving behind a salt-encrusted plain, ruined fisheries and dust storms carrying pesticide residues. Since independence, the region's states have had to [[balance]] competing needs – upstream countries wish to release water through hydropower dams in winter when they need electricity, whereas downstream farmers need it in summer. Afghanistan's construction of the Qosh Tepa canal, designed to draw water from the Amu Darya, has added a new source of concern.

Similar tensions run through other basins. Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, begun in 2011 to generate electricity for a country where millions lacked power, alarmed Egypt, which relies on the Nile for nearly all its fresh water. Despite years of negotiations involving Sudan, the three countries struggled to agree on rules for filling and operating the reservoir.

It is tempting to conclude that water shortages will lead to “water wars”. The historical evidence suggests otherwise. Researchers at Oregon State University, led by the geographer Aaron Wolf, compiled a database of thousands of interactions over shared rivers during the second half of the twentieth century. They found that cooperative events outnumbered conflictive ones by roughly two to one, that most disputes were settled through negotiation, and that no modern war had been fought primarily over water. Hundreds of international water treaties have been signed.

The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, brokered by the World Bank, is often cited as proof that cooperation can [[withstand]] hostility: it allocated the eastern rivers of the Indus system to India and the western rivers to Pakistan, and endured through several wars. Yet it has come under increasing strain, and in 2025 India announced that it was suspending its participation – a reminder that treaties depend on political will.

As climate change shrinks mountain glaciers and makes rainfall more [[erratic]], shared rivers will face growing pressure. Experts argue that flexible agreements, data sharing and joint institutions offer the best protection. Water can divide nations, but managed wisely it can also give them a powerful [[incentive]] to cooperate.

text: Water is the most [[indispensable]] of resources and, in much of the world, among the most contested. Roughly 310 river basins straddle international boundaries, sustaining around 40 per cent of humanity. On each of them, upstream decisions – to [[impound]] water behind a dam, divert it for agriculture or discharge effluent – are transmitted downstream. Hydrology thus creates structural asymmetries: the upstream state commands the tap, while the downstream state inherits the consequences.

Central Asia offers a sobering illustration. The Amu Darya and Syr Darya, fed by glaciers and snowmelt in the Pamir and Tian Shan ranges of Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, traverse the arid plains of Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan. From the 1960s, Soviet planners channelled their waters into an immense network of irrigation canals to turn desert into cotton fields. The Aral Sea, deprived of inflow, lost around nine-tenths of its volume, its retreat leaving a toxic, salt-crusted seabed whose dust storms have been linked to respiratory illness across the region. Independence turned an internal Soviet allocation problem into an international one. Upstream states seek to store water and release it through hydropower plants in winter, when their demand for electricity peaks; downstream states require it for irrigation in summer. Years of friction have been eased in part by improved regional diplomacy since the late 2010s, but the construction of Afghanistan's Qosh Tepa canal, intended to draw a substantial volume from the Amu Darya, has introduced a new and largely unregulated [[claimant]].

Comparable dynamics are visible on the Nile, where Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, under construction from 2011, promised electricity to a population in which tens of millions lacked access. Egypt, which depends on the Nile for the overwhelming majority of its freshwater, regarded the project as an [[existential]] threat, and protracted negotiations among Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan failed to yield a binding agreement on how quickly the reservoir would be filled and how it would be operated during droughts.

Such disputes have fuelled a popular narrative of impending “water wars”. The empirical record is more reassuring. A team led by the geographer Aaron Wolf at Oregon State University catalogued interactions over shared waters across the second half of the twentieth century and found that cooperative events outnumbered conflictive ones by about two to one, that violent conflict was rare and that no modern war had been fought primarily over water. States, it seems, generally find negotiation cheaper than confrontation, not least because water infrastructure is vulnerable and rivers cannot easily be [[annexed|annex]].

The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, mediated by the World Bank, has long been the emblematic example. By allocating the eastern rivers of the Indus system to India and the western rivers to Pakistan, it [[insulated|insulate]] water from a fraught relationship and survived several wars. Its recent troubles – culminating in India's announcement in 2025 that it was placing the treaty in [[abeyance]] – show, however, that legal arrangements are only as durable as the political consensus beneath them.

Climate change will intensify these pressures as glaciers retreat and precipitation becomes more erratic. The lesson of past cooperation is that adaptable treaties, transparent data sharing and permanent joint commissions can absorb shocks that rigid arrangements cannot. Shared rivers will remain a source of friction; whether they become a cause of conflict depends largely on the institutions built around them.

text: Of all the resources over which states might come to blows, water is the most [[elemental]] and, in an age of climatic disruption, among the most fraught. Some 310 river basins traverse international boundaries, sustaining roughly two-fifths of the world's population. On every one of them, upstream interventions – the impoundment of water behind dams, its diversion to irrigation, the discharge of effluent – are propagated downstream, so that hydrology inscribes a structural asymmetry into interstate relations: those at the source command the flow; those at the mouth inherit its residue.

Central Asia furnishes perhaps the starkest cautionary tale. The Amu Darya and Syr Darya, nourished by glaciers and snowmelt in the Pamir and Tian Shan, descend from Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan to cross the arid lowlands of Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan. Soviet planners, intent on cotton self-sufficiency, diverted their flow on a colossal scale from the 1960s onwards. The Aral Sea, once the planet's fourth-largest inland body of water, lost around ninety per cent of its volume; its exposed bed, laced with salt and agrochemical residues, now generates dust storms implicated in respiratory and other illnesses far beyond its shores. The dissolution of the Soviet Union converted what had been an intra-state allocation problem into an international one, pitting upstream states' desire to release water through hydropower plants in winter against downstream states' need for summer irrigation. A [[rapprochement]] in regional diplomacy since the late 2010s has eased some of these tensions, but Afghanistan's construction of the Qosh Tepa canal, designed to withdraw a substantial share of the Amu Darya's flow, has introduced a new claimant outside existing frameworks of coordination.

The Nile presents a parallel drama. Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, under construction from 2011, embodied the aspiration of a populous, power-starved nation to electrify itself. For Egypt, almost wholly dependent on the Nile for fresh water, the project raised the [[spectre]] of reduced flows during drought, and a decade of tripartite negotiations with Sudan failed to produce a binding accord on filling and operating rules.

These disputes lend surface plausibility to the much-repeated prophecy of “water wars”. The empirical record is considerably more reassuring. Aaron Wolf and colleagues at Oregon State University assembled a database of interactions over international waters spanning the latter half of the twentieth century and found that cooperative events outnumbered conflictive ones by roughly two to one, that acute violence was rare and that no modern war had been waged primarily over water. The explanation is partly strategic: water infrastructure is acutely vulnerable, rivers cannot readily be seized, and states sharing a basin are locked into perpetual interdependence – precisely the “shadow of the future” that game theorists identify as conducive to cooperation.

The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, brokered by the World Bank, long served as the paradigmatic demonstration that water could be [[quarantined|quarantine]] from wider hostility. Allocating the eastern rivers of the Indus system to India and the western rivers to Pakistan, it survived several wars. Its recent [[tribulations|tribulation]], culminating in India's declaration in 2025 that it would hold the treaty in abeyance, are a salutary reminder that legal architecture is no stronger than the political consensus underpinning it.

Climate change will test these arrangements as never before. Retreating glaciers may initially swell river flows before diminishing them, and precipitation is becoming more [[capricious]]. The lesson of past cooperation is that institutions designed for variability – adaptive allocation formulas, real-time data exchange, standing joint commissions with dispute-resolution mechanisms – fare better than rigid volumetric divisions predicated on a stable climate that no longer exists. Shared rivers will continue to generate friction. Whether that friction escalates into conflict is less a matter of hydrology than of institutional [[foresight]].

text: In almost every democracy, young adults are less likely to vote than older citizens. In the 2020 United States presidential election, around half of [[eligible]] voters aged 18 to 24 voted, compared with about three-quarters of those over 65. Similar gaps exist in Britain and much of Europe. This matters, because governments tend to listen most to the people who vote.

It is often said that young people simply don't care about politics, but research suggests this is not true. Young people are more likely than older people to sign petitions, join protests, boycott products and discuss political issues online. Many are [[passionate]] about climate change, housing costs and education. The problem is not a lack of interest but a [[gap]] between this interest and the ballot box.

Several practical [[obstacles|obstacle]] help explain the gap. In some countries, people must register before they can vote, and young people who move often – for university, work or cheaper rent – may not register at their new address. First-time voters may also feel unsure about how and where to vote. Some say they do not know enough about the candidates to choose.

There is also a cycle. Because young people vote less, politicians often focus their promises on older voters, for example by protecting pensions. Young people then feel that politics isn't for them, and they vote even less. Political scientists also point out that voting is partly a habit: people who vote in the first elections after they turn eighteen are much more likely to keep voting for the rest of their lives.

Several ideas aim to break the cycle. Some countries register citizens [[automatically]]. Austria lowered the voting age to 16 in 2007, and Scotland allowed 16-year-olds to vote in its 2014 independence referendum. Supporters argue that 16-year-olds, who usually still live at home and attend school, are more likely to form a voting habit. Better civic education in schools may also help. After all, a democracy works best when all [[generations|generation]] take part.

text: Across established democracies, a persistent pattern emerges at election time: the young vote least. In the 2020 US presidential election, roughly half of eligible citizens aged 18 to 24 cast a ballot, against around three-quarters of those aged 65 and over. Comparable age gaps appear in Britain, Canada and much of Europe. Since politicians, quite rationally, pay closest attention to those who turn out, this gap has real consequences for whose interests shape policy.

A popular explanation holds that young people are [[apathetic]]. The evidence does not support it. Surveys consistently find that younger citizens are at least as interested in political issues as their elders and are more likely to participate in “non-electoral” ways – signing petitions, joining demonstrations, boycotting brands or campaigning online. Movements on climate change, racial justice and housing have been driven largely by the young. The disengagement, in other words, is specific to voting rather than to politics as a whole.

Researchers point to a combination of practical and psychological [[barriers|barrier]]. Early adulthood is a period of frequent moves – to university, to new jobs, between rented flats – and in systems that require voters to register, each move can mean dropping off the electoral roll. First-time voters often lack the practical knowledge of how, where and when to vote, and many report feeling insufficiently informed to choose between parties whose policies seem distant from their own lives.

Political scientists also emphasise that voting is habit-forming. Studies of individual voting records suggest that people who vote in one election are significantly more likely to vote in the next, and that the elections immediately after a person becomes eligible are especially [[formative]]. Those who skip their first few elections may never develop the habit. This creates a vicious circle: low youth [[turnout]] encourages parties to [[prioritise]] older voters, which reinforces young people's sense that politics is not for them.

Several reforms aim to break the circle. Automatic voter registration, used in many countries, removes one of the most common obstacles. A number of democracies have lowered the voting age to 16: Austria did so for national elections in 2007, and Scotland and Wales have extended the vote to 16-year-olds in their own elections. Advocates argue that 16-year-olds, typically still living with their families and attending school, are better placed to cast a first vote – and thus to begin a habit – than 18-year-olds in the middle of moving away. Evidence from Austria suggests that the youngest voters there turned out at higher rates than those just a few years older.

Civic education and outreach matter too. Ultimately, though, the most effective [[remedy]] may be political: when parties address issues such as housing, education and climate with conviction, young people have more reason to believe their votes count.

text: Among the most [[consistent]] regularities of electoral politics is the age gradient in turnout. In the 2020 US presidential election, roughly half of eligible 18- to 24-year-olds voted, compared with around three-quarters of citizens aged 65 and over; similar gaps recur across Britain, Canada and much of continental Europe. Because parties rationally concentrate their appeals on those who reliably vote, the gradient is not merely a statistical curiosity. It shapes the distribution of political attention and, ultimately, of public spending.

The intuitive diagnosis – that the young are apathetic – fits the evidence poorly. Surveys repeatedly show that younger citizens express as much interest in political issues as their elders, and they are markedly more likely to engage through non-electoral channels: signing petitions, demonstrating, boycotting, organising online and joining issue-based movements on climate, housing and racial justice. What declines among the young is not political engagement but its conversion into votes – a pattern some scholars describe as a shift from “duty-based” to “engaged” citizenship, in which participation is seen as a matter of personal expression rather than civic obligation.

Practical frictions account for part of the shortfall. Early adulthood is a period of acute residential [[mobility]], and in systems that require individuals to register, each change of address risks removing a young person from the electoral roll. Inexperience compounds the problem: first-time voters frequently lack the procedural knowledge that older voters take for granted, and many report feeling that they know too little about the parties to make an informed choice – a sense of political [[inefficacy]] that discourages participation.

Perhaps the most consequential finding concerns habit. Analyses of validated voting records indicate that turning out in one election substantially raises the probability of turning out in the next, independently of interest or [[partisanship]]. The first elections after reaching voting age therefore exert a disproportionate influence on lifelong participation. This produces a self-reinforcing dynamic: low youth turnout leads parties to [[court]] older voters, whose priorities then dominate manifestos, deepening young people's [[alienation]] from electoral politics.

Reformers have targeted each link in this chain. Automatic or same-day registration removes a recurrent administrative barrier. Several jurisdictions have lowered the voting age to 16 – Austria nationally in 2007, Scotland and Wales for their devolved elections – on the reasoning that 16-year-olds, still embedded in families and schools, are better placed to cast a first vote and thus to establish the habit than 18-year-olds in the throes of leaving home. Evidence from Austria indicates that 16- and 17-year-olds turned out at higher rates than voters in their early twenties, though critics question whether the effect will persist as the novelty fades.

Civic education, school-based mock elections and targeted outreach can reinforce these institutional changes. Yet the deepest determinant of youth turnout may lie with the parties themselves. Where young voters see their concerns – affordable housing, educational debt, climate change – addressed with seriousness, they have reason to believe that voting is [[efficacious]]; where they do not, the cycle of mutual neglect is likely to continue.

text: If there is an iron law of electoral participation, it is that turnout rises with age. In the 2020 US presidential election, roughly half of eligible citizens aged 18 to 24 voted, as against some three-quarters of those aged 65 and above, and the gradient recurs, with local variations, across Britain, Canada and most of continental Europe. This is not an innocuous demographic quirk. Parties, behaving rationally, direct their appeals towards those who reliably turn out; the age gap in voting therefore becomes an age gap in political attention, and eventually in the allocation of public resources – a dynamic some commentators have dubbed “gerontocracy by [[default]]”.

The commonplace explanation – that the young are apathetic – fares poorly against the evidence. Survey data consistently show that younger citizens are no less interested in political questions than their elders, and markedly more inclined to participate through non-electoral repertoires: petitions, demonstrations, consumer boycotts, digital campaigning and issue-specific movements on climate, housing and racial justice. What diminishes among the young is not engagement but its translation into the ballot. Some political scientists interpret this as a generational shift from “duty-based” citizenship, in which voting is an obligation, to “engaged” citizenship, in which participation is valued chiefly as a form of self-expression – a shift that privileges direct action over the [[mediated]] and episodic act of voting.

Institutional frictions explain part of the shortfall. Early adulthood involves exceptional residential [[churn]], and wherever registration is the individual's responsibility, each move threatens to [[disenfranchise]] in practice someone entitled in principle. Inexperience compounds the difficulty: first-time voters often lack the procedural familiarity that older citizens take for granted and frequently report a sense of insufficient knowledge to choose between parties – what researchers term low internal efficacy.

The most consequential mechanism, however, appears to be habituation. Studies using validated turnout records find that voting in one election raises the likelihood of voting in the next, net of interest and partisanship, implying that participation is partly self-perpetuating. The elections immediately following enfranchisement are thus disproportionately formative: those who abstain then may acquire a durable habit of abstention. The resulting equilibrium is self-reinforcing. Low youth turnout invites parties to court older voters; their priorities dominate manifestos; and young citizens, seeing little of themselves in the offer, find their [[estrangement]] confirmed.

Reformers have targeted each link in this chain. Automatic and same-day registration remove a recurrent administrative hurdle. A growing number of jurisdictions have lowered the voting age to 16 – Austria for national elections in 2007; Scotland and Wales for their devolved elections; and the UK government has signalled its intention to follow suit for general elections. The rationale is less about maturity than about timing: 16-year-olds, still embedded in families and schools, are arguably better positioned to cast an inaugural vote, and so to initiate the habit, than 18-year-olds amid the [[upheaval]] of leaving home. Austrian evidence that 16- and 17-year-olds turned out at higher rates than voters in their early twenties lends this argument some support, though sceptics caution that novelty effects may decay.

Civic education, mock elections in schools and targeted mobilisation can [[buttress]] such reforms. Yet structural fixes cannot substitute for a substantive one. Where parties address the material concerns of the young – housing costs, educational debt, precarious employment, climate – with credibility, voting acquires a plausible connection to outcomes. Where they do not, the reciprocal neglect between young citizens and the parties that might represent them is liable to persist, and the iron law will continue to hold.

text: Tourism is one of the world's biggest industries. Before the pandemic, international tourist arrivals reached about 1.5 billion a year, and the number has now recovered. For many places, visitors bring jobs and income. But in some of the most famous destinations, residents feel that tourism has gone too far. They even have a word for it: “overtourism”.

Venice is the classic example. Its historic centre has fewer than 50,000 [[residents|resident]] – less than half the number of fifty years ago – but receives tens of thousands of visitors on busy days, many arriving by cruise ship or coming just for the day. Locals complain about crowded streets, high rents and shops that sell only souvenirs. In 2024, Venice became the first city in the world to charge day-trippers an entry [[fee]] on its busiest days.

Other cities are taking action too. In Barcelona, thousands of residents marched against mass tourism in 2024, and the city announced plans to stop licensing short-term holiday flats, which many people blame for [[pushing|push]] up rents. Amsterdam has limited new hotels and cruise ships and has run campaigns asking noisy groups of young tourists to stay away.

Overtourism also damages nature. Maya Bay in Thailand, made famous by a Hollywood film, was closed from 2018 to 2022 after boats and swimmers [[destroyed|destroy]] much of its coral. When it reopened, swimming was banned and visitor numbers were limited. In the Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan, tourists pay a daily fee to help protect the environment and culture.

Not everyone agrees with these measures. Some say fees punish ordinary travellers while the rich can still visit. Others point out that tourism workers [[depend]] on visitor numbers. However, most experts agree that the problem is not tourism itself but too many people in the same places at the same times. Travelling outside peak season, choosing less famous destinations and staying longer can help spread the [[benefits|benefit]] more fairly.

text: Tourism has become one of the largest industries on Earth. International arrivals approached 1.5 billion in 2019 and, after the collapse caused by the pandemic, have returned to similar levels. For many regions, visitors are an economic lifeline, supporting hotels, restaurants, transport and countless small businesses. Yet in a growing number of popular destinations, residents complain that the [[sheer]] volume of visitors is making their home towns unliveable. The term “overtourism”, barely used before the mid-2010s, has entered the vocabulary of urban politics.

Venice has become its emblem. The population of the historic centre has fallen below 50,000, less than half of what it was in the 1970s, while on peak days the city receives many times that number of visitors, a large share of them day-trippers who spend little but add to [[congestion]]. Residents complain of overcrowded alleys and water buses, rising rents and a landscape of shops selling masks and fridge magnets. After years of debate, Venice in 2024 became the first city to [[impose]] an entry fee on day visitors during busy periods, and it had earlier banned large cruise ships from its central lagoon.

The backlash has spread. In 2024, tens of thousands of people demonstrated in Barcelona, some spraying tourists with water pistols, under slogans demanding that visitors “go home”. The city responded by announcing that it would not renew licences for some 10,000 short-term rental flats, which critics blame for driving up housing costs. Amsterdam has capped overnight stays, restricted new hotels and cruise ship calls and launched campaigns discouraging stag parties. Dubrovnik, whose old town became famous as a filming location for a television fantasy series, has limited the number of cruise passengers allowed in at once.

Fragile natural sites face similar pressures. Thailand's Maya Bay, popularised by a Hollywood film, lost much of its coral to boat anchors, sunscreen and trampling, and was closed between 2018 and 2022 to allow the ecosystem to recover. Bhutan has long pursued a policy of “high value, low volume” tourism, charging most international visitors a daily sustainable development fee.

Such measures are [[contentious]]. Fees can make travel a privilege of the wealthy, while businesses dependent on visitors fear the loss of income. Some economists also question whether day-tripper charges are high enough to change behaviour. Nonetheless, there is a broad [[consensus]] that the core problem is one of distribution: too many people concentrated in a small number of places at the same times of year.

Travellers can play a part by visiting outside peak seasons, choosing lesser-known destinations, staying longer and spending money in locally owned businesses. Governments, for their part, increasingly recognise that managing tourism, rather than simply maximising it, is necessary to keep popular places [[viable]] for those who live there.

text: Few industries have grown as [[relentlessly]] as international tourism. Arrivals approached 1.5 billion in 2019, collapsed during the pandemic and have since rebounded to comparable levels, sustained by cheap flights, cruise ships, short-term rental platforms and the visual allure of social media. For many economies, tourism is an [[indispensable]] source of employment and foreign currency. Yet in a handful of celebrated destinations, the concentration of visitors has provoked a backlash so pronounced that a new term – “overtourism” – has moved from academic journals into everyday political debate.

Venice is the paradigm. The population of its historic centre has dwindled to under 50,000, less than half its level in the 1970s, as residents have been priced out by soaring rents and the conversion of homes into holiday lets. On peak days, visitor numbers dwarf the resident population, and day-trippers – who contribute relatively little to the local economy while adding substantially to congestion – make up a large proportion. In 2024, after years of [[deliberation]], the city introduced the world's first entry fee for day visitors on its busiest days, having already barred large cruise ships from the Giudecca Canal. Critics dismissed the fee as too small to alter behaviour and as a gesture that [[commodified|commodify]] the city further; supporters saw it as a first step towards managing demand.

Resentment has surfaced elsewhere. In 2024, mass demonstrations in Barcelona – where some protesters doused diners with water pistols – pressed for curbs on tourism, and the municipal government announced that licences for around 10,000 short-term rental apartments would not be renewed by 2028, citing their effect on housing. Amsterdam has capped annual overnight stays, halted new hotel construction in much of the city and reduced cruise ship calls, while Dubrovnik, whose fortunes were transformed by its role as a television filming location, restricts the number of cruise passengers permitted in its old town simultaneously.

The ecological dimension is no less acute. Thailand's Maya Bay, catapulted to fame by a Hollywood film, suffered such severe coral degradation from boat traffic, anchors and sunscreen that it was closed from 2018 to 2022; it reopened with a ban on swimming and strict daily [[quotas|quota]]. Bhutan, meanwhile, has long positioned itself as the antithesis of mass tourism, levying a substantial daily fee on most international visitors under its philosophy of “high value, low volume”.

Such interventions raise [[thorny]] questions. Charges risk making certain places accessible only to the affluent, and tourism-dependent workers fear that restrictions will cost them their livelihoods. There is also a risk of displacement: limiting visitors in one honeypot site may simply divert crowds to neighbouring places less equipped to cope. Most analysts nonetheless agree that the fundamental problem is not tourism per se but its extreme spatial and seasonal concentration.

The emerging consensus favours management over maximisation: dynamic pricing, timed entry, regulation of short-term rentals, and the promotion of off-season and lesser-known destinations. Travellers can contribute by staying longer, travelling outside peak periods and spending in locally owned businesses. The goal, as some planners put it, is to ensure that cities remain places to live in, not merely places to visit – lest they become, in the [[pejorative]] phrase of critics, theme parks of themselves.

text: International tourism has been one of the most [[inexorable]] growth stories of the past half-century. Arrivals neared 1.5 billion in 2019, all but vanished during the pandemic and have since recovered, propelled by low-cost aviation, ever-larger cruise ships, short-term rental platforms and the self-perpetuating imagery of social media, which channels millions towards the same photogenic vistas. For many economies tourism is a lifeline, generating employment and foreign exchange where alternatives are scarce. Yet in a small number of celebrated destinations, the concentration of visitors has generated a backlash sufficiently intense to [[spawn]] its own [[neologism]]: “overtourism”, a word scarcely in circulation before the mid-2010s.

Venice is its locus classicus. The historic centre's population has dwindled below 50,000, less than half its 1970s level, as rents have soared and housing stock has been converted into holiday lets. On peak days visitors vastly outnumber residents, a substantial share of them day-trippers who contribute disproportionately to congestion and comparatively little to the local economy. In 2024, after protracted deliberation, the city became the first in the world to levy an access charge on day visitors during peak periods, having already banned large cruise ships from the Giudecca Canal. The measure attracted criticism from both directions: from those who considered the fee too modest to alter behaviour, and from those who saw in it a further step in the conversion of a living city into a ticketed attraction.

Discontent has proliferated. In Barcelona, mass protests in 2024 – memorably including the dousing of terrace diners with water pistols – demanded limits on tourism, and the city council undertook not to renew licences for roughly 10,000 short-term rental apartments by 2028, citing their inflationary effect on housing. Amsterdam has capped annual overnight stays, halted new hotel construction across much of the city, reduced cruise ship calls and run campaigns explicitly discouraging certain kinds of visitor. Dubrovnik, whose fortunes were [[transfigured|transfigure]] by its role as a location for a television fantasy series, now limits the number of cruise passengers admitted to its walled old town at any one time.

The ecological costs can be still more acute. Thailand's Maya Bay, catapulted to celebrity by a Hollywood film, suffered such extensive coral degradation from anchors, boat traffic and sunscreen that it was closed between 2018 and 2022, reopening under a swimming ban and strict quotas. Bhutan has long [[cultivated|cultivate]] the opposite model, levying a substantial daily fee on most international visitors in pursuit of “high value, low volume” tourism – an approach admired by some and criticised by others as [[exclusionary]].

The policy dilemmas are genuine. Charges and caps risk transforming certain places into preserves of the affluent; workers whose livelihoods depend on visitor volumes reasonably fear for their incomes; and restrictions in one honeypot may simply displace crowds onto neighbouring communities less equipped to absorb them. There is also an uncomfortable irony in rich-world cities seeking to deter the very mass tourism that their own citizens practise abroad. Most analysts nonetheless converge on a diagnosis: the problem lies less in tourism per se than in its extreme spatial and temporal concentration – too many people, in too few places, at the same moments.

The prescriptions that follow are managerial rather than prohibitive: dynamic pricing and timed entry, regulation of short-term lets, redistribution of demand towards the off-season and lesser-known destinations, and fiscal arrangements that return a larger share of tourist spending to the communities that bear its costs. Travellers, for their part, can stay longer, travel off-peak and spend in locally owned businesses. The underlying aim is to preserve cities as places to inhabit rather than merely to consume – lest they become, in the [[mordant]] phrase of their critics, theme parks of themselves.

text: When you visit a new country, what do you remember most? For many travellers, the answer is the food. Food tells us a lot about a country – its history, its weather and its people.

In Uzbekistan, plov is much more than a meal. Families cook it for weddings and holidays, and men often cook it in a big pot called a kazan. In 2016, UNESCO added the Uzbek plov [[tradition]] to its list of world cultural heritage.

Every country has its own food [[manners|manner]]. In Japan, it is polite to make noise when you eat noodles – it shows you enjoy them. In Uzbekistan, people treat bread with great respect and never put it upside down on the table.

Many tourists eat only in hotel restaurants or at famous international chains. But if you want to [[understand]] a place, eat where local people eat. Visit a market, try street food or go to a small family café.
And don't be afraid to [[try]] something new. Ask local people what they recommend. A shared meal is one of the easiest ways to make new friends, even if you don't speak the same [[language]].

text: Ask travellers about their best memories, and many will describe a meal: grilled fish on a beach in Greece, steaming noodles at a night market in Taiwan, or fresh bread from a tandoor oven in Samarkand. Food is often the fastest way to understand a new culture, because what people eat – and how they eat it – reflects their history, geography and values.

Some food traditions are considered so important that UNESCO lists them as part of humanity's “intangible cultural heritage”. They include the French gastronomic meal, Japanese washoku, Korean kimchi-making, Neapolitan pizza-making and, since 2016, Uzbek plov. In Uzbekistan, plov is cooked for weddings, funerals and celebrations, often by men in a huge cauldron called a kazan, and sharing it is a sign of [[hospitality]] and [[community]].

Eating habits also teach visitors about local manners. In Japan, slurping noodles loudly is perfectly acceptable and even shows enjoyment. In many Central Asian homes, bread is treated with such respect that it is never thrown away or placed upside down. In some countries, guests are expected to finish everything on their plate; in others, leaving a little food shows that the host has been [[generous]].

Food can even be a tool of international politics. In 2002, Thailand's government launched a programme to increase the number of Thai restaurants around the world, hoping to [[promote]] tourism and Thai products. Experts call this kind of policy “gastrodiplomacy”.

Of course, many tourists never leave the safety of their hotel buffet or familiar international chains. Travel writers suggest a different [[approach]]: eat where the locals queue, visit markets, take a cooking class and ask questions. Not every dish will be to your taste, but each one is a small lesson in how other people live. And sitting down to eat together is one of the oldest ways humans have of turning strangers into [[friends|friend]].

text: Ask people to recall the highlights of a journey abroad and a surprising number will describe not monuments or museums but meals: a bowl of pho on a plastic stool in Hanoi, a plate of plov shared at a long table in Samarkand, a slice of pizza folded in half on a street in Naples. Food offers perhaps the most direct and [[sensory]] way into an unfamiliar culture, because cuisine encodes geography, history, religion and social relationships in a form that can be tasted.

The cultural weight of food is increasingly recognised. UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage includes not only rituals and crafts but culinary traditions: the French gastronomic meal (inscribed in 2010), Japanese washoku, the Korean practice of kimjang – communal kimchi-making before winter – the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo, Singapore's hawker culture and, since 2016, the culture and tradition of Uzbek plov. In Uzbekistan, plov is cooked for life's milestones, from weddings to funerals, typically by men in a cast-iron kazan, and serving it to guests is an act of hospitality that carries social [[obligations|obligation]] on both sides.

Meals are also a crash course in local [[etiquette]]. In Japan, slurping noodles is not merely tolerated but regarded as a sign of appreciation. In much of Central Asia, bread is treated as almost sacred: it is broken by hand rather than cut, never placed upside down and never thrown away. Attitudes to leftovers vary strikingly – in some cultures a clean plate compliments the cook, while in others it implies that the host has not provided enough.

Governments have noticed food's [[persuasive]] power. In 2002 Thailand launched its “Global Thai” programme, offering support to entrepreneurs to open Thai restaurants abroad in the hope of boosting tourism and agricultural exports. Scholars now speak of “gastrodiplomacy”: the use of cuisine to build a country's international image, a form of what political scientists call soft power.

Food tourism, however, raises questions of [[authenticity]]. Restaurants near famous sights often adapt dishes for foreign palates, and local residents may be priced out of the places they used to eat. Some critics also caution against treating other people's food as an exotic spectacle rather than as part of ordinary life.

For travellers who want more than a hotel buffet, the advice of food writers is consistent: eat where locals queue rather than where menus come in five languages, explore markets early in the morning, take a cooking class with a family, and approach unfamiliar dishes with curiosity rather than suspicion. A shared meal [[transcends]] language barriers in a way few other experiences can – which may be why the oldest form of hospitality remains one of the most effective forms of cultural exchange.

text: Ask seasoned travellers what they remember of a journey and, more often than not, they will describe a meal: pho eaten on a low plastic stool in Hanoi, plov ladled from a vast kazan at a Samarkand wedding, a folded slice of pizza on a Neapolitan street. Food is perhaps the most [[visceral]] point of entry into another culture, because a cuisine distils centuries of geography, trade, migration, religion and social hierarchy into something that can be smelled, tasted and shared.

The cultural significance of food has gained institutional recognition. UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity now includes a range of culinary practices: the gastronomic meal of the French (2010), washoku, the traditional dietary culture of the Japanese (2013), the Korean practice of kimjang, in which families and neighbours prepare winter kimchi together, the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo, Singapore's hawker culture and, since 2016, the culture and tradition of palov in Uzbekistan. Uzbek plov illustrates why such practices are classed as heritage rather than recipes. It marks the milestones of life, from circumcision feasts and weddings to funerals; it is traditionally prepared by men, sometimes for hundreds of guests, under the direction of a master cook; and its preparation and sharing [[reaffirm|reaffirm]] bonds of [[kinship]], neighbourhood and mutual obligation.

Dining practices also serve as an education in implicit norms. In Japan, slurping noodles signals appreciation; in much of Central Asia and the Middle East, bread is treated with a [[reverence]] bordering on the sacred – torn rather than cut, never set face down, never discarded. Conventions about leftovers diverge sharply: in some cultures, an empty plate honours the cook; in others, it suggests that the host has been [[parsimonious]]. Such details are trivial only to those who do not share them.

States have become alert to food's capacity to shape perceptions. Thailand's “Global Thai” initiative, launched in 2002, offered training and financial support to encourage the opening of Thai restaurants abroad, with the aim of promoting tourism and agricultural exports. Scholars of international relations have since coined the term “gastrodiplomacy” to describe the deployment of national cuisines as instruments of soft power – South Korea, Peru and Malaysia have pursued similar strategies.

Food tourism is not without tensions. Restaurants clustered around famous sights frequently adapt dishes to foreign palates, raising questions about authenticity, while the popularity of particular neighbourhoods can drive up prices and displace the residents whose everyday food culture attracted visitors in the first place. Critics also warn against an [[exoticising|exoticise]] gaze that treats other people's meals as spectacle rather than as part of ordinary life.

For travellers seeking more than a hotel buffet, food writers offer consistent advice: eat where the queues are local and the menus monolingual, visit markets early, accept invitations into homes, take a class with a family cook, and meet unfamiliar dishes with curiosity rather than [[squeamishness]]. A shared table can bridge gaps that language cannot, which is perhaps why the most ancient form of hospitality remains among the most potent forms of cultural exchange.

text: Interrogate any seasoned traveller about the residue a journey has left, and the answer is as likely to be a meal as a monument: pho on a squat plastic stool in Hanoi, plov ladled from a cauldron at a Samarkand wedding, a slice of pizza folded like a wallet on a Neapolitan pavement. The persistence of such memories is no accident. Cuisine is among the most [[palpable]] archives a culture possesses, compressing geography, trade routes, migrations, religious prescription and social hierarchy into something that can be smelled, tasted and – crucially – shared.

Institutional recognition has followed. UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity now encompasses a growing array of foodways: the gastronomic meal of the French, inscribed in 2010; washoku, the traditional dietary culture of Japan; kimjang, the collective preparation of winter kimchi in Korea; the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo; Singapore's hawker culture; and, since 2016, the culture and tradition of palov in Uzbekistan. The Uzbek case [[elucidates|elucidate]] why such practices are understood as heritage rather than recipes. Plov punctuates the life course – circumcision feasts, weddings, funerals – and is traditionally prepared by men, sometimes in quantities sufficient for hundreds of guests, under the supervision of a recognised master, or oshpaz. Its preparation and distribution enact and reaffirm networks of kinship, neighbourhood and reciprocal obligation; to be served plov is to be drawn, however briefly, into those networks.

The table is also a seminar in tacit norms. In Japan, audible slurping of noodles signals appreciation rather than [[boorishness]]. Across much of Central Asia and the Middle East, bread commands a reverence approaching the sacramental: it is torn rather than cut, never laid face down, never discarded. Conventions regarding leftovers diverge almost diametrically – in some societies an empty plate honours the cook, in others it implies the host's insufficiency. Such codes appear trivial only to those who have not been raised within them, and transgressing them is among the commonest ways in which visitors unwittingly give offence.

Governments have grasped the persuasive potential of the plate. Thailand's “Global Thai” initiative of 2002 sought to multiply Thai restaurants abroad through training and finance, aiming to stimulate tourism and agricultural exports. Scholars have since adopted the term “gastrodiplomacy” for the strategic deployment of national cuisines as instruments of soft power, and South Korea, Peru and Malaysia, among others, have pursued comparable campaigns. Food, on this view, is not merely a reflection of national identity but a medium through which that identity is curated and projected.

Culinary tourism nonetheless generates its own [[contradictions|contradiction]]. Establishments clustered around famous sights often recalibrate dishes for foreign palates, prompting perennial debates about authenticity – debates that can themselves be naive, since cuisines have always evolved through contact. The fashionability of particular districts can inflate rents and displace precisely the residents whose everyday food culture attracted visitors. And critics warn of an exoticising gaze that renders other people's [[sustenance]] as spectacle, aestheticising poverty or tradition for consumption by outsiders.

For the traveller who aspires to more than the hotel buffet, the counsel of food writers is remarkably consistent: seek out queues of locals and monolingual menus, visit markets at dawn, accept invitations into homes, apprentice oneself for an afternoon to a family cook, and greet the unfamiliar with curiosity rather than squeamishness. [[Commensality|commensality]] – the act of eating together – is among the oldest of human institutions, and it retains a capacity to [[dissolve]] distance that few other forms of exchange can match. The guest who sits at a stranger's table and eats what is offered has, in a sense, already learned the most important rule of all.

text: Imagine a city where you can walk or cycle to everything you need in fifteen minutes: your school or work, shops, a doctor, a park and a café. This is the idea of the “15-minute city”.

A French [[professor]], Carlos Moreno, made the idea popular. In 2020, the mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, used it in her election campaign. Since then, Paris has built many new bicycle lanes and planted more trees. Some streets near schools are now closed to cars.

Other cities have similar plans. Barcelona has “superblocks”: groups of streets where cars must drive slowly and children can play safely. Melbourne in Australia wants “20-minute neighbourhoods”.

But not everyone likes the idea. In big cities with long roads, it is difficult to have everything [[nearby]]. Some people are worried that they will not be able to use their cars. Planners say the aim is to give people more choice, not to [[stop]] them driving.

text: How long does it take you to buy bread, see a doctor or get to a park? In many modern cities, the answer is a long drive or a crowded bus ride. The “15-minute city” is an idea that aims to change this: everything people need for daily life should be within a fifteen-minute walk or bike ride from home.

The concept was developed by Carlos Moreno, a professor at the Sorbonne University in Paris. It became famous in 2020, when Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo made it a central part of her re-election campaign. Since then, Paris has added hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes, turned car parks into green spaces and closed many streets outside schools to traffic during school hours.

Supporters say the [[benefits|benefit]] are huge. Walking and cycling improve physical and mental health. Fewer car journeys mean less pollution and fewer accidents. Local shops get more customers, and people who meet their neighbours in the street often feel less lonely. Parents also [[appreciate]] being able to let their children walk to school safely.

The idea is not completely new. In the 1960s, the American writer Jane Jacobs argued that the best neighbourhoods mix homes, shops and workplaces, creating busy, [[lively]] streets. Many cities later did the opposite, separating housing from offices and shops and building wide roads for cars.

Other cities are now experimenting. Barcelona's “superblocks” group nine blocks together, limiting traffic inside so the streets can be used for play, trees and benches. Melbourne aims to create “20-minute neighbourhoods”. Critics, however, argue that the model works better in [[dense]], old European cities than in spread-out cities built around cars. Others worry that improving an area can make housing more expensive. text: For much of the twentieth century, urban planners designed cities around the car. Homes were separated from offices, shops were gathered in out-of-town malls, and wide roads carried commuters between them. The result, in many places, was congestion, pollution and long, stressful journeys. The “15-minute city” proposes the opposite: neighbourhoods where residents can reach most daily needs – work or school, food shops, healthcare, parks, culture – within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle.

The concept was formulated by Carlos Moreno, a professor at the Sorbonne, and propelled into global debate in 2020 when the mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, made la ville du quart d'heure the centrepiece of her successful re-election campaign. Paris has since added hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes, converted thousands of parking spaces into terraces and gardens, and created “school streets” closed to traffic at the start and end of the school day. The pandemic, which confined millions to their neighbourhoods, gave the idea an [[unexpected]] boost: many people suddenly discovered how much – or how little – was available close to home.

Advocates point to a wide range of benefits. Active travel improves cardiovascular and mental health; fewer car journeys reduce emissions, noise and road deaths; local businesses gain footfall; and streets [[populated|populate]] by pedestrians tend to feel safer and more sociable. The vision echoes the work of the urban writer Jane Jacobs, whose 1961 book The Death and Life of Great American Cities championed mixed-use neighbourhoods and lively streets against the car-centred planning of her time.

Other cities have developed their own versions. Barcelona's superilles, or superblocks, combine nine city blocks into units where through-traffic is diverted to the perimeter, freeing interior streets for play areas, trees and seating. Melbourne's long-term plan promotes “20-minute neighbourhoods”, and cities from Bogotá to Seoul have adopted related policies.

The idea has also attracted criticism. Some urbanists argue that it suits compact European cities better than [[sprawling]] metropolitan regions in North America or Australia, where jobs may be concentrated far from homes. Others warn of [[gentrification]]: as neighbourhoods become greener and more pleasant, rising property prices can push out lower-income residents. In 2023 the concept became the target of online conspiracy theories, which falsely claimed that 15-minute cities were a plot to confine people to their districts – a misreading of plans, such as traffic filters in Oxford, that restricted certain car routes rather than people's [[movement]].

Supporters respond that the goal is not to prevent anyone from travelling, but to make long journeys a choice rather than a necessity. In that sense, the 15-minute city is less a rigid blueprint than a [[yardstick]] for measuring how well a city serves the people who live in it.

text: For much of the twentieth century, the dominant [[paradigm]] in urban planning was functional separation. Zoning laws segregated housing from employment and commerce, out-of-town retail parks replaced high streets, and expanding road networks stitched the fragments together for the benefit of the motor car. The costs became apparent over time: congestion, air pollution, sedentary lifestyles, social isolation and commuting times that consumed hours of each week. The “15-minute city” is a deliberate [[repudiation]] of that model. Its premise is that most of life's essential functions – living, working, shopping, caring, learning and enjoying – should be accessible within a quarter of an hour's walk or cycle from home.

The concept was articulated by Carlos Moreno, a scientist and professor at the Sorbonne, and catapulted to international prominence in 2020, when Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo built her successful re-election campaign around la ville du quart d'heure. Paris has since undertaken a substantial reallocation of street space: hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes, the conversion of tens of thousands of on-street parking places into greenery and terraces, and the creation of rues aux écoles, streets outside schools [[pedestrianised|pedestrianise]] at the start and end of the day. The COVID-19 lockdowns, which abruptly shrank millions of lives to the scale of their neighbourhoods, lent the idea unexpected [[resonance]].

Proponents cite an impressive array of benefits. Walking and cycling yield well-documented gains in cardiovascular and mental health; reduced car dependence cuts emissions, noise and traffic casualties; local retailers benefit from increased footfall; and streets animated by pedestrians foster the informal social contact that the urbanist Jane Jacobs called the “ballet of the sidewalk”. Jacobs's 1961 polemic, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, attacked the car-centred modernism of her era and championed dense, mixed-use districts – an intellectual lineage the 15-minute city openly acknowledges.

Variants have proliferated. Barcelona's superilles group nine blocks into units from which through-traffic is excluded, reclaiming interior streets for play, planting and seating; evaluations have reported reductions in noise and nitrogen dioxide. Melbourne's metropolitan strategy promotes “20-minute neighbourhoods”, and related initiatives have been pursued in cities as diverse as Bogotá, Seoul and Ottawa.

The model has nonetheless drawn [[cogent]] criticism. Urban economists note that it maps more readily onto compact, historically dense European cities than onto sprawling metropolitan regions whose labour markets are concentrated in distant employment centres. Others warn that the amenities it promises can catalyse gentrification, raising rents and displacing the lower-income residents who stand to benefit most. More bizarrely, in 2023 the concept became entangled in online conspiracy theories portraying it as a scheme to confine citizens to their districts – a [[distortion]] of measures, such as traffic filters in Oxford, that restricted particular driving routes rather than personal movement.

Its defenders insist that the aim is not to curtail mobility but to make long journeys optional rather than obligatory. Understood in that light, the 15-minute city functions less as a rigid template than as a heuristic: a way of asking how [[equitably]] a city distributes the everyday necessities of life.

text: For the better part of the twentieth century, urban planning was governed by an ethos of functional segregation. Zoning codes partitioned the city into discrete domains for dwelling, work and commerce; retail decamped to peripheral malls; and an ever-expanding road network was charged with stitching the fragments together for the convenience of the private car. The [[externalities|externality]] accumulated quietly – congestion, particulate pollution, sedentary habits, attenuated community life and commutes that devoured hours of every week. The “15-minute city” is an explicit [[riposte]] to that legacy. Its organising premise is that the essential social functions – living, working, provisioning, caring, learning and leisure – should lie within a quarter of an hour's walk or cycle of every resident's front door.

The formulation belongs to Carlos Moreno, a scientist at the Sorbonne, but its global celebrity dates from 2020, when Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo made la ville du quart d'heure the centrepiece of a successful re-election bid. What followed was one of the more ambitious reallocations of street space in any major Western city: hundreds of kilometres of cycle infrastructure, the conversion of tens of thousands of [[kerbside]] parking spaces into planting and café terraces, and the designation of rues aux écoles, closed to vehicles at the bookends of the school day. The pandemic, which [[telescoped|telescope]] millions of lives into the radius of their neighbourhoods, conferred on the idea an unanticipated topicality.

Its advocates marshal a formidable inventory of benefits. Active travel confers well-attested cardiovascular and psychological gains; reduced car dependence diminishes emissions, noise and road casualties; local commerce profits from heightened footfall; and pavements thronged with pedestrians cultivate the casual, repeated encounters that Jane Jacobs memorably termed the “ballet of the sidewalk”. Jacobs's 1961 polemic against car-centred modernism, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, is the movement's acknowledged ancestor, and its insistence on density, mixed use and street life reads today less as nostalgia than as prophecy.

Variants have multiplied. Barcelona's superilles aggregate nine blocks into cells from which through-traffic is banished, reclaiming interior streets for play, greenery and seating, with evaluations reporting measurable falls in noise and nitrogen dioxide. Melbourne's metropolitan plan enshrines “20-minute neighbourhoods”, and kindred schemes have taken root from Bogotá to Seoul.

The model is not beyond reproach. Urban economists observe that it maps more naturally onto compact, historically dense European cores than onto [[polycentric]] or sprawling metropolises in which employment is concentrated far from residential suburbs; for many workers, the nearest suitable job will never be fifteen minutes away. Others caution that the very amenities it furnishes can catalyse gentrification, capitalising into higher rents and [[displacing|displace]] those residents with most to gain. In 2023, more strangely, the concept was swept into online conspiracy theories casting it as a covert scheme to confine citizens to their districts – a grotesque misreading of measures, such as Oxford's traffic filters, that constrained certain driving routes rather than anyone's freedom of movement. The episode was a reminder that urban planning, however technocratic its vocabulary, is never insulated from the politics of identity and distrust.

Its defenders maintain that the objective is not to curtail mobility but to render long journeys elective rather than compulsory. Understood thus, the 15-minute city is less a template to be imposed than a diagnostic: a way of interrogating how equitably a city distributes the ordinary necessities of life, and of revealing, neighbourhood by neighbourhood, where that distribution [[falters|falter]].

text: Many people are always busy. They work long hours, check emails in the evening and fill their weekends with activities. When they have a free minute, they look at their phones. But is it good to be busy all the time?

In the Netherlands, there is a word for doing nothing: “niksen”. It means sitting quietly, looking out of the window or [[lying|lie]] in the grass, without any goal. In Italy, people talk about “dolce far niente” – the sweetness of doing nothing.

Scientists say that rest is good for our brains. When we do nothing, the brain does not stop. It [[connects|connect]] ideas and memories. That is why we often have good ideas in the shower or on a walk.
But doing nothing is not easy. In one experiment, people sat alone in a room with no phone for fifteen minutes. Many of them found it very [[uncomfortable]].

Some countries now protect free time by law. In France, many workers have the right not to answer work emails in the evening. So try it: put your phone away, sit down and do nothing for ten minutes. It may be the most [[useful]] thing you do all day. Your body and mind need a [[break]].

text: Many of us feel [[guilty]] when we are not busy. Our calendars are full, our phones are always with us, and even our free time is filled with exercise classes, online courses and social plans. Being busy has become a kind of [[status symbol]]. But a growing number of psychologists argue that doing nothing at all – really nothing – is an important skill we are losing.

The Dutch have a word for it: “niksen”, which means doing something without any purpose, such as staring out of a window or listening to music without checking your phone. Italians speak of “dolce far niente”, the sweetness of doing nothing. These are not lazy habits, supporters say, but a way to [[recover]] from stress.

Neuroscience supports the idea. In the early 2000s, scientists discovered that when people stop focusing on a task, a group of brain regions called the “default mode network” becomes more active. This network seems to help us process memories, imagine the future and make connections between ideas. Many people find that solutions to problems appear when they are relaxing, a phenomenon psychologists call “[[incubation]]”.

Yet doing nothing can be surprisingly difficult. In a 2014 study at the University of Virginia, participants were asked to sit alone with their thoughts for six to fifteen minutes. They could also give themselves a mild electric shock if they wanted. Amazingly, many chose the shock rather than sit quietly – about two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women.

Overwork has real costs. In 2019, the World Health Organization recognised burnout as an occupational [[phenomenon]] caused by chronic stress at work. Some countries now protect rest by law: since 2017, many French employees have had a “right to disconnect”, meaning they don't have to answer work messages outside working hours, and several other countries have introduced similar rules. Experts suggest small [[steps|step]] too: short breaks without screens, walks without headphones and evenings without email. Doing nothing, it turns out, is not a waste of time – it may be one of the best uses of it.

text: In many workplaces and social circles, busyness has become a [[badge of honour]]. Asked how they are, people answer “crazy busy” with a hint of pride; calendars are packed, phones never leave our hands, and leisure itself is optimised – a run tracked by an app, a podcast at double speed, a holiday filled with activities. Against this background, a modest counter-trend has emerged: the [[deliberate]] practice of doing nothing.

The Dutch call it niksen – an activity, or rather non-activity, without purpose, such as gazing out of a window, sitting in a café without a phone or simply letting the mind wander. Italians have long celebrated dolce far niente, “the sweetness of doing nothing”. Advocates stress that this is not laziness but a necessary [[counterweight]] to constant stimulation and productivity.

Neuroscience lends the idea some support. In 2001 the neurologist Marcus Raichle and colleagues described what became known as the “default mode network”, a set of brain regions that is more active when people are not focused on an external task. The network is involved in remembering the past, imagining the future and thinking about ourselves and others. Psychologists have also documented the “incubation effect”: stepping away from a problem can make a solution more likely to [[surface]], which may explain why insights so often arrive in the shower or on a walk.

Yet idleness does not come easily. In a 2014 series of experiments led by Timothy Wilson at the University of Virginia, participants left alone in a bare room with nothing to do but think for six to fifteen minutes found the experience unpleasant. In one version, they could press a button to give themselves a mild electric shock – which most had earlier said they would pay to avoid. Two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than sit with their thoughts.

The costs of never switching off are increasingly recognised. In 2019 the World Health Organization included burnout in its International Classification of Diseases as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Several governments have [[legislated|legislate]] to protect rest. France introduced a “right to disconnect” in 2017, requiring larger companies to agree rules limiting out-of-hours emails; Portugal and Australia have since passed related laws.

None of this means abandoning work or ambition. The argument is rather that rest is not the opposite of productivity but one of its preconditions. Experts recommend building small pockets of [[idleness]] into the day – a walk without headphones, a train journey spent looking out of the window, an evening with the phone in another room. In a culture that rewards constant activity, choosing to do nothing may require more discipline than doing something.

text: In much of contemporary working life, busyness has acquired the status of a virtue. Asked how they are, professionals report being “slammed” or “crazy busy” with barely concealed pride; calendars are colonised weeks in advance, and leisure itself is subjected to the logic of productivity – runs measured by apps, podcasts consumed at double speed, holidays itemised like project plans. Some sociologists argue that, in societies that once displayed status through leisure, conspicuous busyness now [[signals]] that a person is in demand. Against this backdrop, a quiet counter-movement has emerged that treats doing nothing not as a failing but as a skill worth cultivating.

The Dutch term niksen, which attracted international attention in the late 2010s, denotes purposeless activity – gazing from a window, sitting in a park without a phone, allowing the mind to drift. It has a southern European cousin in the Italian dolce far niente, the “sweetness of doing nothing”. Proponents are careful to distinguish such idleness from [[procrastination]], in which one avoids a task while remaining preoccupied with it, and from passive screen consumption, which keeps the mind continually stimulated.

Neuroscience offers a plausible rationale. In 2001 Marcus Raichle and colleagues described a constellation of brain regions – later termed the default mode network – that becomes more active when people disengage from externally focused tasks. Far from idling, this network appears to support autobiographical memory, the simulation of future scenarios and reflection on the minds of others. Research on the “incubation effect” suggests that setting a problem aside can facilitate its solution, perhaps because unconscious processing continues once deliberate effort ceases – a finding consistent with countless anecdotes of insights arriving in the shower or on a walk.

Doing nothing, however, proves strikingly [[aversive]] to many people. In a widely publicised set of studies led by Timothy Wilson, participants asked to spend between six and fifteen minutes alone with their thoughts, without phones or reading material, generally reported finding it difficult and unpleasant. In one experiment, participants could administer a mild electric shock to themselves; despite having previously stated that they would pay money to avoid it, 67 per cent of men and 25 per cent of women did so at least once. The authors concluded that the [[untutored]] mind does not like to be alone with itself.

The consequences of perpetual activity are increasingly acknowledged by institutions. In 2019 the World Health Organization incorporated burnout into the eleventh revision of its International Classification of Diseases, defining it as an occupational phenomenon arising from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Legislators have begun to [[intervene]]: France's 2017 “right to disconnect” obliges larger employers to negotiate limits on out-of-hours communication, and Portugal and Australia have since enacted comparable provisions, though enforcement and coverage vary.

None of this amounts to a rejection of work. The case for idleness is, paradoxically, partly instrumental: periods of rest [[replenish]] attention, consolidate memory and foster creativity, making them a precondition of sustained productivity rather than its antithesis. Yet advocates also make a more [[radical]] claim – that time without purpose has value in itself, and that a life in which every moment must justify its existence is impoverished, however efficient it may be.
