text: Busyness has become one of the more curious status markers of late modernity. Asked how they are, professionals profess themselves “slammed” or “crazy busy” in tones that hover between complaint and boast; calendars are colonised weeks in advance; and leisure itself has been annexed by the logic of optimisation – runs logged by apps, audiobooks consumed at accelerated speed, holidays itemised with the rigour of a project plan. Sociologists have noted an inversion of an older pattern: where the elites of Thorstein Veblen's era displayed status through conspicuous leisure, today's professionals often signal their worth through conspicuous [[overwork]], advertising that they are in demand. It is against this background that a small counter-current has gathered momentum, one that treats the capacity to do nothing as a skill to be recovered rather than a vice to be overcome.

Its emblem is the Dutch word niksen, which enjoyed a brief international vogue in the late 2010s and denotes activity stripped of purpose: gazing through a window, sitting in a square without a phone, permitting the mind to drift where it will. The Italian dolce far niente, the “sweetness of doing nothing”, expresses a [[cognate]] ideal. Proponents take pains to distinguish such idleness from its counterfeits – from procrastination, in which a deferred task continues to occupy the mind, and from the passive consumption of screens, which merely substitutes one stream of stimulation for another.

Neuroscience supplies a suggestive, if incomplete, rationale. In 2001 Marcus Raichle and colleagues identified a constellation of regions – subsequently christened the default mode network – whose activity rises when attention is withdrawn from external tasks. Far from representing neural idling, this network appears integral to autobiographical memory, prospective simulation and the modelling of other minds. Studies of the incubation effect indicate that disengaging from a problem can facilitate its resolution, perhaps because associative processing persists below the threshold of awareness – a mechanism that would account for the [[proverbial]] [[epiphany]] in the shower.

And yet the unstructured mind is, for many, an uncomfortable place. In experiments led by Timothy Wilson and published in 2014, participants instructed to entertain themselves with their own thoughts for six to fifteen minutes, deprived of phones and reading matter, generally found the task difficult and disagreeable. Given the option of administering a mild electric shock to themselves – one they had earlier said they would pay to avoid – 67 per cent of men and 25 per cent of women did so at least once. The authors' dry conclusion was that “the untutored mind does not like to be alone with itself”. Solitude without stimulus, it seems, must be learned.

Institutions have begun to register the costs of perpetual activity. In 2019 the World Health Organization included burnout in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, characterising it as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Legislatures have also intervened, if [[tentatively]]. France's 2017 “right to disconnect” requires larger employers to negotiate limits on out-of-hours communication; Portugal and Australia have since enacted related provisions. Critics observe that such laws are weakly enforced and largely irrelevant to the self-employed and gig workers for whom the boundary between labour and leisure is most [[porous]].

The case for idleness is often made in instrumental terms: rest replenishes attention, consolidates memory and nourishes creativity, and is thus a precondition of sustained productivity rather than its antithesis. That argument has the merit of persuading managers. But it [[concedes]] the very premise the counter-movement seeks to question – that time is valuable only insofar as it is useful. The more radical claim is that unproductive time possesses intrinsic worth, and that a life in which every hour must justify itself is, however efficient, impoverished. Doing nothing, on this view, is not a means to an end. It is one of the ends.
